After I watched the entire season, I realized I was thoroughly entertained and without a single scene of gratuitous violence or sex, something that much of today's programming relies on vs. back in the 80's or earlier. I found it refreshing and yes it's something a family can actually watch together (although very young children might be frightened by the monster). The only reason I did not rate this show a 10 is I thought Ryder's character was a bit too much at times. The constant hysterics wore me out for the first half of the season but it did get better in the second half. I understand she was a panicked mother so I can't put a finger on it. author: ashley_walton
title: Bloomin' brilliant!
content: OK, I know I'm late to the party but glad I made it! I'm a predominantly fan of films rather than tv series (which is a reason why I hadn't watched it yet), but having run out of films to watch (mainly due to few releases because of the pandemic) I finally watched it. And I'm glad I did!My problem with tv series vs movies is how do you keep everything seem fresh and enjoyable for more than 1 hour 30 minutes? I love how film manages to get a story into a small timeframe whilst introducing key characters and their backstories. Too many times I find that tv series elongate screen time by adding backstories and other "information" that does little for entertainment but explains about the characters. Apart from some instances of this for the psionic Elle, it was hardly evident anywhere. Instead, the writing allows all the characters to live their own lives and interact with each other with their own unique personalities whilst dealing with all the things that go on around them.I watched series 1 and loved it so much that I didn't want to start the second incase it didn't live up to that standard. Although the second dipped in parts, in my opinion (the episode where Elle finds out about her past wasn't my favourite), it still hit so many levels, such as heartfelt emotion, laughs and drama. The writing, effects, acting, score (I love eighties music!) and direction are exemplary.Will the third series be as good? I hope so. I can't wait to find out.

title: The best Netflix show to date
content: I've seen all the episodes of Daredevil, House of Cards, Master of None, Narcos, and several other of Netflix's brilliant shows. This is definitely the best one to date. All of the actors--including the young kid actors and the adult actors--are brilliant and give outstanding performances. Literally each one of them could be nominated for an Emmy. The fact that they're all unknown actors (save for Winona Ryder) adds to the mysteriousness of the show, and their chemistry and dialogue is spot-on. There's nothing predictable about Stranger Things--each episode had something happen that I never would've predicted. Most shows have moments where you can pretty much guess what's going to happen at certain parts, but NEVER in this show. Once I started the first episode, I ended up binge- watching the rest of the season in one weekend, which is the shortest period of time it ever took me to watch a single show. Really looking forward to season 2!

author: harcool
title: Stranger Things 4: Volume One and Two Review (And Show in General)
content: GENERAL THOUGHTS ON THE SHOW: This show is just amazing in every way possible. The way it combines the 80's and Horror without being cheesy is just groundbreaking on its own.. but it has likeable characters, such as Eleven, Steve, Mike, Dustin, Robin, etc. And also delves into trauma and The Upside Down is a very creative way to show us a backwards Dimension of our own. It's fun, sad, heartbreaking, tragic, happy, joyful, scary, horrific and everything else.VOLUME ONE OF S4: The Darkest, Goriest Season to date became my personal favourite season. It explores every single one of our characters and what they are going through after the events of Season Three. The Scenes with Hopper in the Russian Prison are heart-shattering and there is one conversation he has with a character in the Season that will melt your heart. And we explore the past and trauma of Eleven in flashback scenes that are so brutal, and Vecna.. the villain.... oh my gosh! Easily the best villain we've gotten in Stranger Things so far. He is intense, malicious, evil and at the same time... human. You feel his emotions and the twist that happens with the character in the Season is shocking, though it makes sense. We see all of our characters split up, and though a lot of people didn't like that... I really enjoyed it. Cutting back to every one of the storylines through the movie-length episodes was always great! The deaths are gruesome, the characters are great... this Season was a total win for Netflix and fans of ST. Can't wait for the final two episodes in July!VOLUME TWO OF S4: This is perfection from Start to Finish. Thrilling, gory, exciting, and emotional. I will not drop any Spoilers here.. but there is a scene with a character that dies that breaks you from the Inside Out. All the storylines mash together and it's just an amazing time! This is the best TV has been for a long time. That's all I can manage to say right now... holy moley.

author: Jxfiles
title: Brilliance Betrayed
content: This show didn't stumble out of the gate. It sprinted. Season one was lightning in a bottle: disciplined storytelling, genuine suspense, emotionally grounded characters, and a mystery that earned its reveals. It trusted pacing. It trusted restraint. It trusted the audience. The supernatural worked because it was anchored to something human-friendship, fear, loyalty, loss.For a while, the show understood its assignment.But somewhere around the middle seasons, things began to slip-not all at once, but subtly. The mystery became less coherent. The tone wobbled. Plot threads multiplied without payoff. What had once been tight and intentional started to feel bloated and self-indulgent. The show began confusing scale with depth.Flash forward to the fifth and final season-and what do we have now?We have a story that no longer knows what it's about. The mystery that once drove the narrative gives way to a series of non-sequitur plot beats that feel stacked rather than structured. Lore piles on top of lore. Stakes escalate, but logic evaporates. The rules of the world bend whenever the script needs them to. It starts to resemble the final season of Lost: lots of ominous monologues, lots of emotional noise, and very little narrative clarity.And layered on top of that confusion is a noticeable shift in priorities.Roughly 20% of the characters are now gay, and this isn't incidental background detail-it's a major plot point. Coming out arcs are foregrounded, emphasized, and narratively privileged in a way that actively competes with the core story. Instead of character serving plot, the plot bends to accommodate declarations. Representation stops being texture and becomes obligation.What do we have now?We have male characters who are largely written as bumbling, fearful, indecisive, and ineffectual-constantly doubting, constantly panicking, rarely leading. And opposite them, we have women portrayed as uniformly headstrong, fearless, decisive, and morally certain. They're the drivers. The solvers. The heroes-often without meaningful flaws or consequences.This isn't empowerment. It's inversion without depth. And inversion without depth quickly becomes parody.The great irony is that Stranger Things once understood balance. Early seasons allowed characters to be strong because they were flawed. Courage meant something because fear existed. Victory mattered because failure was possible. By the end, the characters feel less like people and more like symbols moving through a foggy, incoherent narrative.Are there good moments in the final season? Yes. There are flashes of what once was-solid performances, effective horror imagery, the occasional emotional beat that lands. But those moments feel orphaned. Isolated. Like echoes from a better version of the show struggling to be heard over the noise.In the end, Stranger Things doesn't collapse from lack of talent or budget. It collapses from misplaced priorities. Storytelling takes a backseat to messaging. Mystery is replaced with monologue. Meaning is announced instead of discovered.What began as one of the best genre shows of its era ends as a self-conscious parody of itself-loud, bloated, and convinced of its own importance.That's not how legends end.That's how brilliance gets betrayed.

author: Snow12456
title: A Phenomenal Story Held Back by Inconsistency
content: Stranger Things is a show I can respect more than I can fully love. What ultimately pulled me in was never the acting across the board, but the vision of the Duffer Brothers. When the writing is firing on all cylinders, it's some of the most captivating storytelling Netflix has ever produced. The world-building, the pacing (at its best), and the way the mystery unfolds are genuinely impressive. The overarching story is phenomenal, and watching the characters grow over multiple seasons is rewarding; especially considering how easily this could've become disposable "Netflix content" and faded into obscurity within weeks. Instead, they created something lasting and culturally significant.That said, the show has always had uneven performances, and for me, Millie Bobby Brown has been a consistent weak point. I've never connected with her acting, even from the beginning, and time hasn't changed that. Her performances often feel flat or forced, and her other roles outside Stranger Things haven't done much to change my opinion. While she has a very distinctive look and screen presence, that alone doesn't translate into strong acting for me. Recent off-screen controversies only made it easier for me to disengage entirely. It's frustrating seeing widespread praise finally turn into criticism now, when these issues felt present from the start.On the opposite end of the spectrum, Caleb McLaughlin and Sadie Sink are genuinely surprising in the best way. Their performances consistently carry emotional weight, and you can feel that they understand the script rather than simply reciting it. Even without always being positioned as the central focus of the show, they command the screen when it matters most. They bring authenticity, restraint, and real emotional depth. Qualities that elevate the material around them. I sincerely hope both of them have long careers ahead, because their talent feels earned, not manufactured.This contrast highlights a bigger issue in modern casting: too often, actors move from project to project based on influence or visibility rather than actual ability. Nobody wants to keep watching weak performances coast on popularity. Acting like McLaughlin's and Sink's is what earns lifelong respect and praise from audiences; and they've absolutely earned it from me.The quality of Stranger Things also fluctuates heavily from season to season. Some arcs are tightly written and emotionally resonant, while others feel bloated or dragged out. Still, even at its weakest, the show benefits from strong concepts, memorable moments, and a clear creative identity.Overall, Stranger Things is absolutely a show worth watching at least once in your life. Not because it's perfect, and not because the actors are now twice there characters age, but because when it works, it really works. Its strengths lie firmly in its writing, atmosphere, and long-form storytelling, even if some performances and later choices prevent it from ever being truly great for everyone.

author: aimansuliman
title: A Show That Lost Its Way After Season 2
content: I loved Stranger Things from the start. Season 1 was a masterclass in suspense, with the mystery at its core hooking me immediately. The atmosphere, pacing, and storytelling were tight and compelling - it's easy to see why it became such a phenomenon.Season 2 had a lot to live up to, and while it expanded the story and raised the stakes, it sometimes felt like a faster, repeated version of the first season's premise. Certain story choices kept key characters apart for too long, and some new plot threads went nowhere, but overall it was a solid follow-up and felt like a natural conclusion.Unfortunately, things took a downturn from season 3 onwards. The writing seemed to lose focus, with some storylines feeling unnecessary and tonal shifts that undercut the tension. Attempts at humour sometimes clashed with serious moments, and some explanations for ongoing threats felt vague.Season 4 tried to raise the stakes again but ended up scattering the characters across too many locations, making it harder to maintain the same emotional impact. While there were still good moments, the writing often felt stretched, and the show lost much of the mystery and atmosphere that made it special in the first place.In short, Stranger Things shines brightest in its first two seasons but struggles with its later instalments. Still worth watching for its nostalgia and characters, but the drop in focus and tone left me disappointed.

author: amirmustafa
title: A surprising breath of fresh air for Netflix - nostalgia blended with original premises.
content: STRANGER THINGS was a pleasant surprise. It sprawled comfortably on Netflix's browsing page very recently. Needless to say, I binged all eight (8) episodes in one sitting.STRANGER THINGS, as mentioned in several other reviews, is the "fruit smoothie" of 80s culture. Take in a tablespoon of Stephen King, a few dashes of Spielberg, and a whole lot of 80s horror/thriller culture, blend it together and you essentially have STRANGER THINGS.To start off, the fact that this is NOT a reboot or sequel to a film or television show that debuted in the 80s time period is actually relieving. Not that I necessarily have anything against that, but this series really goes to show that an original concept can still be filled with nostalgia but have its own identity. Hopefully, that will encourage future film/series creators.Regarding the show itself, I found myself on several occasions praising the acting (ESPECIALLY by the children), and engrossed with the plot. I can most definitely appreciate the choice of having this as a television show as opposed to a short movie. It really gave a chance to flesh things out. The plot, while relatively simple, is filled with several cliché tropes - however, they are utilized much differently, which is another thing I happened to enjoy. The "walking backwards and accidentally tripping over something" action DOES NOT lead to a death. The car engine actually STARTED. The girl actually doesn't give too much of a damn (romantically) about the nerdy/weird/outcast guy EVEN AFTER EXPERIENCING A LIFE-CHANGING SITUATION together. Again: a breath of fresh air.My only real gripe with the show had to be the ending. However, this is all hypothetical and essentially not solid. The plot really showcases itself as a one season deal - however, the show creators already confirmed that season two would be a sequel to season 1. I felt that season one's ending should have been more conclusive as opposed to purposely leaving many loose ends to pick up in season two. HOWEVER, if season two does pick up these loose ends and thread them into something even more awesome, then it's a win-win situation and I will be happy with season one's ending. Also, to nitpick, the underlying themes of "mystery" and "folklore" seem to be muddled and messy. Individually, the themes are very strong from an episode-to- episode basis; sadly, as a whole, the show really loses these themes and you're left with a pure thriller-adventure as opposed to the cool dark sci-fi feeling.+awesome characters+superb acting+engrossing plot-possibly weak ending-muddled directionSTRANGER THINGS - binge-worthy - 9/10

author: TheRealPetraeus
title: The Whole Series, 1 Review
content:
*NO SPOILERS*
Since I don't think I can write a review on each season, I will make a review for each season in this one review, starting with Season 1, of course. (Also expect a lot of typos because I'm tired and this review is over 1000 words long)(TLDR for each rating of each season at the end of the review)Season 1: An unexpected hitThe start of the show. The set up for what's to come, and it's the second best season of the show. The atmosphere is creepy and unsettling, but it's not all too grim as actually funny humor is able to prevent the show from becoming too bleak. The plot is simple and easy to follow, but it doesn't feel like it's trying to be overly simple. Simple plots aren't always a bad thing, and this is a great example. The mystery builds up throughout the show making you wonder what the truth is, and it keeps you second guessing yourself. The acting is superb, and that's a common trend throughout the show. Almost all of the characters are likeable and don't feel one dimensional. The buildup is slow and it works. It doesn't feel drawn out, and nothing feels like it's meant to be filler. Everything feels like it has a purpose in the grand scheme of things. The tension is really good even though majority of the protagonists are children and you doubt anything bad is going to happen to them. The cgi is a bit rough when the Demogorgon is shown in full feel, but aside from some other problems this season is amazing. An easy 9/10.Season 2: More of the sameSo much hype. And for some it lived up to that hype, but for others this season failed to meet expectations and was disappointing. I can't fully say if it lived up to the hype for me because when Season 2 started, I started Season 1. But even though this Season has flaws, which we'll talk about, it's still fun and enjoyable, and adds to the foundation of Season 1. This Season had 2 big standout flaws. First, it felt like too much like a rehash of the first season, and 2nd, the "The Lost Sister" episode. Starting with the first big flaw, I think it's a fair criticism. Once again Will is the target of the villain, but instead of the villain being the Demogorgon we get a brand new big bad, The Mind Flayer. An interesting villain, and something we see turn into a very big character throughout the show, but let's not get side tracked. Nothing really in this Season felt different from the first aside from a couple of new characters. Those characters are, Max, and Billy. Both are great characters and play big roles in the show. But the reason this Season still isn't hated or viewed extremely negatively is because the first Season had such a winning formula that fans weren't unhappy with more of the same, and I understand that. But no amount of good formula can save the episode titled, "The Lost Sister." What a terrible episode. It added very little to the story, was boring, had uninteresting characters, and felt unnecessary. We could have gone without this entire episode and the show would be the same. But this Season overall was still pretty fun, and enjoyable. Overall, it's a 7.5/10.Season 3: Oh boy where do I start?Ugh... This season. It could have been really good. That might be one of the worst parts about this season. The visuals, colors, and vibe was great, but nearly everything else was not. The story makes no sense. I'm just going to get that out of the way now. Massive plot holes. It's the 80s and no one in a small town in Indiana notices the massive Russian base underneath the very popular mall. How? Who knows? The design of this base is terrible too. Why does it look like it was ripped out of a canceled Spy Kids movie? The plot wasn't very interesting either. The whole "Flayed" plot was boring and uninteresting. The way the "Flayed" act is so dumb and unoriginal. They're basically zombies! The Hopper and Joyce storyline wasn't very good, and Alexi is an overrated and a lazy character. Giving a character one trait that makes them "funny" doesn't count as a character. And the humor is also pretty bad. Little jokes are funny, and the jokes happen too much. It also has a Terminator knockoff for no reason, and the entire story is extremely predictable. The massive tonal shifts don't help this already mediocre season. Whos idea was it to have a "funny" comic relief scene cut to a torture scene? It's so out of nowhere. This season isn't all bad, and it introduces one of my favorite characters, Robin, but the cons outweigh the pros, by a lot. The final episode isn't too bad though.Sadly, this Season is a 5.5/10.Season 4: Back on track baby!This Season is great! It has the best moments of the show, best episodes, best villain, best story, best mystery, best action, and best cgi. Also the best soundtrack. This season starts off slow, and has the longest episodes of the series, each being at least an 75 minutes long. The tension is high in this Season, and so is the fun. Max gets a great character arc, and Vecna, the new big bad, is the best villain of the show. His origin and story is so interesting, and his way of killing his victims is... Chilling to say the least. I feel like I could talk about this Season forever so I'll keep each topic short-ish, but this Season tops Season 1. It brings back the perfectly timed humor and exciting mystery but cranks those up to 11 (no pun intended.) The episodes don't feel overstuffed either, instead they take their time, and build things up slowly. Even though all of our main characters are split up around the world, each group's story feels fleshed out and well balanced with the others. The best story is the Hawkins story, but each has their own pros and cons. This Season also introduces an amazing new character, Eddie. This dude rocks! What a great character. So likeable, but he isn't just in the show for comic relief. This season is also the most intense of the series, and has the best writing in my opinion. Season 4 was split up into 2 parts/volumes and it really only built hype. We didn't have to wait long for Volume 2, and the ending of Volume 1 was great. The acting from the old cast, and the new, is the best of the series, and overall amazing. The visual effects hit an all new high and the high budget was worth it. This Season tops the first, and is the best of the show. 9.8/10Overall this show is amazing, and even if not all the Season are top tier, its still a classic, and I can't wait for Season 5.TLDR:
Season 1: 9.0/10
Season 2: 7.5/10
Season 3: 5.5/10
Season 4: 9.8/10.

author: Marpi
title: Nostalgia driven nightmare
content: New 80s is trending right now. However, this series offered a sense of nostalgia rarely felt in other movies and series such as this one.Character exploration is beautifully done, and most characters have idiosyncratic traits which makes them quite interesting. Each character's history also ties into the main story line perfectly, leaving few loose ends. The acting is on point with some strong performances and directing is brilliant in regards to the mood being created and the intricate details of the 80s era. Together they've certainly been able to create a wonderful and terrifying world with an original and fascinating story-line.This series features kids, teens and adults and I really feel as if they are there to offer that enhanced sense of nostalgia. I certainly doubt it was to appeal to younger kids which this series is obviously not directed towards. Most of us have lived through such experiences and ordeals, so it offers that sense of ubiquitous normalcy, but which is set against the backdrop of complete chaos which shatters that false sense of security, the perfect way to create a reality-disrupting nightmare.One of the few drawbacks was its predictability. I didn't even have to try to guess what would happen next, I just did. I might have enjoyed a few sleight of hand misdirection plot twists but this still really falls in line with classic 80s movies, so even that was welcomed here.and the soundtrack is just an absolute bonus.Which is why I gave this a 10/10, they couldn't have done it any better. I am certainly bias, being a huge fan of everything 80s, sci-fi, horror and new retro wave, but this is an absolutely memorable series that will stay with me for a very long time.

author: LuisValencia
title: Truly Outstanding
content: I wholeheartedly believe this is one of the best TV shows in recent years - maybe even of the decade. Season 1 felt more like a long, drawn out, excellent movie than an ordinary series, and this can be attributed to many reasons.Visually, "Stranger Things" is stunning. The production value and cinematography are the best, unlike any other I'd ever seen in a TV show. Normally the contrast of visuals between a show and a movie is clearly apparent - usually because of budget and staff - but such is not the case here; one could play an episode marked as part of a movie and no one would be the wiser. There's also of course, the 80s homage feel that is conspicuously displayed in most of the scenes. To many, it serves as an item of nostalgia or a reminiscence of similar classic 80s movies.But even though 'the 80s feeling' seems to be the focus of many people when watching the show, I sense that they forget to look at the other aspects that makes "Stranger Things" great. One of those aspects is the characters. All of them play some part or role in the movie, and they all have profound personalities. As the story progresses each of the sets of characters make their own developments to solving the conflict, and the way they were able to eventually intertwine their efforts was a satisfying inclusion. Even the child actors were able to pull off very convincing and pretty strong characters.This is a show that can easily have you finding yourself suspend disbelief and feel the story come to life, despite the very otherworldly premise. It's funny how greatly it makes you long for a misadventure with your friends as kids. Overall, the way the sequence of events build up, the way the plot unravels to the impending climax, the way the mysteries keep you glued to the screen, the way the magical soundtrack takes you back in time and the way the experience finally comes to a powerful conclusion and wraps up in a fashion that very few TV shows can imitate, makes "Stranger Things" an evoking installment that perhaps only good movies are.

author: sachin_rautela
title: An Absolute Gem 💎
content:
Stranger Things is one of those rare web series that gets almost everything right - storytelling, characters, music, emotions, and nostalgia.What makes this series stand out is that there is no single hero or heroine. Every character feels important, every storyline matters, and everyone gets their moment to shine. It's truly an ensemble-driven show where every character feels like a main character.One of the most satisfying aspects of the series is how, at a certain stage, everything connects back to the initial event. Watching all the threads come together makes the storytelling feel rewarding and well thought out.Steve Harrington's character arc deserves special mention. From an initially unlikeable high-school bully to one of the most loved, brave, and selfless characters in the show - his transformation feels organic and earned. Easily one of the best redemption arcs in modern television.The Russia storyline, especially when Hopper ends up there, adds a fresh and intense layer to the series. It expands the world beyond Hawkins, raises the stakes, and gives Hopper's character more emotional depth.Among all the characters, Dustin and Hopper stand out the most. Their personalities, emotional range, and screen presence make them not only the best-written characters but also personal favourites.Flaws:
The Kali (008) storyline was poorly executed and ultimately wasted a character with strong potential.Also, Mr. Wheeler felt largely useless throughout the series, contributing very little to the overall plot.Final Verdict:
Despite a few flaws, Stranger Things remains an absolute gem. Its interconnected storytelling, memorable characters, and emotional depth make it a must-watch and one of the best series of its time.

author: virindra
title: A nostalgic, thrilling, and emotional ride through the Upside Down.
content: I truly enjoyed watching Stranger Things, all the way through Season 4 and I'm very much looking forward to Season 5. What makes this show so special to me is not just the story, but the time period: 1983-1986. I was a boy during those years, and watching the series brings back memories in the most vivid way, much like It (2017) did, also starring Finn Wolfhard. The music, the clothes, the bikes, the cars... it all feels authentic. It's a beautiful tribute to a time that shaped many of us.There's something Harry Potter-like in how we get to see these kids grow up together, facing danger, discovering themselves, and dealing with both trauma and friendship. The core cast is fantastic: Eleven, Mike, Dustin, Lucas, Will, Max, Nancy, Jonathan, Steve, along with Joyce and Hopper. Their chemistry and development bring the show to life. Even the nearly 2.5-hour Season 4 finale flew by.The decision to split up the group was bold. At first, I thought it might have been a budget decision; less screen time, fewer costs, but it turned out to be a smart storytelling choice. Watching each character fight Vecna from different fronts, while also being attacked emotionally and physically (Papa, Chrissy's obsessed boyfriend) added real depth.Still, I was sad to see great characters leave the show like Billy (Dacre Montgomery), Bob (Sean Astin), and especially Eddie (Joseph Quinn). Eddie became a fan favorite for a reason.If I had to mention one weak link in the casting, it would be Maya Hawke as Robin. It reminds me a bit of Harry Potter's casting of Evanna Lynch as Luna; a misfit character that just didn't land. Maya comes across as trying, but lacking the same depth or presence as her co-stars. Despite having incredibly talented parents, I simply don't find her performance convincing.But all in all, Stranger Things has it all: horror, suspense, action, emotion, romance, humor. It's a thrill to watch. Even my 16-year-old daughter enjoys watching it with me and sharing that experience across generations is a blessing I don't take for granted.Stranger Things isn't perfect, but it has heart. It's eerie, exciting, and deeply nostalgic.

author: phaylen
title: A True Homage to 80's Sci-Fi
content: Stranger Things are what television and movies used to be about. Imagination, fun, mystery, suspense, a dash of comedy. Before youth was force fed Marvel Comic adaptation after adaptation after reboot after remake after sequel, there was seriously good, quality material to sink your chops into.Thank goodness for Netflix because without them, "Stranger Things" would never have gotten made. I'm so glad it did. This was a tour de Force of filmmaking, with stellar performances by Winona Ryder, Millie Bobby Brown and a wonderfully eccentric cast of beloved misfits you embrace from the first episode. You will hear a lot of people compare it to classic 80's films The Goonies, but it's less like those films and more like what would have been created by the Masterful 80's filmmakers that created the flicks that became iconic.This series demonstrates with unapologetic glory what entertainment could be if we allowed more original content into our sphere, rather than the regurgitations and comic saturation that obliterated the blockbuster and dumbed it down to the IQ of a gnat. This is why we remember the 80's films so fondly. They were better.Star Wars was a film that changed the industry, much thanks to the young pioneer George Lucas. Following him through that gate of genius was Steven Spielberg, Robert Zemekis, Ron Howard and so many artists with stories to tell. The Duffer Brothers are a hugely welcome, long overdue addition to that club, and so is their series, "Stranger things."Packed with nods to yesteryear cinema, it never has to rely on sex, drugs and exploding cars to pull you in, but instead grips you with a brilliant storyline and powerful performances. It lets you have fun again, without beating you over the head with the common "Look how much money we spent" plague.I hope for a second series. There is no question, this is full of tomorrows biggest stars, especially Millie Bobby Brown whose turn here is mind blowing. Emmy should hand them their awards now.

title: Season 4 Review - Best Season Yet!
content: After watching the final two episodes of "Stranger Things: Season 4", I appreciate the decision to make them into longer episodes - I understood the importance of wrapping up two essential story arcs: that of Papa and El and then Vecna and...everyone else. Well...so to speak. When all is said and done, I can't help but think of Plato's Allegory of the Cave.Metaphorically, Chapter 8 is about self-discovery, enlightenment, and creating healthy boundaries. Chapter 9 is about venturing into the darkness, facing your fears, and standing up for yourself.We do arrive at a conclusion of sorts that readies us for season 5. Loaded with resonating emotion and nuanced human connection, the ending is rockin' rolling fun, thrilling and frightening, and sometimes too bombastic and overstuffed with fighting conflicts for its own good.All the characters have an opportunity to shine through a combination of earnest and vulnerable conversations and near-impossible feats that once again puts them in extreme and hopeless peril. The stakes are higher than ever. And I loved it. I loved the sacrifices, the deceit, the teamwork, the reunions, and the action.I will say that while I do love Kate Bush's "Running Up That Hill", I felt it was overused, which took away from its brilliant use in Chapter 4. The ending of the series may have benefited from the reintroduction of another cool, theme-appropriate hit.

author: jas-cenn-chargers
title: From School Bully to Selfless Hero: The Magic of Hawkins
content: Stranger Things is a fantasy horror drama set in the fictional town of Hawkins, Indiana, during the 1980s. The series follows a group of friends and their families as they uncover government conspiracies and battle supernatural threats. The conflict begins when the Hawkins National Laboratory accidentally opens a portal to a dark parallel dimension known as the Upside Down while conducting secret experiments on Eleven, a young girl with psychokinetic powers. This breach allows monstrous entities to enter the real world, starting with the mysterious abduction of a young boy named Will Byers-an event that forces the town's residents to confront the horrors of the paranormal to save their own.One of the greatest strengths of Stranger Things is its authentic 1980s atmosphere, as the Duffer Brothers successfully captured the "Amblin" feel found in classic films like The Goonies or E. T. This vibe is reinforced by a synth-heavy soundtrack, period-accurate fashion, and a lack of modern technology that naturally raises the stakes; because the characters cannot simply text for help, they must rely on walkie-talkies and bicycles to navigate danger. Furthermore, the series stands out among other horror shows by providing genuine stakes rather than relying on "plot armor," making the threats from the Upside Down feel truly dangerous. This evolution from the "monster of the week" style of the first season to the complex psychological horror of Vecna in Season 4 demonstrates the impressive maturity of the show's storytelling.My favorite character is Steve Harrington because of his incredible growth throughout the series. While he is introduced in the first season as a stereotypical "popular jerk" or "80s movie bully," Stranger Things subverted those expectations. Instead of being killed off or remaining a villain, he evolved into a selfless protector who frequently puts himself in physical danger to save the younger kids.I would highly recommend Stranger Things to several types of viewers because of its unique blend of genres. First, it is a "must-watch" for nostalgia seekers, specifically Gen X and Millennials, as it perfectly captures the 1980s aesthetic through its music and nods to adventure films like Poltergeist. Second, it appeals to fans of "found family" stories, focusing on a group of outcasts who overcome individual traumas to form an unbreakable bond. Finally, the series is a perfect fit for horror and sci-fi enthusiasts; it offers "gateway horror" that is genuinely creepy while providing the sci-fi crowd with intriguing government conspiracies and the mystery of the Upside Down.Overall Rating: 10/10 - A masterclass in heart, horror, and 80s magic.

author: TheVictoriousV
title: I still hold the show in high regard but man, what a shame about that final season
content: Many people have made the same point about the final season of Stranger Things and, by extension, the way in which serialized media is produced/released in the streaming era: It's wild how long the franchise has been with us, yet how little there actually is of it. With 5 seasons and only 40-something episodes over the course of 9 years, it stands in stark contrast to such TV shows of old as The X-Files, which had a shorter run yet contained more episodes. The COVID-19 delays and the 2023 strikes explain some of it, but it's still pretty dang remarkable.Now why am I, of all people, bringing this up? Am I not usually the first person to complain when things get released hurriedly on a strict schedule at the expense of quality (especially when something that once took its time and planned things out carefully, e.g. The MCU, starts pumping out dozens of titles a year, with plain results in production values and world-building clarity) and acceptable work conditions? Isn't it good that these people get to take their time and release things only when they're done? I suppose so, but it does raise a question of whether, of all things, that lovely little Amblin Entertainment/Stephen King call-back from 2016 (that also took the 2010s "'80s nostalgia" craze to new heights), warrants this kind of grandiosity.Does it need this many characters? Episodes as long as movies? MCU-type apocalyptic (yet deathless) action scenes? The word "overproduced" decorated reviews of the prior season, and I can kind of see why. (Having slept on the Season 5 announcement, I was even dead-certain that 4 was going to be the end, and that may well have been the plan at one point; everything in the season finale, sans the cliffhanger, had an air of finality.)And let's not forget the frequently-clowned-on consequence of the long production time, namely that the kid characters -- who aren't recast at any point -- are now played by actors in their mid-20s. (In fairness, what could be more "80s" than that?) The characters age too, yes, but there are certainly some drastic changes, and the age of the characters in this final season (it takes place after a time skip) can only explain so much.Be that as it may, I was periodically moved and mostly enjoyed the cast -- which now also includes a delightfully unhinged fat kid (who is also absolutely right that Vecna has "too many names") and Linda Hamilton for that extra 80s-ness. A few years ago, I proposed that the only way this show could go "even more 80s" would be to include 1950s nostalgia. (Recall the motifs in Back to the Future, Top Secret!, and one of Stranger Things' inspirations, Twin Peaks, which started production in the late 80s.) In the new season, this basically comes true (and also made me think of the vastly superior Netflix sci-fi series Dark). Still, the 80s nostalgia thing has gotten old. If the "nostalgiacore" TikTok feed is anything to go by, people are all about Y2K music videos and Windows XP now.Because of this -- as well as the insane plot armor levels, increasingly demystified supernatural elements, boring planning scenes, awkward comedy, generally awkward staging, expensive-looking yet often murky effects, and way too much of Noah Schnapp attempting big acting moments -- Stranger Things leaves us on a pretty lame note that rushes and drags in the wrong spots. I'm sure it will continue to be fondly remembered, and that it may go down in history as the last true unifying TV event; I'm less sure about people remembering specifics of the final season, save for Millie Bobby Brown's memeable lip filler. One more positive comment: the sidelining of Winona Ryder, whose big "comeback" was supposed to be this show back in 2016, was sort of made up for in the finale.I almost wish it had ended sooner so that I'd be even sadder about seeing it go; I want to miss it more than I do. Then again, can we trust that Netflix is done milking the town of Hawkins?

author: paulodlourenco
title: Stranger Stranger Things... - Season 5
content: The first thing that hits you like a brick in this season is seeing these young adults still playing the roles of children. It's genuinely distracting, impossible to ignore, and compromises the entire experience. But that's what we have, that's just how things are and there's nothing we can do about it!Following a trend that has become common practice in contemporary Hollywood writing, the series suffers from somewhat lazy and inconsistent storytelling. The rules of the fictional world often shift depending on what each scene requires, frequently contradicting earlier events and undermining internal logic.In this season, the one-dimensional portrayal of the "evil military" villains is a perfect example of the writing's laziness, while the demogorgons - effortlessly defeating a heavily armed military force one moment and then being scared off or defeated by cartoonish traps set by kids or mothers wielding broken bottles and axes the next - illustrate the inconsistency and convenient shifting of rules depending on whether the scene involves the protagonists or mere background characters. Such dramatic fluctuations completely undermine the sense of danger and stakes.Characterization has also suffered. Eleven now exhibits an extremely annoying girl-boss attitude, and her powers - as one might expect - are inconsistent, sometimes overwhelmingly powerful, and at other times merely capable of minor tricks that do little more than buy time.The series is riddled with clichés, and the dynamics between characters have lost some of their original emotional engagement. Some even feel a little superfluous, like Robin Buckley, Erica Sinclair, and even Murray Bauman, who seem exaggerated and overly stylized - occasionally amusing, but lacking depth and failing to contribute meaningfully to the narrative. On top of that, there are simply too many groups doing too many different things at once. Some plotlines are confusing, messy, and often unnecessary.Equally disappointing is the shift away from the original premise: a scientific experiment that accidentally opens a portal to a dark parallel dimension. Instead, everything is now pinned on Vecna as the mastermind behind all events, stripping away the mystery and tension that made the early seasons so compelling. The increasingly blatant use of these "memberberries" is also tiresome. Originally more of an organic reflection of the setting and period, they have now become a cheap, overused trick - not just in Stranger Things, but across modern Hollywood. Rather than taking risks with new ideas, studios increasingly rely on these quick dopamine hits to keep audiences engaged, feeding off their dependence on nostalgia and instant gratification...From what we've been given to see so far in Season 5, the series takes a step down from Season 4, which had briefly revived the show after the weaker Seasons 2 and 3 (although I actually kind of enjoyed Season 3, even if it almost felt more like a spin-off).This decline serves as the ultimate proof that much of the hype surrounding this series stems less from its inherent quality and more from the desperate hope of audiences that it would be genuinely as good as its first season seemed to promise. This is particularly true for those of us who were children in the 1980s, growing up on E. T., The Goonies, Gremlins, Explorers, and all the other stuff that clearly inspired Stranger Things. In its first season, this series, which is nothing more than a patchwork and a pastiche of all these influences - and we fans were willing to accept that - seemed to know exactly how to use them to fill the nostalgia gap effectively. But in reality it proved to be fundamentally fragile, with only Seasons 1 and 4 standing out as genuinely strong and cohesive entries, and yet rather inconsistent with each other.That said, there are moments - rare, unfortunately - that are genuinely good, beautiful, and inspiring, hinting at the potential this series could achieve, especially given the production quality and budget involved. These flashes make the show's wasted potential even more frustrating.

author: xpics
title: Amazing characters, intriguing world, multi-genre entertainer!
content: Every season of 'Stranger Things' seems like an elaborate suspense-thriller franchise film. It has its start-middle-end and a definite season closure, though leaving a subtle seed for the next season. The show very interestingly creates a sci fi world (particularly in Season 1) and then explores different elements of suspense, thriller, fantasy, action, drama, comedy, romance, bromance and also horror (in some portions) very smartly and keeps you riveted all through. Thankfully it never muddles or messes up with its multiple genres.Each season follows a format where multiple tracks run in parallel from the very start until they merge together in the pre-climax and thereafter the group divides into smaller units to get set on one common mission in the finale. The format works perfectly for the show as it keeps its ensemble characters employed in different subplots and keeps you engaged with the variety. However, the editing pattern is so brisk that just when you expect to delve more into one particular track, the narrative erratically cuts into another plot and then another and then another. This happens largely in Season 2 and 3 and, at times, the pattern irritates. Another pattern is a match-cut transition from one scene to another which happens so often that it seems overdone. The pacing of the show is fast, not giving you any breathers to sit back and relax or analyse. Thankfully the makers have kept the flavour in true-blue suspense-thriller zone without making it a slow burn or dark drama.Beyond the premise and promise of an imaginative world, Stranger Things largely works because of its varied colourful characters. Whether it is El, Hopper, Joyce, Nancy or the four friends - each one is unique and has an interesting part to play. Also each character is written so robustly that you cannot pick any one of them as the central protagonist or rate anyone as the supporting cast. This is one of the few shows (or perhaps the only show) where almost every character has equal weightage, not just in screentime but also in their contribution to the story and also how you keep rooting for each of them. Even characters who seem to be just the supporting cast in the start come to fore more prominently over seasons. The best example is of Steve Carrington who comes across as the typical evil campus guy in season 1 but turns more likeable eventually. So is Erica, Max or Billy!The intrigue that was created in Season 1 dilutes down in Season 2 and 3 as you get more and more accustomed to the world. Season 3, in particular, stretches at times with an action track of a Russian mercenary chasing Hopper, resulting in some long-drawn-out action sequences in a fun-fair setup - something that seems forced and not in sync with the primary genre of the show. Then there is one break episode (Season 2, episode 7) that is just unconnected with the overall plot of the series and you aren't surprised when you see it is the lowest rated episode on IMDb. You could give this one a complete miss and still nothing would change in your viewing experience or story flow of the show.The show is subtly set in the early 80s era and the period reference is never in your face. The narrative is so gripping that you never consciously notice the absence of cellphones or other modern gadgets. Every episode ends on a definitive hook point which wants you to keep going ahead. Despite having adult overtones of creature horror and verbal abuse, the show still palpably captures the innocence of childhood friendship in a very organic way.

author: SickBoyGoreHound
title: Sequel done right
content: As expected, true to his '80s nostalgia nature, the second season of "Stranger Things" takes the sequel path - and it does so in the best possible way: it's definitely in the alley of "Empire Strikes Back" or "Aliens" rather than the trite "more of the same" approach.The story builds on the previous installment as we find the characters where we left them at the end of the last season. The attention to details, the '80s feeling, the references - that were the trademark of season 1 - are all still there while the character driven narrative moves forward.The idea of splitting the main characters is a risk that pays off, giving each character room to breath and to grow on their own. The newbies also work, although a couple of them aren't as focused as they could've been.The story is cohesive and well told, a little darker in places and a little more action-y at times (but not to the point of becoming pointless or annoying) - and it manages to be perfectly self-contained, while still planting enough seeds for future seasons to grow around.The usual amount of references and homages (with several new ones throw in the mix) prevent it from be really innovative or deeply creative, but that's not a bad thing, here, and the material is very well executed.Great cast all around, strong performances - although, someone must've told young Finn Wolfhard that he was one of the best actor from the previous season as he tries to overdo himself, here, sometimes going a bit overboard (and, at times, it feels like he's using his character to audition for a young Kylo Ren in the Star Wars franchise). Nothing major, though, and it doesn't subtract from the enjoyment.All in all, the numerous 10 stars it's getting are definitely over- rating, but it's a solid, well rounded 8/10 experience.

author: Dan_W_Reviews
title: Riveting and Suspenseful, An Excellent Standard of Writing, Acting & Production Value Throughout (S1-4)
content: Stranger Things is set in the 1980s in the fictional town of Hawkins, Indiana and follows a group of friends as they uncover supernatural mysteries and government conspiracies.Throughout all four seasons so far, I believe Stranger Things has maintained an extremely high level of quality in its writing, acting, and production value. The show's very memorable and likable characters, along with its riveting storyline and highly suspenseful moments, grabbed my attention and kept me invested and immersed in the show. The show's nostalgic elements, like its soundtrack and references to pop culture from the 80s, were also a highlight for me and one of my favourite aspects of the show.The first season sets a great foundation for the series, introducing the main characters and setting the stage for the strange events that occur in Hawkins. Each subsequent season expertly builds upon the previous one and no episode feels wasted, each expanding the show's intriguing mythology and exploring new themes and characters. The show's attention to detail and its commitment to its 1980s setting have helped to create a unique and immersive world that is both comfily familiar and creepily strange.In conclusion then, Stranger Things's combination of compelling storylines, impactful characters, and excellent attention to detail make it a standout Netflix series that is definitely worth watching from start to finish.

author: glyn-25860
title: Lazy Sci-Fi Series
content:
Can't understand the following that this has. This show has not got an original idea in it's head. It's like watching The Force Awakens 3 times in a row!
The set up of character and story is exactly the same with every season, with annoying characters and stupid sub-plots thrown in for good measure.Season 1 IS NOT brilliant television which some people will tell you it is. This is not The Wire or The Sopranos. This show isn't in the same Galaxy as those classic TV Shows.The first season copies everything from The X-Files to Stephen King to nostalgia Spielberg films from the 80's. It also plays on the 'there's a government conspiracy cover up'. Because we haven't seen that before have we.Season 2 has the same set up about a place called the upside down where a monster comes from so the kids get together (like they did in S1)
They have to fight a monster (like they did in S1)
Eleven has to defeat the monster (like she did in S1)
Season 2 is actually worse because this has a 7th episode that has absolutely nothing to do with the episode prior or after it and can be ignorned completely. They only put this in because Milly Bobbie Brown wasn't getting enought screen time and clearly her agent was upset about this!! If you have seen any of her press conferences with her co-stars she clearly has to be the centre of attention and everything has to be about her!!Season 3 starts with yet another monster coming over from another dimension and yep you guessed it the gang get back together and Eleven saves the day yet again. At no point during this overlong and tired series do you fell that any of these kids are going to be in danger.
Season 3 is by far the worse however as they fell the need to force left wing politics into it's storytelling just like the trash Disney films are doing.
There is also a ridiculous subplot between Winona Ryder and David Harbour that fells that is should be in another show. It's just them arguing that fells like an episode out of Eastenders.Non of these characters have progressed over three seasons. Eleven is as powerful in Season 3 as she was in Season 1. The character arcs are terrible that have no development. They are there to serve a creature feature.
The effects are ok but you've seen all this before. The kids are average but nothing special even though they are clearly written as The Goonies.Season 4 threatens to do the exact same predictable and boring set up with no emotional pay-off. At this stage I am completely uninvested in any of these characters because S4 will follow the same predicable and safe formula.Hugely overrated!!

title: Sometimes Shows Just Outstay Their Welcome
content: As many other reviewers here have already noted, Things have gotten worse with each successive season. What started as something fresh yet familiar, has just become a re-tread each season revisiting the ageing actors and following their character arcs -- except the characters just don't seem all that engaging anymore either.Season 3 introduced the daughter of Uma Thurman and Ethan Hawke as a gay character, because.....it was somehow essential to the story that she be gay. Probably the same reason gratuitous nudity and sex scenes were somehow essential throughout 'Game of Thrones'.Season 4 seems determined to recreate some 'Carrie' vibes further cementing the homage to Stephen King. However, the least appealing storyline is the Russian gulag and watching Winona Ryder relentlessly overact. To be fair, Winona has been overacting since season one, but the better story helped distract from it back then.Winona is not the only distracting actor in this show. Some of the kids seem to have become anorexic the older they have gotten. It is truly disturbing watching young people who look like they have actually spent time in a gulag, especially since they weren't involved in that story line.Look, if you are just wanting to dip your toes back into the Stranger Things world every year or two, then each new season will not disappoint you. However, if you really enjoyed the first season and want to cherish your good memories of that...then this show has truly worn out its welcome.

author: gfargas-97361
title: Don't judge it as being a "silly kid show". It won't disappoint.
content:
For years I looked at this show and thought to myself "this is some stupid kid show there's no way it lives up to its hype". I'm here to say that I was gladly mistaken by a long shot. The storyline is meticulous in building this world similar to the style of Stephen King. It is set in the 80's surrounding a group of adventurous kids who love science and playing D&D. It's quite ironic that they always seem to find themselves in unspeakable scenarios that seem quite similar to the game they love so much. It all starts when one of their buddies goes missing and they come across a new friend, a young girl with powers who doesn't speak much but seems to be connected to the disappearance of their friend. The kids play their roles wonderfully, even alongside the veteran actress Winona Ryder. There's also the older teen group who find themselves entwined in the same creepy situations as the younger kids. They often find themselves working together as the adults probably wouldn't believe the monstrosities they have witnessed. Jim Hopper is the macho man sheriff who is the protector of the town with a troubled past which has shaped him into the man he is. The spookiness of the show is often followed up with some comic relief which will have you filled with suspense while laughing at the same time. Especially that of one of the kids, Dustin who has a condition with his teeth that gives him a lisp that only makes him funnier. Murray also provides much of the shows comedy, he's a conspiracy theorist who to regular folks seems like a straight up nutcase obsessed with crazy Soviet Union theories. However, to those in Hawkins aware of the things happening around them his theories will be more than helpful.Season 4: 10/10
Season 3: 9.5/10
Season 1: 9.2/10
Season 2: 9/10.

title: It deserves higher ratings.

Tying D&D into this whole series was really neat and a nice journey back to the 80s-- malls, and actually talking on a land line telephone.They went a bit overboard on the whole surfer stoner guy. Was it forced to have a trans counselor from their school!? I wish they played more popular 80s music in all 4 seasons-- being that music was very much a part of the what really made the 80s. The background synth music in the score more than made up for it, but still 80s really was about how the music shaped the 80s.A visit with Suzie was a nice surprise and home life there was even more of a didn't see it coming surprise.S04 started out a bit anticlimactic and a bit Smallville-ish, since we waited 3 years. Character development started flat and didn't have the charm or wonder as it did in S01. Almost like they didn't know how to develop them. The build up to see what was going on took a bit longer, or rather nothing was really happening to get to that point.They pulled it off though, once they got it kick started, with a very nice season ending. I do think though for shock value and to emphasize their struggle and pain, that the one main character in question should have been sacrificed. The fact that it maybe 2 more years before the season 5 finale, very sad and depressing.Thanks for the awesome adventure... 1982 only seemed like a few years ago to be honest.

author: christianimal
title: All Noise, No Plan
content: Season 5 of Stranger Things feels less like a carefully planned finale and more like the writers' room emptying the junk drawer. The story is overloaded with convoluted plot threads and extra lore that bury what used to be a simple, sharp emotional core. Characters keep leaping to strangely precise conclusions off the thinnest hunches, not because it makes sense, but because the plot needs to move, and their dialogue often strains for quotable one-liners and "viral" moments in a way that feels obvious. Instead of paying off years of setup, the season often plays like they are making it up as they go, stacking twists on top of half-resolved ideas. By the time you reach the ending, the constant cross-cutting, multiple almost-endings, and desperate push for something epic leave it feeling scattered rather than satisfying.

author: TheCaribbeanBlue
title: Used to be good series, that faded fast.
content:
Surfing through the best series in IMDB ratings, you can find Stranger Things up there. Season 1 brought a lot of freshness to the table with it's 80's theme and well chosen actors. Those kids will win you over quick and you just see the natural aura going on the set. It really felt like an adventure you want to be part of, by going through every single episode. Fair to say that 2nd season carried through well, as it managed to bring new ideas to the table and season one would have required a proper ending. I wouldn't want to go into detail with these seasons, as they were nearly perfection in my opinion. You just have to see it for yourself.Now I wish that the 3rd season had not had happened - at least not this way. I feel that it is no surprise, as film companies now try to milk out every cent of successful series or movies, till it becomes unbearable. I felt that they had tried to dumb it down for mainstream watchers, but that was not the fan club you built this show up from. I'd rather not go into the dialogues and humor (which felt very awkwardly forced upon this season), as it seemed to be the least of this season's problems. I'm just going to count up the problems that made me lose any interest for the series:
1) Actors with their attitude and relationship problems. It felt that the main characters all had to be paired up romantically. All series shouldn't feel like some reality TV show on MTV, where you just put a group of people together and every one develop feelings. These are just episode fillers, that you have to sit through, as nothing else is going on.
2) Time management. The whole season felt like it's put together as if sometimes time runs still and other times are fast forwarded. Opening the gate, building of the Mind Flayers - at times it felt it was happening so fast and all of the sudden, it all froze, as it was not the season finale yet. Then, when it came to switching locations that were far away to help your friends or closing the gate - it happened in a heart beat.
3) The whole story. Russians, and their uniforms; secret underground base, which is "heavily guarded". Oh boy, how I would not have gone there - Russians?! The Russian terminator that took his joke role too seriously. It felt like suddenly robots have been introduced to the series, that I have missed out on. It wouldn't have been so bad, if he was meant to be somebody significant and who got plenty of screen time. Somehow had to stand out of all the Russians, who were already after every one. The secret base, which dropped all the way to earth's core, it's corridors unnecessarily long and empty, where every Russian footsoldier wore a uniform. You are trying to blend in with your secret base and you wear a uniform? And after all that seriousness it was like the creators of the show dropped every logic when they made it to a children's playground, where you could almost walk around with no security. Finally the overly powered Mind Flayer, who freeroams around the city, being unstoppable. The only ones to be concerned about it, are the kids with the help of their parents.In conclusion:
Season 1-2 were superb and season 3 lacked of thrills and story. Even at the very end (the sneak peak to season 4), they left no hope for this fading show to end with season 3. Hard to give a fitting rating to this show, as it's probably near 5/10 in the end of season 4.

content: Just finished binge watching it. I'm just in love with the setting, the universe they bring back to us. Did you ever wanted that E.T or Goonies went on for 8 hours??? This was it. Just top notch production top to bottom, easter eggs everywhere and many goodies to enjoy a fine piece of work. Characters are lovable an relatable. The story arch was clear and well designed even with twists like the redemption of the douche jock and the "odd couple born from distress" not ending up together, with a just enough open ending that probably will stay like that and that's fine (I won't complain if there's a second season, but these guys will probably end up getting some big franchise to write and direct like the Russo brothers did (What is it about brothers working together... Just Magnific. Even the Washowskis in some points)Obviously this doesn't reinvents the genre, but it was an excellent work from everybody involved in the production. You can feel the 80 's alive in this one and if you have little boys you can show them how it felt to be a kid back then, to be a child watching the world through TV and movies.And to the hipsters that think that this was an average series i tell them to go a write a soul for them. Because if you go and find these mediocre "at best" (as someone said) i feel really sorry for you and probably your family hates spending Christmas with you.I'm 37 years old and for 8 hours i was 7 again. And that's priceless for me.Just watch it. Really...

author: jeroen-106
title: Season 4: entertaining, but not without its flaws.
content: Boy, you can surely tell the budget went up for this season. There is so much happening and every shot seems to be an expensive one, either because of the practical or digital effects.I liked this season, but it has serious issues.First and foremost, everything seems to drag on forever, which creates a feeling I'm eating an overstuffed turkey. Whether it's the rainbow room segments, The Sovjet storyline, all scenes seem to take up too much screen-time.It feels as if the extra long episodes were a requirement and now suddenly the writers and director had to fill up the extra time they've been given.Also, some characters are there but don't have a lot of interesting things to do. Will Byers and Mike Wheeler for example are plain annoying and the conflicts they have feel forced, which the directors mask by sprinkling melodrama. I've had to roll my eyes in several occasions and ask myself when the hell they were gonna shut up.It doesn't help they've grown up. At least as kids they were cute and their actions were perceived as the ones of kids. Now they seem to act younger than they really are. But you can't really kill them off, now can you, dear directors?I recommend the directors to reduce the episode duration to what it was before and avoid us having to sit through a single episode in multiple sessions, which also forces them to write, direct and edit with rigor.Luckily, many of the cast members are consistently entertaining and they can still carry the show. Production quality is excellent.Having said that, 5 seasons is plenty. We've enjoyed the show for several years and it's time to bring it to a conclusion before the overstuffed turkey burns in the oven.

author: moviegeeekk
title: heart, soul, thrilling direction and heart wrenching performances.
content: The second last season of Netflix's now mega-popular series is inescapably, formulaic. The previous 3 seasons were quiet enjoyable but none of them feel as grand-esque as S4 does. S4 feels more scary, more frightening, more disturbing and more heartbreaking. The season exquisitely rounds off all the characters journey subsequently giving each of the them moments to shine. But it's not all touchy-feely heart-to-hearts, though - the action set-pieces have stepped up a gear, too and the gang's big showdown with Vecna is a glorious, slow-mo affair. And yes, there's more 'Running Up That Hill'.Stranger Things S4 is beautifully crafted. The writing is great, sublimely exploring different characters whilst also giving them heart. But despite having a plethora of characters to manage everyone is given a moment to shine. Will and Jonathan restoring their brotherly bond beautifully, Mike realising El still needs him no matter who powerful she is, Steve opening up to Nancy about his feeling and Max's tearful speech about the dark thoughts that made her so susceptible to Vecna's curse. Every character gets their moments to shine and all the actors put forth compelling, heart wrenching and commendable performances.The last episode being 2h 30m seems undeniably self-indulgent on paper but it is well earned on screen. The last 2 episodes don't have a lot going on with respect to moving the story forward but it's more about the build-up and establishing stakes which makes it more interesting when things don't go as planned. What the last season lack in surprises, it more than makes up for in heart, soul, thrilling direction and heart-wrenching performances. A strong closing chapter that makes the idea of returning to Hawkins one last time more appealing than ever.

author: CKohls
title: Possibly the greatest accomplishment in television history.
content: Let's set The Twilight Zone, Alfred Hitchcock Presents, Maverick, Quantum Leap, Seinfeld, and Breaking Bad to one side a moment. These were shows that were great not only for their brilliant writing and production value but also for their originality. They either created, defined or redefined a genre. Stranger Things is another thing entirely. Another, completely NEW thing which is, in itself, original.But I doubt this will ignite an entire genre, and this is why I consider it unique and incomparable to traditionally groundbreaking shows. Stranger Things is retro. This is obvious and has been noted by everyone. But I don't know if many people have noticed the ASTONISHING attention to detail. Lots of shows are set in history. And lots of shows do a good job of it. But Stranger Things is perfect. It's perfect, not in that it is a perfect reflection of the 80s. It does a damn good job of that. But it goes several steps further. Stranger Things also captures the cinematic style of the 80s. And it does it with such acute accuracy that it is truly mind blowing for a writer and filmmaker who grew up on 80s cinema and was primarily influenced by it as a child. (Me).I'd like to take a moment to specifically note the props. When I was a boy in the 80s, that was the furniture we actually owned. It is perfect in every detail. The girl's room could have been my sister's room. My sister literally had that exact music box with the ballerina in it. Furthermore, the show draws attention to brands that were popular in the 80s. This adds a touch of authenticity. Sure. But what is so brilliant about this is that it's done in the kind of obvious way that 80s movies did it.I'd also like to address the brilliance of the casting. I realized something about attraction many years ago. There is traditional look, there are unique looks, and there are fashionable looks. In every major era of cinema, there are particular "types" that the industry, for whatever reason, tends to like to cast. The 80s had an extreme version of this. And almost everyone in this cast is straight out of 80s casting. (Winona Ryder is an exception. I actually love Winona Ryder, but I think casting her in this was a mistake). The daughter is a great example of this. She reminds me of the actress from The Great Outdoors Lucy Deakins (I just looked that up) and several other actresses from the era. I honestly don't understand how these filmmakers are getting these performances out of these actors. My guess (and this really is just a guess) is that much of this was casting. I think probably the actors they chose, not only were perfect because they fit the 80s look, but also because they fit the 80s style of acting. Much of acting is exploiting natural quirks in your real character, and my guess is that many of these actors all had a natural tendency to be this way. Tendencies that might not be particularly charming in a typical 2016 project, but that are perfect for this. The filmmakers may also have had them watch 80s performances to try to emulate. Either way, credit needs to be given to the filmmakers for this.But the writing is where it all begins. The foundation of it all. Here's why I'm so impressed with the writing. They didn't just include a lot of good 80s stuff, they included 80s clichés. And not even good clichés. They added clichés that are kind of lame like completely senseless character motivations that we're just supposed to buy because it's movie logic. This show really steeps itself in movie logic and I LOVE IT. I usually hate this but, in this case, it's a beautiful homage to 80s films. And what really works for me is that they do it with a real reverence. Any time they include movie logic, the do it with the same straight face as was done in the 80s. There is no tongue in cheek; it's a perfect mimeograph.There are so many little touches. Kids-on-bikes being a signature of 80s cinema, especially with Spielberg. A lot of this seems to be very Spielbergian, but there are so many 80s films that this project draws from that I wouldn't define the influence so narrowly. As a writer and filmmaker myself, I can't help but watch, jaw open, astonished and mesmerized by this project. It's truly incomparable to other films or television projects. It's something entirely new and different, and I think it will stand apart for a very long time. I've never seen this level of accuracy in the depiction of an era, and I lived through the era. And maybe that's why it's so compelling to me. The first 10 years of my life were 1980-1990 and, in many ways, those are the most important year of one's life. It's one's introduction to the world, to one's self, to sights and sounds and smells, music, food, entertainment, etc. I don't think about the 80s all that much. I didn't love it. But I can tell you, there are things about my childhood that I haven't thought about for years, that this show has drawn back into the forefront of my mind. Wonderful things. And something makes me think that, maybe, our world is a little more synthetic today. Somehow the world was more "real" back then. I don't tend to buy into this idea that everything was better before smartphones, but... maybe some things were better. I don't know. I suppose, love it or hate it, this show has made this viewer think about some things, and that's one of the most important things great art can do.

The storytelling, the cinematography, the acting (including the child actors), the pacing, the music, the 80's nostalgia and pop-culture references, even something as trivial as the opening credits and title screen... everything about this show screams perfection. I'm curious what Netflix will throw at us next. I don't expect they will be able to maintain this level of quality with their future productions, but even coming close to it every now and then would probably put them ahead of the competition, including HBO.In summary, i think Stranger Things is a masterpiece and pretty much the best TV production i've ever seen. author: wnvyvcgc
title: That's it?!
content: I went into the finale hoping it would finally fix the long-standing plot holes and tie everything together in a satisfying way. Instead, what we got was mostly flashy visuals, overly easy fights, and more than anything, terrible timing. So many events in this episode could have happened earlier, but they didn't, simply because it "wasn't the moment." Not for logical reasons, not because the story demanded it, but because allowing them to happen earlier would have prevented other plot points. Rather than rewriting events creatively, the show chose convenience.That issue shows up clearly in how certain characters are handled. I kept wondering what Joyce was even doing up there in Dimension X for most of the episode, only for it to finally lead to her talking and reacting in what felt like a manufactured, long-awaited drama scene. It didn't come naturally from the situation; it felt delayed on purpose just to squeeze out an emotional moment, even if it made her presence feel pointless for far too long.What makes this even more disappointing is how many genuinely smart fan theories were floating around. Theories that connected past seasons, characters, and mysteries in ways that would have elevated the finale into something memorable. Almost all of them turned out to be wrong, not because they were far-fetched, but because the finale itself just wasn't operating on that level of depth or ambition. The hype built by the fandom ended up being better than the actual writing.The final plot twist didn't land either. It was painfully predictable. I had already convinced myself that the Duffer Brothers wouldn't have the courage to permanently let a major character go, so once you accept that assumption, the only question left is "how?" And the answer turned out to be exactly what you'd expect, nothing complex, nothing bold, just the safest possible route.Kali's character also felt largely unnecessary. Her presence didn't meaningfully impact the overall story; she existed mainly to give Eleven a proper or emotionally neat ending, just as many people had already imagined. Beyond that, her role had little weight, especially considering how much potential her storyline once seemed to have.They also teased a deeper connection to Will's disappearance, implying that everything would finally come full circle, but that promise went nowhere. The connection was either extremely shallow or simply abandoned.In the end, the finale suffers from too many unresolved plot holes, moments of weak acting, cliché dialogue, and above all, poor writing choices driven by bad timing. It doesn't feel like a conclusion that grew naturally from the story. It feels like one that avoided risks just to reach an ending.
