author: aadarshkhule_16
title: Stranger Things isn't just a TV show
content: Stranger Things isn't just a TV show - it's an emotion that grew with us, season by season. It's the perfect blend of '80s nostalgia, supernatural mystery, and heartfelt friendship that never loses its soul, even when the monsters take over Hawkins.Season 1 was pure magic - a perfect introduction to the small town of Hawkins and the strange, eerie energy of the Upside Down. The bond between the kids, Eleven's mysterious powers, and the haunting disappearance of Will Byers made it feel like a dark fairytale mixed with a Spielberg adventure. It wasn't just scary; it was emotional. You could feel the innocence of childhood colliding with the terror of the unknown.Season 2 deepened that bond. The characters matured, the danger grew, and we saw how trauma lingers - especially in Will's haunting storyline. Eleven's search for her identity and belonging was beautifully emotional. It wasn't as mysterious as Season 1, but it made us care more deeply for everyone. The family-like warmth between Joyce, Hopper, and the kids really stood out here.Season 3 was visually brighter but emotionally darker. The Starcourt Mall setting added so much color and style - a nostalgic love letter to the '80s. Beneath all the neon lights and humor, though, the show hit hard with themes of growing up and moving on. Hopper's fatherly love for Eleven and his final letter still feels like a punch to the heart. It was action-packed, emotional, and full of tension - a true turning point for the series.Season 4 took everything to another level. It wasn't just horror anymore - it was psychological, tragic, and cinematic in scale. Vecna became one of TV's best villains, connecting every mystery from previous seasons in such a chilling way. The separate storylines - from Hawkins to Russia to the desert - somehow tied together perfectly. Max's emotional arc and "Running Up That Hill" moment were unforgettable. This season didn't just scare you; it broke you and healed you at the same time.Now, as we wait for Season 5, Stranger Things has become more than a sci-fi series - it's about friendship, loss, courage, and growing up in a world that keeps changing. The show gave us laughter, heartbreak, goosebumps, and a reminder that even when life turns upside down, love and loyalty bring us back.

author: aki_vlahodimos
title: Excellent retro love-in - ignore the naysayers
content: As you read some of the negative reviews for Stranger Things, you begin to realise just how messed up modern society is when it comes to judging the quality of movies and TV.There seems to be a completely false misconception that in order for something to be good or 'original' it needs to be filled with brand new ideas that no one has ever seen (or thought of) before.Frankly, this is rubbish and the people spouting utter codswallop about it on this site clearly have way too much time on their hands or just enjoy being negative.It genuinely feels as though some people are just panning this show so they can demonstrate their knowledge of movie and TV history, mentioning a moment in the decades of movies that have gone before, where a scene was similar to one shown in Stranger Things. If that is how we judge things nowadays, it's a bit of shame.Apologies, rant over.This show is excellent. Really it is. I personally found it so engrossing that I was – for the duration of each episode – transported back in to the 80s. Credit goes to the actors - especially the kids, for making it seem so real despite having no first-hand experience on which to draw from.The way this is filmed, the lighting, the vast amount of electronic music used, the graininess in the opening credits, the cars and technology, the bicycles, the clothes and the haircuts – it's all first rate. Actually, let me just say that again. The soundtrack is awesome.As mentioned, the acting is also good. I agree with another reviewer who said that our old friend Winona Ryder wails like a slightly mentally unstable person for the majority of her time on screen but this just about bearable given the context.David Harbour is excellent as a run-down but hard-nosed local cop and all the kids are outstanding. Mathew Modine is a little under-used, but he almost feels like a last minute addition to the cast anyway so it's no real loss.The CGI and special effects are pretty solid. I think the dark settings and low lighting obviously helps. Indeed, as we get to the later episodes and the CGI becomes more important and more frequently used, you start seeing the inevitable shortcuts that were taken to support a TV series versus a blockbuster summer movie.For me the best thing about this series is the fact that it made me want to see more episodes. I found it hard to stop watching. And the interesting thing is that I couldn't quite put my finger on one single thing that made me want to watch. It really was a bit of everything.Yes, I could see where the story was heading from fairly early on, but I still wanted to see it unfold because the experience was, well, a whole lot of fun.And I guess this brings me full circle to my initial rant.There are countless references to countless 80s + 90s movies and TV series. If you're old enough, you'll spot most of them. But this didn't pose a problem for me, nor did it reduce the level of enjoyment of watching. On the contrary, it made me smile and briefly think back to my own childhood.The whole series treads a very unusual line between thriller, horror, and retro-spoof. Now, you can could say that drawing all these genres together is boring and unoriginal, but I beg to differ.Putting them all together in this way is not something I've seen before. Maybe it has been done, but I haven't seen it, and I watch plenty of series.The fact that so many people are giving this 10 stars speaks volumes, so please don't be influenced by the negative reviews without first giving at least one episode a go.This series draws you in and it's enjoyable, funny, cheesy and mildly frightening right to the very predictable ending/intro to season 2. To be fair, I'm not entirely sure how else they could've ended it.You can choose to miss it if you think everything that comes of out of Hollywood needs to be something we've never seen before – but honestly, I dare you to find a single thing on a planet of 7.6 billion people and countless series, books, movies etc. that no one has thought of or done before.Watch it. Stranger Things is fun because it's different to most of the other things out there.

author: LorenzoS-754
title: A great show brought down by a safe, disappointing finale
content: Stranger Things was once one of the most exciting and emotionally engaging shows on television.The first three seasons are outstanding: tense, imaginative, scary, and full of heart. Even season four, despite some flaws, still carried ambition and scale.Unfortunately, the final season undermines everything the series built.The problem is not the themes, but the execution. The finale avoids real consequences, explains too much, and plays it safe when it should have been bold. The supernatural threat loses its power, the sense of danger evaporates, and the story prioritizes introspection and reassurance over tension, loss, and sacrifice.What made Stranger Things special was its ability to show fear and mystery without over-explaining it. In the end, the unknown becomes manageable, the stakes feel lowered, and the emotional payoff never truly arrives. Characters who should have paid a price are protected, and the ending lacks the weight and courage expected from a show of this caliber.This is not a terrible ending - but it is a deeply disappointing one.Stranger Things deserved a finale that hurt, that risked dividing the audience, that felt inevitable rather than comfortable.An incredible series that could have become legendary, but chose safety over impact.

title: Teen horror at its peak

author: Kysugo
title: A must-watch show that ties Sci-Fi, Horror, Drama, bits of Comedy and good ole 80's nostalgia
content: Stranger Things is a must-watch show. It is without a doubt one of the best shows to come out in the past 15 years. Saying that it's a great show is a gross understatement. The Duffer Brothers have created something very special here that only comes once in a while and I'm glad that we are all able to experience it. Everything from the production quality, the acting, the special effects, the ideas, the music, the storytelling, the world that they've created - everything is top tier. The music is fantastic. Not only the songs they use from the 80's, but also the original soundtrack that they've created. They make full use of lush pads and synth noises that are reminiscent of the 80's and it definitely sets the perfect tone for the show. The intro theme song is iconic. The whole idea of the upside down along with the Demogorgon and all the creatures that they've conceptualized are all incredible ideas. They pull a lot of inspiration from movies like E. T., Alien, The Thing, The Goonies, Poltergeist, Stand By Me, and Nightmare on Elm Street which are all fantastic movies from the 80's. They've really outdone themselves with the storytelling and the way they tell the story - the story flows beautifully and feels natural. The way they jump around from one characters journey to another's is just chef's kiss - it's very Pulp Fiction-esque in that sense. The scene transitions in this show are very clever and brilliant. Stranger Things accomplishes one of the hardest things to do in media - creating a seamless ebb and flow. By this I mean that the show does a beautiful job at showing the dark scary moments and then contrasting them with lighter more comedic moments at the right time. The show does a wonderful job at capturing that 80's feel and in turn makes it feel nostalgic. The show has also managed to deliver with each season. There hasn't been a bad season and that's definitely worth noting.

author: claudioafc
title: Nostalgia bait with impressive visuals and awful acting
content: First of all, let me say that "Stranger Things" was the first show that I ever binge watched.That first season was quite impressive when it came out and it still holds today. The way they captured the 80's feeling in a cleaner and modern aesthetic still makes it feel timeless, and apart from many other modern shows.The hairstyles, clothes, music, etc, all fit so nicely and the impressive visual effects that are throughout the whole five seasons are definitely the main highlight of Stranger Things.However, the plot is either a constant hit and miss, especially on the latter seasons/episodes.See, as many other TV shows, it's quite normal to follow a plot and then not lead anywhere, as there are other more important plots to continue the story. And many get resolved with the main plot. But here, a lot of them are just fillers and completely pointless.And somehow, on the later seasons, the episodes get full of pointless plots and extremely long runtimes. It's like the creators didn't really know what they wanted to do anymore and decided to just add everything at once.That was probably one of the biggest changes when compared to the first season.The show went from each episode being entertaining to watch to then becoming a complete drag to finish one single chapter.The other noticeable change was the acting.Earlier seasons you could use the age of the protagonists as an excuse to overlook a lot of it, but later on you just realize that some of them are just bad actors overall.Millie Bobby Brown (Eleven) and Noah Schnapp (Will), when compared to the rest of the cast they're just awful (especially on the last seasons).Joe Keery's (Steve) and David Harbour (Jim) do have some great charater development's, but then they get relegated to even less than secondary roles.They did add some great characters later on. Billy, Eddie, even Robin were all entertaining to watch. And most of the times they were better than the main cast.But sometimes the characters themselves are nonsensical. Winona Ryder (Joyce Byers) goes from entertaining focused maternal figure on the 1st season to completely pointless (and sometimes idiotic) on the following chapters. It's as if she filled her role and then they didn't know what to do with her anymore.And the stupidity/smartness of most of them keeps flipping in between seasons or episodes. In the end you don't care much about any of them anymore because what they do on one season doesn't really follow up to the next.Overall, Stranger Things season 1 is still probably one of the best things to come out of Netflix in that genre.But if you don't watch the rest of the series, you won't be missing much.

author: iazurdiaCR
title: A great throwback to nostalgia in the early seasons, but the finale stretched the story, rushed some parts, and was full of the 80s style plot armor
content: It's been a long time since season 1 aired, but I remember a well-written, well-executed show from the start, with great characters and an incredible nostalgic feel.That vibe stuck around, but it got weaker with each new season - until we got to this last one. The show still looked and sounded cool (even if this time it's more CGI-esque), but it had way more plot armor, convenient twists, and overcrowded storylines.Don't get me wrong - the finale had great moments, especially the closure of some iconic relationships. But if you strip away all the scenes designed to make you cry (which lean on nostalgia, the show's biggest strength), they stretched a story that could had its resolution in earlier seasons (and we could have avoided the dissonance between the actors' ages and their characters' supposed ones).Plus, ironically, some conclusions were rushed - they either needed more time to breathe or shouldn't have been crammed in at all. Typical of a final season: one kind of pacing throughout the ride versus a completely different one to wrap it all up.In the end, the finale was bittersweet and fun, but it could've been resolved years ago and with a simpler narrative.PS. I liked the Will coming-out scene, though I wasn't a fan of how his overpowered abilities played out in the end with Vecna.

author: swaneliott
title: Amazing 1st season, and a questionable following
content:
Let me start by saying I love season 1. I thought it was the perfect start for young horror fans and it was able to boost Netflix's popularity so they could go on and make more originals, such as Dead to Me, Big Mouth, The Babysitter ect. It was perfect and I wouldn't change a thing.
However,
But the time season 2 rolled along, I started to roll my eyes. I thought it was good, but nowhere near as amazing as the 1st season. It felt a bit unfocused at times and very forgettable. I remember every plot point in season 1, and about 2 scenes in season 2. And if you want to see one of the most pointless and out of place episodes in the history of TV, watch the 7th episode of season 2. But it did wrap all the stories up nicely and gave us a satisfying ending.
Until now,
Season 3 was great, it was so much better than season 2 and felt like the show found it's feet again. But because of my distaste for season 2, I no longer cared for the characters. All of the big character driven, heart felt scenes that are made to make teenage girls cry their eyes out, and the chemistry between the characters, no longer felt like something I could identify with and therefore it made me feel a bit bored, wanting it to just hurry up and finish.
And thank God it did.
Season 3 perfectly ends the show. All the characters have reached the end of their progression. They have nowhere else to go. Done, completed, now let's move on.
But wait, THERE'S MORE!!!
My instincts tell me that Netflix has already ordered Season 4, completely ruining the ending of 3. Don't over milk the cow! Everyone will be satisfied if the show ends here, and we can move on and Netflix can make more influential originals. But knowing American TV shows, they will milk the cow dry, leaving a sour taste in everyone's mouth, when we should be remembering what a great show it was.

author: RaushanK-7130
title: About it
content: Stranger Things is one of those rare shows that feels instantly iconic while still surprising you at every turn. From its very first episode, the series pulls you into a world that is both nostalgic and unsettling, blending 1980s small-town charm with genuine, edge-of-your-seat suspense. What makes the show truly outstanding is how effortlessly it balances genres-science fiction, horror, mystery, and heartfelt coming-of-age drama-without ever losing its identity.The storytelling is sharp and emotionally grounded. At its core, Stranger Things is about friendship, loyalty, and growing up in a world that suddenly becomes far more dangerous than it should be. The characters feel real, flawed, and deeply human, which makes the supernatural threats even more terrifying. You don't just watch the danger-you feel it, because you care about the people facing it.The performances across the cast are exceptional, especially from the younger actors, who bring remarkable depth and authenticity to their roles. Their chemistry is natural and believable, making every quiet moment just as compelling as the intense ones. The older cast members add emotional weight and complexity, ensuring the story resonates with viewers of all ages.Visually and musically, the show is a masterpiece. The cinematography captures both the innocence of a quiet town and the dread lurking beneath it, while the synth-heavy soundtrack perfectly amplifies the tension and nostalgia. Every detail-from lighting to sound design-feels carefully crafted.Ultimately, Stranger Things succeeds because it has heart. It's not just about monsters or alternate dimensions; it's about courage, sacrifice, and holding on to hope when everything feels wrong. It's gripping, emotional, and unforgettable-a modern classic that fully deserves its place among the best television series ever made.

author: felixborre
title: "Stranger Things" (2016)
content:
IntroductionStranger Things is a science-fiction horror series created by the Duffer Brothers that premiered on Netflix in 2016. The show combines elements of 1980s nostalgia, supernatural mystery, and small-town drama in the fictional town of Hawkins, Indiana. It quickly distinguished itself through strong ensemble performances, meticulous period detail, and a blending of horror, adventure, and coming-of-age drama.The series' popularity is partly due to its interweaving of adolescent perspective with high-stakes supernatural conflict, creating a layered narrative that appeals both to nostalgia-driven adults and young viewers.Narrative Structure
Serialized Mystery with Episodic Beats:
While each episode contributes to a larger story arc (the disappearance of Will Byers, Eleven's powers, the Upside Down), the episodes also include self-contained suspense and small-resolution plot points, giving viewers multiple narrative gratifications.Multiple Viewpoints:
The story unfolds through the perspectives of the children, their families, the town authorities, and shadowy government agencies, providing a multi-layered narrative tension.Each viewpoint intersects organically, particularly during climactic sequences, demonstrating strong narrative orchestration.Escalating Stakes:
Season 1 gradually builds from a missing-child mystery to a confrontation with a full-scale interdimensional threat, balancing personal stakes and cosmic horror.Themes and Motifs
Friendship and Loyalty
Central to the show is the bond among Mike, Dustin, Lucas, and Will, which drives much of the emotional resonance.The children's resilience, courage, and ingenuity provide a human anchor to the supernatural chaos.Nostalgia and 1980s Americana
Visuals, music, and pop-culture references evoke a carefully curated sense of time and place, from arcade games to Dungeons & Dragons sessions.This nostalgic grounding enhances character relatability and thematic depth.Otherness and Power
Eleven embodies the intersection of innocence and dangerous potential, reflecting themes of isolation, trauma, and the ethics of power.The Upside Down operates as both a literal and metaphorical manifestation of hidden fears, societal anxieties, and unseen threats.Government Secrecy and Ethical Ambiguity
Hawkins National Laboratory embodies scientific hubris and moral compromise, providing a critique of institutional authority and unchecked experimentation.Character Development
Eleven (Millie Bobby Brown):
Central to the narrative, Eleven evolves from a silent, traumatized test subject to a socially aware, fiercely loyal member of the Hawkins circle.Her arc balances vulnerability with escalating agency, culminating in decisive confrontations with the Demogorgon.Mike Wheeler (Finn Wolfhard):
Represents the emotional and moral compass of the children's group, demonstrating courage, strategic thinking, and empathy.Will Byers (Noah Schnapp):
His disappearance and subsequent exposure to the Upside Down frame the first season's central conflict.Will's trauma is depicted with subtlety and emotional authenticity, providing the series with a lasting thematic resonance.Jim Hopper (David Harbour):
Embodies the grizzled, emotionally complex adult archetype: flawed, haunted by personal loss, but capable of profound bravery and sacrifice.Hopper's arc balances procedural authority with paternal instincts, particularly toward Eleven.Supporting Ensemble:
Characters like Dustin, Lucas, Nancy, and Joyce contribute to interpersonal drama, humor, and investigative intrigue, ensuring the ensemble is more than a backdrop.Production Values
Cinematography: Moody, atmospheric lighting and practical effects evoke creepy small-town horror with cinematic flair.Sound Design and Music: The synth-heavy score reinforces the 1980s aesthetic and intensifies suspense.Visual Effects: Practical effects and CGI combine seamlessly, particularly in Depictions of the Upside Down and the Demogorgon.Strengths
Tightly Constructed Mystery: Gradual revelation of the Upside Down and Eleven's origins keeps viewers engaged.Strong Ensemble Performances: Child actors deliver nuanced portrayals, maintaining believability under high-stakes fantasy scenarios.Period Accuracy: Meticulous attention to 1980s visual and cultural detail enhances immersion.Emotional Core: Friendship, loyalty, and family dynamics create resonant stakes beyond mere horror tropes.Weaknesses / Critiques
Occasional Genre Pastiche: Some episodes rely heavily on homage to 1980s films, which may distract from narrative originality.Predictable Procedural Elements: Certain investigative sequences follow standard suspense/horror beats, reducing tension.Limited Diversity: Season 1 largely centers on a predominantly White cast, with minor roles for characters of color, reflecting a lack of broader representation in the central narrative.Overall AssessmentSeason 1 of Stranger Things is a masterclass in genre blending, combining horror, suspense, and coming-of-age drama. Its emotional resonance, stylistic authenticity, and ensemble performances make it a standout entry in 2010s television. While it leans on nostalgia and occasionally predictable procedural structures, the series' careful character work, thematic depth, and inventive supernatural mythology ensure it remains compelling and influential.Key Themes: Friendship, trauma, power, government secrecy, otherness, 1980s nostalgia
Audience Appeal: Viewers of horror, science fiction, and coming-of-age dramas, especially those attuned to 1980s cultural references
Legacy: Set a high standard for serialized streaming drama, combining cultural nostalgia with modern storytelling sophistication.

about but the sci fi mystery genre put me off a little.I can only judge the first season but already can see that the series creators the Duffer brothers Matt and Ross have hit gold .Stranger Things author: AlenD-9
title: Disappointing last season
content: The ending season of Stranger Things was deeply disappointing because it failed to live up to the massive potential the series had built over the years. The first four seasons were intense, emotional, and genuinely scary, with strong storytelling, memorable characters, and a constant sense of danger that kept viewers hooked. The show once balanced horror, mystery, and friendship perfectly, making it feel fresh and powerful. However, in the final season, that tension disappeared-what was once a dark and frightening series slowly turned into something that felt more like a joke. A bunch of teenagers defeating an interdimensional monster in just five minutes made the threat feel laughably small and completely undermined the danger that had been built up for years. The stakes no longer felt real, the horror was weakened, and moments that should have been terrifying or emotional felt forced or overly dramatic. It was frustrating to see a show with such a strong foundation and so much unused potential end in a way that didn't respect how great it once was.

author: nidhunmoviebuff
title: Volume 4 takes the franchise to dazzling, cinematic levels!
content: When you stretch the run-time of each episode of your already lengthy 9-episode season to over an hour-long, culminating in a mammoth 2-hour long finale, the makers of Stranger Things needed to ensure that the narrative justified its length and the time invested by the viewers. And the Duffer Brothers and Shawn Levy achieve just that, seamlessly combining the coming-of-age and horror-thriller genres to deliver a sparkling, almost-cinematic experience that will set new benchmarks on the levels a series can aspire to reach.We rejoin our beloved Eleven (Millie Bobby Brown) and her rag-tag bunch of compatriots as they look to navigate the vagaries of high school, all-the-while keeping at bay the nefarious forces of the other-dimensional "Upside down", where a new power has surfaced, a demonic being known as "Vecna". While the core coming-of-age storyline continues to go from strength to strength, the makers deftly split the narrative into three branches, deftly switching back and forth between the POVs of Eleven, her adopted father "Hopper" who is trapped in Russia and the enterprising "Dustin", my personal favorite character in the entire franchise.The throwback references to the 1980s, where the story takes place, add a superlative charm to the proceedings, with everything from vintage brands to metal music weaved neatly into the storytelling. The writing is top-notch as usual and how they manage to give each one of its 15+ main characters a compelling story arc with seemingly equal importance is beyond my comprehension. Because of the same, it is very difficult to pick a stand-out performer, with everyone from David Harbour ("Hopper") to John Keery ("Steve Harrington") turning in eye-catching portrayals, and even the newly introduced characters like "Argyle" and "Eddy Munson" make their presence felt.The only downside of the 4th season is the romance tracks which seem forced and contrived in places, with the writers seemingly drumming up conflicts where there naturally aren't any and deliberately leaving behind loose ends and unanswered questions just to build anticipation for Season 6, said to be the final season of the franchise. Due to these small shortfalls, Volume 4 will still lag behind the landmark Volumes 1 & 2 for me but still manages to deliver a satisfying, immensely binge-worthy viewing experience. Recommended!

title: Tween Peaks meets Silent Hill
content: Right at the beginning - is this a good show? Yes. Is this the best thing since sliced bread? No. I don't think that the show deserves so much praise as it gets. There's almost a pathological sense of nostalgia nowadays and I would ascribe a lot of the series success to it's setting in the 80's. The feeling of the "good old days" is so abundant in the audience that they'll swallow pretty much anything with the retro vibe and continue to ask for more. So, let's put off those nostalgia glasses and be realistic. The series deserves praise for the execution since it's good enough to keep you engaged and make you binge watch the whole season. On the other hand, so many things have already been seen in other movies/series that there's no sense of originality (at least for me). If you are a long term fan of the genre, there's almost nothing new to see here. But if you're a newcomer, this will be a nice initiation into this type of movies/series and hopefully it will encourage you to dig deeper and find all the other works that inspired this one. author: mumu420yhboi
title: gud review innit
content: Stranger Things is an American science fiction horror drama television series created by the Duffer Brothers, who also serve as showrunners and are executive producers along with Shawn Levy and Dan Cohen. Produced by Monkey Massacre Productions and Levy's 21 Laps Entertainment, the first season was released on Netflix on July 15, 2016. Its second, third, and fourth seasons followed in October 2017, July 2019, and May and July 2022, respectively. In February 2022, the series was renewed for a fifth and final season.Set in the 1980s, the series centers around the residents of the fictional small town of Hawkins, Indiana, as they are plagued by a hostile alternate dimension known as the "Upside Down", after a nearby human experimentation facility opens a gateway between the Upside Down and the normal world. It stars an ensemble cast including Winona Ryder, David Harbour, Finn Wolfhard, Millie Bobby Brown, Gaten Matarazzo, Caleb McLaughlin, Natalia Dyer, Charlie Heaton, Cara Buono, Matthew Modine, Noah Schnapp, Sadie Sink, Joe Keery, Dacre Montgomery, Sean Astin, Paul Reiser, Maya Hawke, Priah Ferguson, and Brett Gelman.The Duffer Brothers developed Stranger Things as a mix of investigative drama and supernatural elements portrayed with horror and childlike sensibilities, while infusing references to the pop culture of the 1980s. Several thematic and directorial elements were inspired by the works of Steven Spielberg, John Carpenter, David Lynch, Stephen King, Wes Craven and H. P. Lovecraft. They also took inspiration from experiments conducted during the Cold War and conspiracy theories involving secret government experiments.One of Netflix's flagship series, Stranger Things has attracted record viewership on the streaming platform. The series has been critically acclaimed for its characterization, atmosphere, acting, soundtrack, directing, writing, and homages to 1980s films. It has received numerous awards and nominations.

author: js-342-386147
title: A real tasty love potion
content: Much have been written about this series love for the early 80s. And it's understandable. The whole period of John Carpenter, Steven Spielberg, teenage horror-movies and cold war paranoia has been mixed together to a real tasty love potion. If you're too young and don't love the 80s for sentimental reasons you probably will after a few episodes of Stranger Things.The story is set in a small rural town and revolves around a missing boy. His friends is soon dragged into a mystery and an adventure. Goonies and I.T. with the BMX bikes, nerds turning into heroes and a friendship story worthy a Spielberg movie. But there is so much more. The older sister have her own problems and her adventure makes an equally intriguing and fun story including all the ingredients for a classic high school horror movie. Under age drinking, skinny dipping and stupid boyfriends. And finally there is the confused and distraught mother and the towns sheriff also trying to solve the mystery.What impresses me the most is how the series manages to keep all three parts of the plot relevant and interesting all the way to the climax. The pacing is mostly perfect and so is the acting. The child characters are all well played, specially Millie Bobby Brown as Eleven and the funny character Dustin played by Gaten Matarazzo. Of course Winona Ryder is brilliant as the desperate mother.The 80s atmosphere is well set with great horror sequences with the mandatory light flickering, scare jumps and electronic music that could have been made by John Carpenter. There is a lot of John Carpenter stuff going on here and it's great. Some of the inspirations for the series are even featured in one way or the other. Stephen King, The Thing, Michael Myers, and a few more.The only weaknesses I can find here is the somewhat uninteresting bad guys. And David Harbours sheriff doesn't do it for me. His character don't add up so to speak. There is something missing there. But these minor flaws are very minor.Stranger Things is defiantly some of the best TV I've seen for the last three years or so.

title: Some still do make'm like they used to.
content: This was the nostalgia itch that I didn't know that I needed scratched. After so many reboots and remakes from my childhood that ultimately fail to deliver more than a hint of what made the originals great, I determined that I must be getting too old and cynical to appreciate things in the same way as I used. It's only a matter of time until I become the "they don't make them like they used to" guy. Stranger Things laughs at the notion that the wonder and adventure from that time period can't be recreated, and makes it obvious what the other attempts at capturing this have missed. It doesn't show you that you are in that you are back in your childhood by putting a kid in an Indiana Jones costume and dressing teenagers in loud clothes with big hair. It makes you feel it with a hundred little details that you forgot about and I can't thank the creators enough. Somebody still makes them like they used to, and apparently, I'm still capable of being able to have the same wonder, joy and investment that I did all those years ago.

author: FlorisV
title: Second season delivers again!
content: Great show where everything is done right: casting, music, writing and visuals. The most eye-catching performance in the first season is a superb Winona Ryder, the second season doesn't have any particular star but introduces some interesting newcomers. The show is chock full of flashbacks to the 80s and not just because it takes place in 1984 but often winks to sci fi classics from the 80s via movie posters, toys (of course, everybody has the Star Wars Kenner toys) dialog references, little TV fragments (The Thing) and what not.The small town setting, which much attention to the personal woes of it's locals, is reminiscent of Stephen King but the focus on it's nerd kids screams Stephen Spielberg louder than E.T. could phone home. It's horror concept of the Upside Down parallel world and it's monsters is very H.P. Lovecraftian. And it's depiction of high school problems is very John Hughes.This is where the criticism comes in: it's very derivative and constantly points out things from the 80s that you loved, or loved to hate, to get that sense of familiarity. For instance, the second season shows the Dragons Lair Arcade game infamous for it's excruciating difficulty and Terminator running in the theaters. You constantly get that tap on the shoulder: "hey, you liked that though back in the day, didn't you?" But if the answer is: hell yes you bet I did"", then there's no problem really.While it would have never been made without the inspiration of many 80s sci fi and horror classics, Stranger Things has enough strength on it's own and has proved with it's second season there's more, much more where this came from. While the first season was too reminiscent of E.T., this second season went into new and interesting directions. Can't wait till the 3rd comes!

author: theopinionatedindian
title: Duffer Brothers Killed It Again!
content: When the first season has garnered rave reviews & has developed a cult following, expectations from the second season of Netflix's hit Show were abnormally high. The Duffer brothers had tough job at hand & had to present a bigger & better second season in order to satiate their show's huge fan base's thirst for quality entertainment. But the Duffer brothers luckily do not disappoint. Netflix has perfected the art of producing quality drama shows & then churn out several seasons of their hit shows. The second season starts off on a high & answers a lot of questions unanswered in the first season. The script is excellent. The show manages to keep you involved & intrigued throughout. Finn Wolfhard (Mike), who probably shot for IT simultaneously, must be given credit for portraying two characters who are polar opposites of each other. Such maturity in acting at such a young age is commendable. Series regulars Winona Ryder(Joyce Byers) & David Harbour (Jim Hopper) continue to perform to our expectations. A few new faces are introduced & we are even told that a much loved character will be a part of the second season as well. The second season delves deeper into Natalie Dyer(Nancy Wheeler)- Charlie Heaton(Jonathan Byers) & Joe Keery(Steve Harrington) as well. The demons are bigger, scarier & more powerful than the first season. The camaraderie between the four friends will make you miss your childhood friends & bring back some pleasant memories from school. Gaten Matarazzo(Dustin) is endearing. Noah Scnapp(Will Byers) who did not have much of a role in the first season has a prominent role in the second season & gives a fine performance. Caleb Mclaughlin(Lucas Sinclair) does a good job of supporting the cast, although he doesn't have much of a role himself. He is probably cast for adding some "color" (pun intended) to the show. The makers have even added a dialogue on these lines. On the whole, the second season will remind you why you feel in love with the first season. The Duffer brothers have to be thanked for not letting us down. Netflix has been kind to add a recap before the first episode starts. The last two episodes are out of this world! We are having withdrawal symptoms already & cant wait for the third season!

author: FortyLMC
title: The series of MY life.
content: I'm writing this at 6:13 a.m., January 1st, 2026, right after finishing the final episode of the series I've loved and enjoyed the most in my life.Well... it's finally over.No more Dungeons & Dragons.No more nights waiting for new episodes.No more theories about what might happen next (we never got them right btw).No more stranger things.If I had to describe this series in a single word, it would be beautiful. Or amazing. Or emotional. Or... I don't know, it is HUGE, it can't be described in one single word.Not just because it told an incredible story, expertly executed, but because HOW it's told it created emotions that maybe we would have never felt without it. The nostalgia for a time I didn't even live through. The excitement of speculating about future seasons. The pure happiness of knowing a new episode had just dropped. And so many other Stranger-and emotional-Things at the same time.There is nothing else like it. It's simply sublime.It's the series that moved me the most, the one that made me the happiest.This review isn't about a specific episode. It's about a series that, in my case, marked my childhood and my adolescence for ten years. I will always remember Stranger Things. There will never be anything like it.Thank you, Stranger Things.Thank you, Duffer Brothers.Thank you to everyone who made this series possible.There will never be anything like this again.I feel sad and happy at the same time.People say that, objectively, there are better series. That it has imperfections. That it isn't realistic. And maybe that's true. But I believe that life-and stories-are defined by how we remember them, and how we choose to tell them.And one day, when I talk to my kids, I'll tell them about the series I loved the most and enjoyed the most.Thanks to the greatest series of all time, of all my life.Thank you, Stranger Things.Thanks for reading, happy new year!

author: trnjamesbond
title: Strange Exciting Nostalgia
content: If your not a Netflix subscriber you've probably never heard of this show, but from what I can see it's getting advertised quite well, so I could be wrong."Stranger Things" is an 80's style sci-fi/horror type of drama, as of today there are eight episodes so far. Winona Ryder is an excellent choice for a pivotal role in this saga. She is a tour de force, watching her on screen brings smiles to my face because she really hasn't been in anything remotely good for a really long time.The series really has a mixture of everything that was cool back in the early 80's it was like I was watching this through the eyes of a 10 year old boy with wonder and amazement. We are introduced to many characters, with roles similar to either "The Goonies" or "Stand By Me" There are also hints of the film "Firestarter" as well. I really don't want to give too much away. So I won't make this a spoiler review. Just a generalization.Every episode seems to have a theme, but sticks to the basic underlying plot and some great tunes from the 80's to go along with it. With the likes of the late David Bowie and so forth. There is also some elements of the X-Files from time to time, but it's not very pronounced and in your face, just a very subtle feeling from that show, even though it was based in the 90's, it still has that feel.It was nice seeing Matthew Modine in this show as well, I haven't seen him in so long I could hardly recognize him. Unknown to me Charlie Heaton plays a really strong role as well, he has a lot of talent. The three main child actors Finn Wolfhard, Caleb McLaughlin, Gaten Matarazzo bring to their roles such passion they make you feel like a kid again."Stranger Things" is a well rounded show, that has allowed forgotten actors from the past to breath new life into television again, with so many shows based on Zombies and Reality, it's nice to sink your teeth into something fun and mysterious such as this show. "Stranger Things" could go anywhere, and do anything the gates are wide open, and it's just amazing the talented writers in this world can still master the marvel of cinematography. I recommend this show to anyone above the age of ten. Some kids might find some scenes frightening, but all in all a definite winner.

author: drau-85780
title: 10/10 A series that made television history
content: Stranger Things is one of those rare shows that manages to captivate from the very first episode all the way to its finale. The story unfolds gradually and thoughtfully. At the beginning you know very little, which sparks curiosity, and with every episode and every season the world becomes clearer and deeper. This slow reveal is exactly what keeps you emotionally invested. The show is highly addictive in the best possible way, with a tension curve that remains strong and consistent over the years while continuously raising the stakes.The casting of the child characters deserves special praise. The choices are nearly perfect, and what truly sets the series apart is that every character goes through real development. Nothing feels static or forced. You grow with them, care about them, and genuinely root for them. Despite the long break between season four and season five and the fact that the actors naturally grew older, this was handled in a very smart and organic way. The final season feels mature, coherent, and deeply respectful of the story that came before it.From acting and directing to CGI, music, and thematic depth, everything works together seamlessly. The series also shines through its loving homage to 80s pop culture and especially to Dungeons and Dragons, which is woven into the narrative again and again. This adds an extra layer that fans of science fiction, fantasy, and nerd culture will especially appreciate. The ending, which is rare for a long running series, is truly successful. It is emotional, satisfying, partly closed yet open enough to linger, and feels like a genuine tribute to the early days of the show.Overall, Stranger Things is a clear 10 out of 10. Anyone willing to embrace science fiction, fantasy elements, and a slowly evolving but deeply engaging story will get exactly what they are hoping for. I can wholeheartedly recommend this series to anyone.

author: nahianalvy-82311
title: copy or not
content: People are saying that Stranger Things Season 5 feels heavily inspired by Apple TV's Invasion, and honestly, I can see why. The overall atmosphere, the global chaos, the mysterious alien-like threats, and the focus on multiple character groups surviving in a collapsing world all resemble elements from Invasion. Even the visual tone dark, grounded, and almost war-movie-like matches that show's style. And you know what? I'm actually totally fine with it. Inspiration isn't necessarily a bad thing, especially when it comes from a well-made sci-fi series.However, what I really expected from Season 5 was something more unique-something that felt like a natural evolution of Stranger Things rather than a shift toward another show's formula. Stranger Things originally stood out because of its nostalgic 80s vibe, its quirky teen adventures mixed with supernatural horror, and its emotional character moments centered around friendship. Seasons 1-3 had a charm that came from the balance of mystery, humor, and heart. Even Season 4, despite being darker, still had a strong identity of its own with Vecna's storyline and the intense psychological horror elements.Season 5 so far seems more militarized and apocalyptic, which isn't necessarily bad, but it does drift away from the classic formula. The Duffers clearly want to go big for the final chapter, and they're leaning more into large-scale world-ending stakes. But in that process, some fans feel like the show is losing the unique essence that made it special in the first place.To be fair, shows evolve, and inspirations from other sci-fi stories are normal. My only hope is that Stranger Things doesn't forget its roots. Even if the concept overlaps with Invasion, there's still plenty of room for originality-emotional payoffs, unexpected twists, deeper exploration of the Upside Down, and character-driven storytelling. As long as the finale delivers something memorable and distinct, I don't mind the similarities at all. In fact, I just want the ending to feel like Stranger Things-the show we've grown up with not just another sci-fi apocalypse scenario.

author: HotTakesAndMilkshakes
title: The Final Review With All Seasons Ranked
content: The show has ended, and it's time to give my piece of heart to it. Here are my final thoughts and the ranking of all seasons, from worst to best.Overall, the show was a thrill ride. It had enough charm to captivate anyone, and its characters were so likeable that even the less likable ones were understandable. The show had grand ideas, but in the first seasons, it held itself spectacularly by staying simple at its core. The characters sometimes led the show instead of the plot because they were just that interesting. Unfortunately, as I'll mention later, Season 5 completely missed that point.Stranger Things is accessible, memorable, and will be considered a classic by many, myself included. What the Duffer Brothers created here will be remembered for a long time. Even though it had noticeable issues at the end, it still concluded on a note that will charm me into rewatching it all over again.Seasons Ranking ( from worst to best )Season 5 - In my opinion, the worst season of Stranger Things. The characters we loved and cared about were sidelined, and the bigger-budget spectacle felt like the show's only concern. It lost much of its charm, especially because it focused on additional characters who took screen time away from the ones we already loved. The stakes were supposedly high, but the season never made us feel any real danger.The writing was noticeably weaker from the very first episode. Worst of all, this season undermines what came before, especially Season 4. Season 4 ended in a mesmerizing way, yet Season 5 continued on a completely different note, almost as if the plot was improvised on the fly. It was messy and lacked the courage to make the story more impactful.Season 2 - Not a bad season at all. I defend it, though it lacked some of the meaningful moments that other seasons delivered. I enjoy this season a lot because Noah showed incredible talent at a young age. The season was full of charm and comedic moments, while still giving us great character development and introducing new characters like Max and Billy. The newcomers were surprisingly well written and blended into the show seamlessly.Season 3 - This season had some of the funniest and most memorable moments of the entire series. It explored themes like growing up, love, and friendship that is dissapearing with time while keeping the main plot in focus. Everything worked perfectly from start to finish. The villain was somewhat forgettable, partly because Season 5 failed to provide meaningful answers about him. Nevertheless, Season 3 is the most quotable, and Dustin and Suzie singing remains a peak moment of the series.Season 4 - The most serious and scary season. It delivered a memorable and terrifying villain who kept us glued to the screen. Despite telling multiple stories across different locations, it tied everything together flawlessly. Our beloved characters had grown, but they were still charming and lovable. This season was the show's biggest spectacle, with high stakes and intense tension, yet its plot remained simple and effective. It felt like a perfect clockwork - precise, balanced, and complete without any unnecessary parts.Season 1 - This is the season that made it all happen. This whole season had a detective mystery vibe but they still managed to twist the story into something supernatural and made it work. The character especially children brought a never before seen charm on our screens. Writting of characters was the strongers part of this season especially when you compare this to season 5 but yet the plot with Eleven was done perfectly. I absolutely love the simplicity and effectivenes of this season.

author: belbagel
title: the end of beginning
content: This show means more to me than I can even put into words. Sometimes I genuinely find it unbelievable how much it means to me. No show will ever live up to this one. It is so incredibly creative, beautiful, different, and-most importantly-homely.I enjoy many, many shows, but this one will forever hold a unique and irreplaceable place in my heart. I grew up with this show. I grew up with the cast. Knowing that it's officially over truly hurts. I spent New Year's Day of 2026 grieving its end. For so many years, I loved, learned, grew, and followed this story. Now, it feels strange and painful to know there's no next season, no next volume, no next episode to wait for-to experience for the first time and be surprised by everything that unfolds in those hour-long (give or take) episodes.This show shaped who I became as a person. And how could it not? When you grow alongside something for so long, it inevitably influences you and becomes a part of who you are. I cherish this show deeply, and I hope that anyone who begins their journey with Stranger Things for the first time will love it just as much as I do.There are so many parts of this story to love and so many characters to hold close. In most shows, you might see pieces of yourself reflected in certain characters-but rarely your whole self. In this show, I truly believe everyone can find someone who makes them feel deeply seen, and that feeling is something incredibly special.The writing of this show is a true masterpiece, and the directing is just as exceptional. It feels unmatched. Upcoming artists may try to live up to what this show started as, what it became, and what it ultimately finished as-but this was something truly special. Something entirely its own. And that is what makes it so beautiful. It captures so much emotion and humanity. It was done with such care, and I will always remember and love it. I know I'll return to this show again and again-when I need comfort, when I miss a sense of home and family. I'll always find my way back to this story, to this home, to this family.I feel forever indebted to the Party, and I am endlessly proud of the cast and crew. If you haven't been introduced to this show yet, I can't recommend it enough. Start it. Experience it. Learn what it means to be part of this fandom-it truly is something extraordinary.P. S. Of course I had my theories, my hopes, and my wishes-but in the end, it never truly mattered how the show ended. I could never hate this story. What felt right was right. I'm just grateful that I got to be there with it, for all of it.And not to mention-the original music in this show is some of the best ever created. The emotions they capture in a single song, the weight and meaning it carries, is impeccable. And the licensed music is just as powerful. They know exactly when to use a song and how to let it speak. The music alone tells stories of its own.

author: LunNaria
title: A Strong Series Undermined by a Confusing and Underwhelming Finale
content: Stranger Things has earned its place as one of the most influential and emotionally engaging series of the last decade. Season 5, overall, delivers on atmosphere, performances and the weight of everything the characters have been through.Unfortunately, the final episode fails to live up to the legacy the show itself built. The confrontation with Vecna, the central villain of the entire series, feels surprisingly short and rushed. After seasons of buildup, his final role is overshadowed not by character driven resolution, but by the faceless "army" and the system behind it. While the idea of a larger evil is interesting, it ultimately diminishes Vecna's impact rather than enhancing it.Will's arc is another major disappointment. He is clearly established as having abilities and a deeper connection to the Upside Down, yet when it truly matters, those powers are barely and poorly utilized. For a character whose suffering has been foundational to the series, this feels like a missed opportunity.The most confusing element is Eleven's fate. Her death or possible survival, is left painfully unclear. The logic of how she could return to the Upside Down makes little sense, especially considering that she entered Hawkins with the others. If she is alive, Kali's projection raises even more questions, since the series strongly implies that Kali is dead. These inconsistencies aren't subtle mysteries, they feel like genuine plot holes.While the open ending is clearly intentional, allowing viewers to form their own interpretations, the problem is that none of the theories truly hold up. There are too many contradictions for any interpretation to feel satisfying or coherent. Mike's apparent acceptance that Eleven might be alive comes across as emotionally understandable, but narratively weak and unsupported by what we are shown.In the end, Stranger Things remains an excellent series, but the final episode feels less like a conclusion and more like an unfinished draft. Ambiguity can be powerful, but only when it is built on solid storytelling. Sadly, this finale leaves more confusion than meaning.

author: mustafaep
title: A Phenomenal Masterpiece - Stranger Things: A Perfect 10/10
content: Stranger Things is not just a TV show; it's a mesmerizing journey that completely captivates its audience from start to finish. With its perfect blend of nostalgia, thrilling storytelling, exceptional cinematography, and unforgettable characters, this show has undoubtedly become a cultural phenomenon.From the very first episode, Stranger Things sets a hauntingly amazing tone that keeps you on the edge of your seat. The excellent pacing and well-crafted plot effortlessly transport you to the enchanting yet eerie small town of Hawkins, Indiana, in the 1980s. The attention to detail is impeccable, flawlessly capturing the essence of the era and indulging viewers in a nostalgic experience.One of the show's greatest strengths lies in its characters. Each one is uniquely developed, and their individual journeys and relationships are brilliantly woven together. Eleven, played magnificently by Millie Bobby Brown, is a standout character whose emotional depth and supernatural abilities add an extraordinary dimension to the plot. Additionally, the talented ensemble cast comprising Winona Ryder, David Harbour, Finn Wolfhard, Gaten Matarazzo, Caleb McLaughlin, Noah Schnapp, and many others deliver performances that are nothing short of exceptional.The writing in Stranger Things is top-notch, filled with witty dialogue, heart-pounding suspense, and unexpected twists and turns. The Duffer Brothers, the masterminds behind the series, expertly balance moments of pure terror with heartwarming encounters, creating a rollercoaster of emotions that keep you hooked throughout every season.Visually, Stranger Things is a feast for the eyes. The beautiful cinematography adds another layer of depth to the show's already gripping narrative. The stunning imagery, coupled with an outstanding score that pays homage to 80s music and synth-filled soundtracks, elevates the viewing experience to new heights.Moreover, the production design and special effects are flawless, giving life to the parallel dimensions, terrifying creatures, and supernatural occurrences that form the core of Stranger Things' mystery-filled universe.Despite its fantastical elements, Stranger Things also delves deep into themes of friendship, family, and the power of human connection. The bonds formed between the characters are so genuine and heartfelt that you cannot help but become emotionally invested in their struggles and triumphs.In conclusion, Stranger Things shines as a television masterpiece that effortlessly captivates its viewers with its impeccable storytelling, exceptional performances, and nostalgic charm. With its flawless execution and homage to 80s culture, this show deserves nothing less than a solid 10 out of 10 rating. It is a must-watch for anyone seeking an unforgettable and thrilling television experience.

title: the show sank in quality
content: TLDR: Season 1 is almost perfect, Season 2 is also great, Season 3 is not as good but a very fun ride, Season 4 is overrated with high highs and lower lows.I love Stranger Things. It's a great season of television with likable characters, an interesting plot, solid writing with lots of heart, and it's very authentic to the 80s setting. It's a 10 in my book.I think Stranger Things 2 is an incredible follow up to the first season. It builds upon the first season well especially with Will's character, some of my favorite scenes in the show take place in this season, the upside down becomes a more dynamic location with new but alike creatures, it's a strong sequel with great new additions. I'd probably have to give it a 9 because of how great the first season is... I also think this season is overhated for doing interesting stuff with it's story and being different from it's predecessor.While Stranger Things 3 is in my opinion a welcome addition to the show, it is the least engaging part. Just about every aspect of the show besides certain characters is just not as good. My biggest gripe with the season is how they handle the 80s setting... in this season the nostalgia and 80s isms are dialed to 11, to the point where the show loses a lot of the authenticity that was cultivated in the first two seasons. Something this season has is it's comedy, though many characters will get pretty goofy for no real reason... it's entertaining if nothing else. I'd probably give this one a 7 just because this is kinda where the show fell off, it's still decently watchable.Now on to Stranger Things 4, my least favorite part of the show. This time around the highs are high and the lows are really darn low. It seems that to be up in arms about how this is the best season of the show and that it's so much better is an acceptable reaction to Stranger Things 4. I'm not saying this to be a lame-o contrarian but I couldn't disagree more. What the show did poorly before this season does repeatedly and horridly, we bounce around between storylines very frequently occasionally giving less than a minute of screen time to a less integral piece every cutaway, the writing is the worst it's ever been (super predictable and uninspired at points), the acting in the now late-teenage main cast is somehow worse than it was when they were like 12, and this season is just kind of blah. Like is said earlier the lows are low, but the highs my friends... the highs are very high. Vecna is a pretty cool villain (could've been scarier but I digress), Sadie Sink is phenomenal as Max, this season gets pretty horrific (I personally am proud that the show went there), and Eddie Munson is probably the best character that will ever grace Stranger Things as a series. Cant say I'm not worried that the finale will disappoint.

author: Ricardo-36
title: Reproduction of the past - mostly succeeds
content: "Stranger Things" is quite an anomaly in today's overly saturated market of media crap and thin drama - and a good one. The 80s are for children what the early 60s were for young men, the "decade du jour" of all things good and valuable: friendship, character building, fantasy, adventure, learning the facts and pains of life without overprotective parents and eyes constantly gazing at iPhones. It was also the high point of the second golden age of cinema, when George Lucas and Spielberg were kings and the highly emotional rollercoasters fun films were the norm - and special effects were meant to dazzle and tell a fantastic story, and not distract us.It's a particular sentiment of comprehensible nostalgia that has been attempted to be "captured" and "reproduced" before by J.J. Abrahams: "Super 8" comes to mind again and again when seeing "Stranger Things". It's like watching a craftsman building a vintage car from scratch: it's the same thing, and at the same time, it is most certainly not. All of the elements are there, complete with slowly fading credits with film scratch marks, but it's impossible to avoid seeing the modern touches of editing, lightning, CGI, and the eventual winks to the audience that this is a period piece (which is particularly painful for those, including myself, who have lived in that era)."Stranger Things" borrows from it all: apart from the obvious "Super 8", there's bits and pieces of "ET", "The Thing", "The Goonies", "Fire Starter", "Akira", and even some nuances of "Neon Genesis Evangelion's" Rei Ayanami on Eleven's speech and behavior. Sometimes it fails, being a "paint by the numbers" replication of those formulas, leaving plot holes and thin characterizations behind like a trail of bread crumbs leading you to what media produces today for the millennial audience unaccustomed with plot and emotion. On some times, it succeeds going beyond that level and portraying an engaging story that invites you to look beyond the clichés and enjoy this series for what it is.All in all, "Stranger Things" can be truly recommended, is a guilt pleasure of the most extraordinary kind, and rarely you will find a moment where, albeit flaws, you are not enjoying it.

From its synth-heavy soundtrack to the perfectly crafted small-town atmosphere, the series pulls you into a world where friendship, mystery, and supernatural danger collide.The young cast delivers performances far beyond their years, making the emotional moments hit just as hard as the jump scares. The Duffer Brothers weave a tight narrative where every subplot-from government conspiracies to teenage drama-feels essential. The balance between heartwarming character bonds and nail-biting suspense keeps you hooked from episode one.Its greatest strength lies in its ability to make you care-about every kid on their bikes, every parent trying to protect them, and every strange shadow creeping at the edge of the screen. With a perfect mix of horror, humor, and heartfelt moments, Stranger Things isn't just a show-it's an experience that stays with you long after you've left Hawkins.

Such a shame for a series that used to be a joy...but dragged out to make everyone lots of money at the expense of fans...an all too familiar plot line for shows that become popular these days.

author: TravelerTai
title: "Stranger Things": A Captivating and Nostalgic Masterpiece
content: "Stranger Things" has taken the world by storm, and for good reason. This Netflix original series is a true gem that combines elements of science fiction, horror, and coming-of-age drama in a seamless and engaging way.The story is set in the fictional town of Hawkins in the 1980s, a time when pop culture was booming and technology was on the cusp of a major transformation. The disappearance of a young boy, Will Byers, sets off a chain of events that leads his friends, including the determined Mike, the intelligent Dustin, and the tough Lucas, on a quest to find him. Along the way, they encounter a mysterious girl with telekinetic powers named Eleven, and together they uncover a dark government conspiracy and a terrifying alternate dimension known as the Upside Down.One of the show's greatest strengths is its characters. Each character is well-developed and has their own unique personality and backstory. The friendship between the kids is heartwarming and feels genuine, and the adults in the show, such as Chief Hopper and Joyce Byers, add depth and complexity to the story. The acting is top-notch across the board, with the young actors delivering performances that are far beyond their years. Millie Bobby Brown's portrayal of Eleven is particularly outstanding, bringing a sense of vulnerability and power to the character.The 1980s setting is also a major draw. The show is filled with references to 80s movies, music, and pop culture, which adds a layer of nostalgia for viewers who grew up during that era. From the iconic synthesizer music to the fashion and hairstyles, every detail is carefully crafted to transport the audience back in time.In addition, the special effects and cinematography are excellent. The Upside Down is a visually stunning and terrifying place, and the creatures that inhabit it are truly menacing. The show also knows how to build suspense and keep the audience on the edge of their seats, with plenty of jump scares and unexpected twists.Overall, "Stranger Things" is a must-watch series that has something for everyone. Whether you're a fan of science fiction, horror, or coming-of-age stories, you'll be hooked from the very first episode. It's a show that will make you laugh, cry, and scream, and it will leave you eagerly awaiting the next season.

author: OlieRendch
title: Really enjoyed the 80s vibe. Kids acting is incredible.
content: Stranger Things seems to have come out of nowhere, I had never heard of it right up until they released the trailer last month. So if you didn't know, Stranger Things is a Netflix original series created by The Duffer Brothers and is set in 1983 Indiana where a young boy goes missing in a small town where strange things are happening and an unusual girl shows up.So right away, this setting is genius. I never lived in the 80s but after this I really feel as though I was there, they didn't bang you over the head with it shoving pop culture references at you every minute but just how they dressed, their hair, the posters on a bedroom wall, it all seemed so natural and not gimmicky at all. The movie Super 8 did this to a certain degree and I enjoy that movie but Stranger Things seemed to make it more real to me. What added to it especially was the music, from the opening credits to the score itself, the use of synth music worked excellently to bring you this mysterious, fascinating and yet nostalgic atmosphere; so all-in-all they really did well with the setting and time-period and will definitely be checking out the soundtrack, all of which served as a brilliant backdrop to the plot.As I said, a kid goes missing; it's something we've seen many times in television and film but because it is such an urgent, fearful, disturbing event you are instantly following the case because you want to know what has happened and you want to see him back; so from the very first episode I was hooked and I was staying. Now the series is only eight episodes and I think that's a good thing; a lot of American shows have upwards of twenty and sometimes that can lose momentum and become very episodic, which works depending on the nature of the series, but I do enjoy a lot of British shows where they usually have between six and thirteen episodes negating the need for fillers and can concentrate on a good script. Here the Duffer Brothers have crafted a simple but very well written story that feels more like a movie; each episode follows on instantly from the previous with no recaps or 'Next Time' trailers so if you were to watch Stranger Things, a binge is required. The also know when to show things and when to not, they spent their budget wisely and paid wonderful homage to the Hollywood of that time giving you visuals reminding you of things like The Goonies and E.T. These callbacks also never detract from the plot and fit the story well; also despite the 80s adventure inspiration, Stranger Things isn't necessarily for the Spielberg audience with one or two darker moments scattered here and there.Now I can't do this review without mentioning the cast. Winona Ryder and David Harbour are really well cast as the adult leads, from the desperate mother who still holds out faith to the driven police chief taking on mysterious government agents. The rest of the cast are largely unknown including the main kids but they were so talented. Millie Bobby Brown and Finn Wolfhard being highlights having to display complex emotions and intelligent arcs. I wish I could mention all of the cast because they were so good, from Joe Keery as high school jock Steve to even the teacher Mr Clarke, each person had a life and character you were invested in.In the end Stranger Things is a really well made original series with some of the best cast, music and writing I've seen in awhile that also has some surprisingly good humour that made laugh out loud. I really hope the series gains traction because I can see the cast and crew going places, as well as a possible season 2.

author: lucasrodriens
title: Duality of Hawkins: How Stranger Things Captivated the World but Stumbled at the Finish Line
content: Stranger Things stands as a defining pop-culture phenomenon of the streaming era. Its genius initially lay in a masterful, heartfelt synthesis of 80s nostalgia, Spielbergian character dynamics, and a genuine undercurrent of cosmic horror. The first two seasons excelled at balancing intimate, small-town stories with a terrifying, expanding mythology. The core cast's chemistry was electric, making viewers deeply invest in the fates of Mike, Eleven, Dustin, Lucas, Will, and Max.However, the series' evolution reveals a critical duality. As the scale ballooned, the intimate horror and coherent world-building often gave way to blockbuster spectacle and narrative convenience. The later seasons, especially the final one, prioritized sprawling set-pieces and Marvel-esque quips over the atmospheric dread and character-driven logic that were its hallmarks. Beloved characters like Will Byers were sidelined, while complex villains like the Mind Flayer were reduced to generic, physical threats.The conclusion, while delivering emotional farewells and spectacular action, felt rushed and anticlimactic. It relied on convenient plot devices, ignored established rules of its own universe, and failed to satisfyingly resolve long-teased mysteries. Ultimately, Stranger Things is a testament to incredible initial execution and character building that struggled under the weight of its own mythos. It remains an iconic, deeply enjoyable ride, but one whose final destination feels less meticulously crafted than its captivating beginning.

author: SJerseyDevil
title: Original Nostalgic Masterpiece
content:
"Stranger Things" is a standout series for many reasons, blending nostalgia, compelling characters, and a thrilling storyline in a way that resonates with a broad audience.1. Nostalgic Appeal
One of the primary reasons I enjoy "Stranger Things" is its nostalgic homage to the 1980s. The show is a love letter to the decade's pop culture, referencing iconic films, music, and even the technological landscape of the time. This retro atmosphere creates a sense of familiarity and comfort, transporting viewers back to a time when things seemed simpler and more straightforward. The attention to detail in the set design, costumes, and soundtrack effectively evokes the era, making it a delightful experience for anyone who has a fondness for 80s culture.2. Engaging Storyline
The storyline of "Stranger Things" is both imaginative and gripping. It combines elements of science fiction, horror, and adventure in a way that keeps viewers on the edge of their seats. The central plot, involving the mysterious disappearance of a young boy and the subsequent discovery of a secret government experiment and a parallel dimension, is both intriguing and original. The show's ability to blend supernatural phenomena with everyday life creates a unique narrative that is both suspenseful and engaging.3. Well-Developed Characters
Another reason I like "Stranger Things" is its richly developed characters. Each character has a distinct personality and arc that adds depth to the story. Eleven, with her telekinetic powers and enigmatic background, is a particularly compelling figure. The show's ensemble cast, including Mike, Dustin, Lucas, and others, each bring their own charm and relatability, making it easy for viewers to become emotionally invested in their fates. The dynamics among these characters, from their friendships to their personal struggles, are portrayed with authenticity and nuance.4. Strong Sense of Community
The depiction of the small-town community in "Stranger Things" adds another layer of appeal. Hawkins, Indiana, is portrayed as a close-knit town where everyone knows each other, and the show's emphasis on community and camaraderie is heartwarming. This setting contrasts sharply with the more sinister elements of the plot, creating a compelling juxtaposition between the mundane and the extraordinary. The show's portrayal of the friendships and family bonds among the characters highlights the importance of support systems in facing challenges, making the story's stakes feel even higher.5. High-Quality Production Values
"Stranger Things" is also notable for its high production values. The special effects, cinematography, and sound design are all top-notch, contributing to the show's immersive experience. The visual style, including the use of practical effects and nostalgic references, enhances the storytelling and helps to create a vivid and convincing world. The atmospheric music and soundtracks further complement the series' tone, adding to the overall sense of suspense and excitement.6. Thought-Provoking Themes
The show also delves into thought-provoking themes, such as the nature of fear, the impact of trauma, and the resilience of the human spirit. The characters' personal journeys and the show's exploration of government secrecy and ethical dilemmas provide a deeper layer of meaning beyond the surface-level thrills. This thematic depth invites viewers to reflect on broader issues while enjoying the gripping narrative.7. Emotional Resonance
Finally, "Stranger Things" resonates on an emotional level. The show's ability to balance intense suspense with heartfelt moments ensures that it appeals not just to fans of horror and science fiction, but also to those who appreciate strong emotional storytelling. The relationships among the characters and their individual struggles add a layer of depth that makes the show's highs and lows feel more impactful.

author: AleshiaH
title: If you either grew up in, or simply love the 80's, then Netflix's Stranger Things is the show for you!
content: This series ticked all the boxes for me, and I can't praise it (or creative geniuses that are the Duffer brothers) highly enough. It's like they took everything you love about movies, TV shows, and books from the 1980's, mashed them all together, added their own origin spin on things, and came up with perfection. The setting is late 1983, and everything from the clothing right down to the toys, feels as if you are really watching something filmed back then – well except the picture and sound are 2016 quality thank god! Genre wise, it's pretty much a mix of everything – sci-fi, horror, supernatural, mystery, fantasy, romance, drama, coming-of-age, and comedy, meaning there's something in there for everyone to enjoy. I wouldn't class it as a family series, but I think that if your kids can make it through the Harry Potter movies without being terrified, then this show would be about the same level of scariness.The acting is flawless, particularly from the young cast. Because of this you instantly grow to love (and care about what happens to) all the characters, from the moment they appear on screen. As a long term fan of Winona Ryder, I had no doubt that she'd be fantastic, and she didn't disappoint. Both the soundtrack (Peter Gabriel, Toto, Foreigner, New Order, and The Clash to name a few), as well as the original musical score (think John Carpenter's Halloween) composed by Kyle Dixon and Michael Stein are superb.Think I'll go and watch it again. 10/10.

author: Falko_h1
title: A nostalgic journey with uneven execution
content: Certainly! Here's your review of "Stranger Things":"Stranger Things" Review: A Nostalgic Journey with Uneven Execution"Stranger Things," created by the Duffer Brothers, has garnered a significant fanbase with its blend of 1980s nostalgia, supernatural thrills, and compelling characters. Set in the fictional town of Hawkins, Indiana, the series begins with the mysterious disappearance of a young boy, Will Byers (Noah Schnapp), and the appearance of a girl with telekinetic abilities, Eleven (Millie Bobby Brown).The show excels in its recreation of the 1980s, with meticulous attention to detail in its set design, costumes, and cultural references. The young cast delivers strong performances, particularly Brown, whose portrayal of Eleven adds emotional depth to the story. The camaraderie among the core group of friends-Mike (Finn Wolfhard), Dustin (Gaten Matarazzo), and Lucas (Caleb McLaughlin)-is heartwarming and authentic.Despite its strengths, "Stranger Things" often relies heavily on nostalgia, which can sometimes overshadow the plot. The pacing can be uneven, with certain episodes feeling like filler rather than advancing the story. Additionally, while the show starts with a strong premise, some of the supernatural elements become repetitive and less impactful over time.The supporting characters, including the adults, have varying degrees of development, with some feeling underutilized. Winona Ryder as Joyce Byers brings intensity to her role, but other characters sometimes lack the same depth and nuance.Overall, "Stranger Things" offers an intriguing mix of mystery, horror, and nostalgia but struggles with consistency. Its initial charm and engaging cast are offset by uneven storytelling and over-reliance on retro appeal.

content: There's not much one can say about this series other than that it's made for true fans of this genre.
