The story is beautifully told and is entwined with themes of friendship, the importance of family, effects of loss, a mother's love and the drive of friends to live out their fantasies and adventures together. Apparently the Duffers brothers have an affinity for Stephen King and I loved the homages to his novels throughout – I almost felt like it could have been based on one of his books. author: midas-jacobs
title: "Should I stay or should I go now?"
content: When a young boy, Will, disappears things start to go wrong. A girl with superpowers appears and a whole crew of bad guys are trying to hunt her down. Who is she? Why are they hunting for her? But that's not all. A monster is there too. It is hunting... That's a bit of a synopsis of the story told in a very vague and short way, but I want to keep it interesting, so hey?The directing of "Stranger Things" was mostly done by the Duffer Brothers, as they are credited, AKA Matt Duffer and Ross Duffer. These two directed six episodes. They were really great. At first I didn't think that they could pull it of, directing with the two of them, but after seeing the pilot, I knew that they could. They made every shot look like a piece of art. But of course, this isn't only thanks to them, also thanks to the brilliant cinematographers. They were great at their job. There was only one shot that I think could've looked better and that was the one in the last episode where Hopper looks up with a bit of teary eyes. This shot just looked a bit of to me. I've praisen the Duffer Brothers, but they weren't my favorite directors of the show. This was Shawn Levy. He only directed two episodes, but he did them well. It was barely noticeable that there was a different director, but some of Levys camera movements were just fantastic. With this I don't mean that the Duffer Brothers didn't have some good camera movements. In the last three episodes they were also fantastic. The editing was handled masterfully, but with some flaws. Sometimes I could see a split-second of another shot, where-after the shot really changed. This I could see around two times in total. This doesn't take away the fact that the editing was great. There were some clever cuts in the second last and the last episode, switching between the perspective of Hopper and Wills mom and the kids. This was also very good, this kept you on the edge of your seat and both sides had different pacings which was very interesting. They were both tense full, but on another way. With the kids it was faster paced than with Hopper and Joyce.In contrast to the cgi. This was fine, but noticeable. Well, it was way better than some of the cgi I see in movies nowadays. I think that they could've made it more scary if they used props instead. I can understand why they didn't do that, though. For practical reasons. But let's not forget that this is still a TV-show - even though it looks like a movie most of the time and that's a compliment - and that it's common that TV-shows don't have great cgi. They did also use some great sets, the sets of the Upside Down world were good looking and had a 'scary' feel to them. The soundtrack was superb. I very much liked the songs, as you can see in the title of my review. I used a part that is song a lot in the movie. The songs fitted the theme quiet well.After this I usually discuss the actors, so let's stay in the trend, shall we? The series has a big cast, so I will select some people out of it. First of we have Winowa Ryder as Joyce or Wills mom. She was very good. She had some bad moments, but these flew away quickly. She showed of her emotional side throughout most of the show and at the end a more relaxed side. It was very cool to watch her switch between both. Mike was the leader of the group if I had to pick one. He was played by Finn Wolfhard. As a kid actor he was fantastic, so were the other kid actors (Millie Bobby Brown, Gaten Matarazzo, Caleb McLaughlin) I want to mention Millie in particular because she was the stand-out to me. She was really good. She played the character of Eleven. I also find it impressive that she shaved of her hair, that's very brave for such a young girl. Natalia Dyer played Nancy. She too was great. author: manuelsbento
title: Season 3 - Rating: A-
content: If you enjoy reading my Spoiler-Free reviews, please follow my blog :)Stranger Things first appeared in our lives back in 2016 with its phenomenal first season, followed by a less amazing yet still entertaining Season 2. I was pretty excited for the third adventure with one of the best (if not the best) young ensemble casts ever. The acting in this show is unbelievable, even more when considering the age of most of the kids (14-17). Millie Bobby Brown is 15-years-old! Fifteen! Weirdly, the show will only be eligible for next year's Emmy's, but if she doesn't get nominated AND win, I sincerely don't know what she needs to do more. The seamless ease that Millie has in showing emotion and delivering those subtle expressions that only the best actors can achieve after years of experience ... She's going to break the Oscar record for youngest Best Actress / Best Supporting Actress winner. It's meant to happen.I started with her because last season I handed the highlight crown to Noah Schnapp (Will Byers) who also gives an excellent performance, even if his character has less to do this time around (similar to the debut season). Of all the young actors, Millie is so much ahead of her fellow colleagues that she indirectly diminishes Sadie Sink's (Max) performance. They have completely different emotional responses to similarly painful events. Not that Sadie isn't able to transmit her feelings (I enjoyed both her and her character a lot more this season), but jumping from Eleven showing 200% of her emotion to any other character is always going to feel that the other actor/actress isn't at her level (truthfully though, they aren't).In addition to Millie, the other standout has to be David Harbour as Jim Hopper. This might be the funniest season so far, as well as the most emotionally powerful. Both are due to Hopper's arc and Harbour's award-worthy performance. He's hilarious, happy, sad, angry, drunk, frustrated, proud, ... His arc is definitely the one that serves as a pillar to this season's structure. Without him, this season wouldn't be near to the quality it is. Harbour's chemistry with Winona Ryder (Joyce Byers) is palpable, and that's basically enough for me to have a great time. However, The Duffer Brothers really deserve a lot of credit. The writing is some of the best I've seen in the last few years.Everyone hated Steve Harrington (Joe Keery) in the first season, but his development got such a fantastic treatment that now everyone loves him. The same happens with Billy Hargrove (Dacre Montgomery). I genuinely hated him last season due to how cliche and lazily written he was. Now, even though his backstory isn't anything innovative, he's undoubtedly seen as a more compelling character, which proves that Stranger Things really doesn't have a single bad character (main or supporting, at least). Max also gets a better script, plus her on-screen time with Eleven helped the character become more interesting. Nevertheless, how's the main gang?!Well, Gaten Matarazzo (Dustin Henderson) spends less time with his original friends, but his side adventure with Steve, Erica Sinclair (Priah Ferguson), and Robin Buckley (Maya Hawke), the newest addition to the show which is also the best surprise of the season, is also pretty entertaining even if it's connected to one of my issues (more on that soon). Mike Wheeler (Finn Wolfhard), Lucas Sinclair (Caleb McLaughlin), Will, Eleven, and Max have a whole romantic subplot that I surprisingly enjoyed mostly due to how realistic and heartfelt The Duffer Brothers wrote it. Obviously, comedy is always a must inside this group, and I wasn't disappointed, having dropped more than just a few laughs throughout the episodes.Finally, Charlie Heaton (Jonathan Byers) and Natalia Dyer (Nancy Wheeler) also have their own inspiring journey, the one that addresses the most how people had to live in the 80s. Dealing with discrimination, workplace injustices, and different lifestyles are put in perspective always through unforced dialogue and/or events. I really loved this season structure. How each group of characters has their own side adventure so that in the end, they can all team-up together to defeat the evil within Hawkins. I never felt bored or less engaged in a story. Season 2 had that horrible episode with Kali (Linnea Berthelson), and some episodes seemed to drag. Season 3 not only has the perfect runtime for each episode, but the story that they cover during each chapter is always remarkably captivating.Of course, I always felt more entertained when Eleven and Hopper were on-screen, so their subplots obviously became my favorites. However, they don't take anything away from the remaining stories or characters. Evidence number one would be the best ending of the show. It's hard to hold off the tears during those last few moments, especially if you went through the same event (which 99% of people definitely did unless you had literally zero friends growing up). Technically, the show proves that you don't need a big budget to provide visual delight. From the appropriated costume design to the addictive 80s' style soundtrack, everything is on-point with tons of practical effects being employed. The CGI regarding the monsters and everything that comes with them are convincing enough, and the action sequences are mostly shot well. The editing gets a little sloppy near the final episodes, but nothing too serious.My main and only issue with this season has to be the actual main plot. The thread that connects all of the subplots and groups of characters that I've been praising so much. Besides being very similar to the last season (monster comes, possesses people, and you know the rest), it's worse regarding the "how" and "why" the monsters came back. There's a whole story involving Russians, secret bases and codes, that feel too cheesy and over-the-top, reaching a level of absurdity that even affected some action scenes "a la Fast and Furious". It's unusual for the main plot to be as cliche and uninteresting as it is, while the side stories are astonishingly good.All in all, Stranger Things delivers yet another fantastic season. Its debut continues to hold the #1 spot, but Season 3 is so much better than its predecessor. Once again, the characters are what make this show a massive success. Even separating everyone into different groups, the cast's phenomenal chemistry remains intact. Millie Bobby Brown takes her crown back from Season 2's highlight, Noah Schnapp, and guarantees herself tons of nominations and hopefully a few awards, due to a perfect display of her emotional range. David Harbour is right behind her, and then comes the rest of the ensemble cast, one of the best to ever grace a TV screen. The Duffer Brothers are masterful screenwriters, presenting extremely developed character scripts, as well as funny, exciting and entertaining side stories. Despite a less strong main plot, Stranger Things finishes this season with the best ending of the entire series. If you're not crying during the last 10 minutes ... I don't know. Can't wait for Season 4, even if I would be more than satisfied to see it end its run now.

author: Tsetso_P
title: The site's AI summary is correct
content: I'll begin with the downsides. First, we waited nine years to get five seasons, and during that time, the cast grew up so much that the youthful spark from the early years disappeared. That would have been fine if they still looked remotely like teenagers, but they didn't. On top of that, the last two seasons easily could have been combined into one. And it's not that I didn't enjoy the show - it's brilliant! In this rare case, stretching out the ending for commercial reasons didn't ruin it, but it still felt unnecessarily prolonged. Then there's the other issue: being a Netflix production, it included characters' (rainbow) arcs that felt forced and unrelated to the core story. Robin was a great character, but her love story often felt inserted rather than organic. And by the second-to-last episode, with the world literally about to end, one of the main characters has a dramatic personal confession, a moment that felt completely out of place given the stakes. It just wasn't necessary, but box-checking. From what could have been a perfect 10, these choices bring it down to one or maybe two stars on that front. Now for the positives, and they're huge... "Stranger Things" is something almost impossible to replicate. The way it captured the aesthetics and atmosphere of the 1980s was extraordinary, and it sparked genuine nostalgia for so many people. The soundtrack is phenomenal, the acting consistently strong, and visually it's one of the most impressive shows I've ever seen. Even though I mentioned earlier that the story felt stretched, it remains incredibly creative and memorable. I'm honestly sad it's over. I'd love to see a short follow-up years from now, perhaps when the characters are adults, or maybe not - I'm not sure. What I do know is that this show stands as one of the best things ever put on screen.

author: itakethesquare
title: Nostalgic escapism!
content:
Netflix has a bad rep for making insanely one-sided content -- that also goes with it's "competitors" with a social commentary message or a re-imagining of home media from a by-gone era. This is one of the only (if only) originals that is any reminiscent of the good ole' days (I'll even put Cobra Kai up there, why not :D)The story is still going on, and it's always refreshing to see how the antagonist(s) are evolving while the protagonists are also evolving by becoming adults or adults with struggles becoming even stronger. What you'll get is a science-fiction, horror, drama, comedy, all mashed into one.(spoiler-free sypnosis)
During the late 70's, a young girl born into Big Pharma/Tech/Government blah blah is being studied for her strong telepathic abilites for reasons unknown and clashes with a group of misfit youths who have a bigger problem when one of them disappears out of thin air. That's it. That's all you need to know -- really.It's a giant time period piece filled with nods to the movies and tv shows that made us love the simpler times. There are homages to the greats like Stephen King, Wes Craven, Steven Spielberg and John Carpenter. Some may say it's fan-service but the Duffer Brothers wanted to explicitly make an original story surrounded by what we loved about PG movies that clearly should have been PG-13 or R (Goonies/Poltergeist) among other things such as how adult-like children were and the rise of heavy metal and Dungeons and Dragons.The film has no political commentary but will make fun of both sides in hints that it's all dumb. The actors look and convince that they were products of the time and is very convincing.Each season is a presented as a sequel to a movie (as sequels were like the baby boomers of media in the 80s), and each one the antagonist grows stronger and every character has a unique utility to out-smart it. Both the adult and youth characters are likable even when they are being butt-heads -- they all grow.Overall, must-watch entertainment especially during Halloween. It's a giant mix of horror and comedy and every scene has an easter egg to film/tv/bpoks during that era and even BEFORE. I'm not a fan of almost all media coming out today as it's heavily pandering to one-side of the aisle but this is heavily recommended. I didn't give it a 10/10 because it's Netflix and their policies are B. S.

title: "Dungeon and Dragons" anyone?
content: For a story where "anything goes" shoots off into the ether and beyond, there isn't a thing you do not understand or not follow for you are sucked into its other dimensional logic without you having to miss a beat. It is an incredible piece of storytelling especially when you assemble all five seasons together! As for the visual razzle dazzles and there are plenty, they are truly amazing to watch, but what is even more amazing is the drama. Especially in Season 5 where some of the moments are truly touching. Some are because of clever twists in writing to iconic expectations of those moments, but even when scenes are written as expected by conventional standards, it is the acting that elevates those familiar moments to something that is above and beyond cliché. The other reason that makes the characters so endearing is between 2016 and now, with 2016 being the launch date of season 1, in that interim, we see actors maturing as real people and with that as an infusion into the characters they played, it adds a dimension of realism and humanity to the show. Lastly, without getting ahead of myself with the hope and expectation of season 6, the ending and closure to season 5 is so well orchestrated, so well written, so well played, and so well edited that it becomes a moving piece of symphony. One that is dusted with a sprinkle of hope and positive values no less. So, while we wait, "Dungeon and Dragons" anyone?

title: Fulfills all the fantasies about a wonderful teenage years!
content: I think the definition of a good tv series is not how intricate the plot is or how profound the theme is. Instead, it is whether the series can give us a sense of immersion. When I was watching the show, I laughed when the kids laughed; I cried when the kids cried; I felt excited when the kids fought; I felt sorrow when the kids lost their partners. So, in terms of sense of immersion, Stranger Things definitely delivered. It reminds me of my own childhood, my own teenager years. Of course, my childhood was not as exciting and colorful as theirs. But that is why I love this series so much. When I was watching those lovely boys and girls, I feel like I was reliving my adolescent years. But this time, it is much more wonderful, just as theirs are. Friendships, loves, loving families, and all those excitements and adventures, these elements that I think a perfect childhood should have are all presented in the series. It shows me how my dreaming life could be like as a teenager. Actually, I kinda envy those children in the show. I hope I can give my future children a childhood like that as well(without the dangers of course).Looking forward to the next season, see you one year later!

title: Stranger Things - A Masterpiece of Storytelling and Character Evolution
content: As someone who's watched every single episode, I can confidently say Stranger Things is one of the best shows ever made. The evolution of the characters over the seasons has been incredible to watch - from kids riding bikes and playing Dungeons & Dragons to young adults facing terrifying, world-ending threats, the growth feels authentic and deeply emotional.Season 4, in particular, absolutely blew me away. It's honestly the best season of any show I've ever seen. The introduction of Vecna was terrifying in all the right ways - haunting, powerful, and yet his backstory was told with such depth and beauty. It's rare to see a villain written and portrayed so masterfully. The cast was phenomenal, as always, and every performance was spot-on.The balance between horror, sci-fi, and heartfelt moments is what makes Stranger Things so special. It's not just about monsters and alternate dimensions - it's about friendship, courage, and growing up in a world that keeps getting darker.I'm beyond excited (and a little nervous!) for the final season. It's going to be emotional saying goodbye to these characters, but if the past seasons are anything to go by, we're in for something truly unforgettable.

title: Step into the Enchanting '80s - "Stranger Things" Review: A Mesmerizing Supernatural Adventure!
content: Stranger Things is a mesmerizing TV series that effortlessly transports viewers to the enchanting world of the 80s. author: The_Right-Brained_Reviewer
title: A masterful blend of 80's Sci-fi and horror
content: If you're a fan of 80s sci-fi and horror flicks, then "Stranger Things" is the show for you. It's set in Hawkins, Indiana during the 80s and follows a group of young friends as they uncover supernatural mysteries that threaten their community. The production design, costumes, and music transport you back in time, and the special effects make the horror scenes even more intense. The entire cast delivers amazing performances, making it easy to empathize with their struggles and triumphs.The series pays homage to classic sci-fi and horror films from the 80s like "E. T. the Extra-Terrestrial," "Poltergeist," and "Alien," among others, while still creating its own fresh story and mythology.But it's not just a fun watch. "Stranger Things" tackles themes like friendship, loyalty, family, community, loss, and trauma, making it a well-rounded and captivating series.Overall, "Stranger Things" is a must-watch show that's got something for everyone. It definitely lives up to its hype, and I highly recommend watching it now!

author: DivyeshB-29
title: Stranger Things Review - A Gripping Mix of Nostalgia, Horror & Heart
content: Stranger Things, created by the Duffer Brothers, is more than just a sci-fi show - it's a cultural phenomenon. Set in the small town of Hawkins, Indiana, the series masterfully blends 1980s nostalgia, supernatural horror, and emotional storytelling.Plot & ThemesAt its core, Stranger Things is about friendship, growing up, and fighting the unknown. The plot kicks off with the disappearance of a young boy and the appearance of a mysterious girl with telekinetic powers. What follows is a suspense-filled journey involving secret government labs, terrifying creatures from the Upside Down, and deep emotional bonds between characters.CharactersThe cast is one of the show's biggest strengths:Millie Bobby Brown shines as Eleven, a girl with incredible powers and a haunting past.The group of kids - Mike, Dustin, Lucas, and Will - bring humor, heart, and realism.Winona Ryder gives a powerful performance as a desperate mother.And the beloved Jim Hopper adds gritty depth and emotional weight.Every character evolves - emotionally and psychologically - making their arcs compelling and memorable.Visuals & SoundThe show's visual effects and creature design are top-notch, especially considering its TV origin. The Upside Down is eerie and unforgettable. But what really sets the tone is the synth-heavy soundtrack, echoing the spirit of the '80s while building tension and mood perfectly.What Makes It SpecialWhat makes Stranger Things stand out is its balance between horror and heart. It's scary, yes - but also warm, emotional, and deeply human. It speaks to the fears of growing up, the power of friendship, and the idea that sometimes kids can be the bravest heroes of all.

author: fredcavalis
title: Amazing show. Final season let me down a bit.
content: Liked Stranger Things Season 5 overall, but if I have to be completely honest, I think I expected a little more from the final season, and that probably informed how I felt about it.There's still a lot to enjoy. The cast is great as always, especially Sadie Sink shines and some of the emotional moments really do hit. You can feel how much care went into giving these characters a proper goodbye, and there are scenes that genuinely feel special, especially if you've been with the show from the beginning.That said, I went in hoping to be completely blown away, and it just didn't fully get there for me. Some story choices felt a bit rushed, and a few moments that were clearly meant to feel huge didn't land as strongly as I expected.The season definitely has heart, and I respect what the creators were trying to do. I just wish the emotional payoff matched the level of anticipation that's been building for years. When something is this hyped, it's hard not to compare what you imagined with what you actually get.So overall, I did enjoy Season 5, and I'm glad I watched it. It's a solid ending to a great series - just not quite the unforgettable finale I was personally hoping for. Still recommend it, especially for longtime fans, but for me it ended up being more satisfying than spectacular.

author: Sir_William_Banana
title: One of the Best Series of All Time
content: Stranger Things is one of the best TV series ever made. Evaluating the script, acting, direction, production, and overall quality, the series excels in every aspect. The core of the story lies in the mystery and intrigue surrounding the characters, keeping viewers guessing and wondering what will happen next. This is combined with the unique theme of a seemingly ordinary town where extraordinary events occur, a philosophical theme of unrest within peace. The series skillfully incorporates historical satire and references to famous conspiracy theories, resulting in a Cold War-era setting of Hawkins that blends American life from the 1970s and 80s, the mysterious underground Hawkins Lab, the CIA's Deep State, and most importantly, the monsters from the Upside Down. It's a perfect blend of mystery and abnormality within a normal world.Another crucial strength is Stranger Things' employed technique, which I greatly admire: the three-part structure. The story is divided into three distinct screens, each featuring a different group of characters, which rotate throughout the episode. This keeps the series from becoming boring because the storyline is constantly exciting, and it distributes screen time equally among all the main characters. This makes viewers feel that every main character is important; their absence could immediately detract from the plot. This is a charm that makes viewers feel like they are journeying and growing alongside each character. The fact that every main character has a significant role gives them depth and a fascinating backstory, and also allows every actor to fully showcase their abilities through their roles.In the transitions between seasons, the director and production team demonstrate that the storyline was meticulously planned. This is evident in some scenes that appear in later seasons, where the child characters have grown up, with flashbacks to their childhood, indicating that scenes were filmed well in advance for multiple seasons. This is a testament to the excellence of the scriptwriting and storyboarding. While Stranger Things might have had slightly too long gaps between seasons in later seasons, creating a time gap between characters and actors, which reduces realism, this isn't a major drawback. The time gap isn't excessive, and the characters are still age-appropriately portrayed.The production quality of this series is top-notch. The visuals, lighting, sound, music, and art direction are all excellent. Everything fits perfectly into every scene, storyline, and situation, enhancing the fun and appeal of the show. Some of the artwork is even good enough to be used as real-life decorations, toys, or souvenirs. Stranger Things' production design not only adds to the fun but also creates memorable moments; for example, "Running Up That Hill" has become widely recognized as the series' theme song.This concludes my review of Stranger Things. In reality, the series has many more fascinating aspects and excellent storytelling techniques that I haven't included here; I encourage you to watch it for yourself. I highly recommend this series; it's a must-watch. If you have the free time, you should watch all five seasons. As a viewer who enjoys reviewing movies and TV shows, I rate Stranger Things as one of the best series of all time, and it deserves a 10-star rating. Thank you for reading to the end.

title: Diminishing returns
content: If I were to rate the series as a whole, from the point of view of someone who had binged it once it was all done, I am giving it 7/10.The first season is excellent. You are introduced to a character, recognizing an cliche archetype only for the character to surprise you by behaving in a way an actual person would, you know with emotions and motivations and not at all as you'd expect from a one note cardboard cutout. All in all, the first season is very strong.The rest? Eh... I don't think things ever get atrociously bad, but it really seems as if the plot wasn't really thought out and constructed beyond that first season so the screenwriters than try to keep adding stuff, keep piling lore on top and inevitably retcon some characters in the process. As the series progress, there is more and more lean on action, cheap horror and 80s nostalgia which sometimes works, sometimes doesn't. Whole plotlines seem pointless and forced, even if they can be entertaining (gulag). Overall, I think it is a fun series worth watching, but claiming it to be amongst the best shows ever might be a bit of an exaggeration.

author: PhoenixGod00
title: God Mode right here
content:
A love letter to the '80s. A masterclass in storytelling. A show that became a phenomenon.The Premise: Sci-Fi Meets Suburbia
Set in the fictional town of Hawkins, Indiana, Stranger Things starts with one simple event: a kid goes missing. But from that single thread unravels a web of government secrets, alternate dimensions, psychic powers, and a growing darkness that turns small-town Americana into something terrifyingly epic.It's The Goonies meets The X-Files with a splash of Stephen King-but with its own voice, its own rules, and a cast that made it legendary.The Core Four: Heart, Humor, and Hell
Mike, Dustin, Lucas, and Will are the emotional foundation of the show. Their friendship feels real-awkward, hilarious, loyal to the bone. They're just kids playing D&D one minute, then risking their lives the next. The show never treats them like side players. They are the story.Mike is the glue-loyal, intense, and brave.Dustin is the comic genius with a surprising amount of heart.Lucas brings the skepticism and the strength.Will is the spark-the quiet kid who endures the most, and keeps on surviving.Eleven: Iconic. Instantly.From her first appearance, El became a cultural icon. Shaved head. Bloody nose. Limited vocabulary. Limitless power. Her journey from lab experiment to found family is one of the strongest arcs in the series.Millie Bobby Brown owns this role. She doesn't just play a kid with powers-she plays a girl trying to find her place in a world that broke her. She's vulnerable, terrifying, innocent, and fierce. Every time she steps into a fight, you feel the ground shift.The Upside Down: Pure Nightmare Fuel
The alternate dimension-known only as the Upside Down-isn't just a cool concept. It's one of the best world-building devices in modern television. It's eerie, rotten, hauntingly beautiful, and always dangerous. It exists just beneath the surface of the normal world, which makes it feel possible-and that's what makes it scary.Each season introduces new threats-from Demogorgons to the Mind Flayer to Vecna-but the real horror is how close it always feels to creeping through the cracks of Hawkins.The Adults: Not Background Filler
Most shows push the adults to the side. Not this one.Hopper is the ultimate reluctant hero: broken, bruised, and willing to burn the world down for his people.Joyce Byers (Winona Ryder's best performance in decades) brings chaotic, anxious, desperate energy-because she knows something's wrong and refuses to be ignored.Steve Harrington went from jerk to legend, becoming the best babysitter in TV history.Nancy & Jonathan carry the journalistic fire-digging deeper while navigating real trauma.Every character evolves. No one is wasted. Even background players eventually get their moment.Tone & Style: A Balancing Act of Genre and Emotion
Stranger Things pulls off something most shows can't: it balances sci-fi horror with pure heart. You'll be laughing in one scene, crying in the next, and gripping your seat seconds later. It's paced with precision and scored like a synthwave fever dream. And the 1980s aesthetic? Authentic without being cheesy.From neon lights to mixtapes, arcades to walkie-talkies-everything feels right. The nostalgia isn't just surface-level. It's woven into the DNA of the show.Themes: Loss, Power, Friendship, and Growing Up
At its heart, Stranger Things is about loss-of childhood, of safety, of normalcy. But it's also about found family, about resistance, about finding strength even when you're terrified.Whether it's El learning what it means to be loved, Will coping with trauma, or Max facing impossible grief-every arc hits hard.Final Word
10 out of 10.Stranger Things isn't just great television. It's modern mythmaking.It captures what it means to grow up in a dangerous world-and to fight back with heart, loyalty, and power you didn't know you had.This show didn't just bring the '80s back.It made us believe again.

author: therealsmooi
title: Nostalgia Meets Supernatural Thrills.
content: Stranger Things is more than just a sci-fi horror series it's a love letter to the 1980s, blending nostalgia, heart, and supernatural mystery into one of Netflix's most iconic originals. Set in the fictional town of Hawkins, Indiana, the show kicks off with the disappearance of young Will Byers, unraveling a chilling tale of government experiments, parallel dimensions, and a girl with extraordinary powers known only as Eleven.The series excels at world-building. The Upside Down is terrifying yet fascinating, a shadow version of Hawkins filled with grotesque creatures like the Demogorgon and later the Mind Flayer. The pacing skillfully balances suspenseful horror with heartfelt character moments, ensuring it never leans too heavily on jump scares.What makes Stranger Things unforgettable is its cast. Millie Bobby Brown delivers a breakout performance as Eleven, capturing innocence, trauma, and strength all at once. The kids Finn Wolfhard, Gaten Matarazzo, Caleb McLaughlin, and Noah Schnapp bring authenticity and charm, evoking the spirit of classic Spielberg adventure films. The adults, particularly Winona Ryder as Joyce Byers and David Harbour as Chief Hopper, ground the story with emotional depth and grit.Nostalgia plays a major role, from retro arcade games and Dungeons & Dragons references to a synth-heavy soundtrack that sets the perfect mood. Yet the show never feels like it's pandering it uses its '80s setting to enhance storytelling rather than just as decoration.Across its seasons, Stranger Things grows in scale without losing sight of its core themes: friendship, loyalty, sacrifice, and the fight against darkness, both literal and metaphorical. Even when the plot stretches into bigger battles, the emotional connections keep it anchored.At once thrilling, heartfelt, and nostalgic, Stranger Things is a rare blend of blockbuster spectacle and character-driven storytelling.

author: ntandoyenkosisibanda
title: Great
content: Stranger Things is a mesmerizing and nostalgic sci-fi horror series that pays homage to the classics of the 80s while still managing to feel fresh and original. The show's creators, the Duffer Brothers, have woven a complex and engaging narrative that masterfully balances elements of mystery, suspense, and coming-of-age drama.From the opening scenes, it's clear that Stranger Things is something special. The show's atmosphere is perfectly captured, with a blend of nostalgia and unease that's both captivating and unsettling. The show's setting, a small Indiana town in the 1980s, is meticulously recreated, with attention to detail that's impressive and immersive.The cast of characters is equally impressive, with a talented group of young actors who bring depth and authenticity to their roles. The show's adult cast is equally impressive, with standout performances that add gravity and complexity to the narrative.One of the standout elements of Stranger Things is its masterful pacing. The show's creators have a keen sense of how to build tension and suspense, expertly ratcheting up the stakes as the series unfolds. The show's use of music and sound effects is equally impressive, adding to the overall atmosphere and sense of unease.Throughout the series, the Duffer Brothers demonstrate a keen sense of storytelling, expertly weaving together multiple plot threads and character arcs. The show's themes of friendship, loyalty, and the power of childhood imagination are timeless and universal, making Stranger Things a show that will resonate with audiences of all ages.Visually, the show is stunning, with a blend of practical and CGI effects that's both impressive and convincing. The show's cinematography is equally impressive, capturing the mood and atmosphere of each scene with precision and skill.Overall, Stranger Things is a must-watch for fans of sci-fi, horror, and coming-of-age drama. With its engaging narrative, memorable characters, and nostalgic charm, it's a show that will captivate and entertain audiences of all ages. If you're looking for a show that will transport you to another time and place, look no further than Stranger Things.The show's creators have done an exceptional job of crafting a narrative that's both nostalgic and original, paying homage to the classics of the 80s while still managing to feel fresh and exciting. With its talented cast, impressive visuals, and masterful pacing, Stranger Things is a show that will leave you eagerly anticipating the next episode.

author: cody_chau-37552
title: Binge-watch worthy first season
content: With only 8 episodes in the first season, this show will certainly not keep you busy for a long time. But after watching it, you will not be disappointed as this wild adventure will keep you guessing and asking for more throughout all 8 episodes. The pace at which the story reveals itself is great, giving almost every character their moment to shine with just the correct length of screen time. This allows the story to flow very well with little to no fillers. It was interesting to see a mashup of character personalities and how they blend together in the show. Since there were distinct focuses on three separate groups of people (the children, young teens, and adults), people from all generations can relate to and find pleasure watching the show. One of the key components that make this a great show is the use of manipulation. As the story-line progresses, there are multiple moments of loud crackles of sound and lights flickering on and off. The sound and lighting manipulations are what drive suspense and thrills that got me hooked on. Furthermore, I also think the method used to reveal the antagonist is clever. The antagonist is revealed a little more, during every encounter, in every subsequent episode. This made me look forward to watching the remaining episodes even more. In addition, the overall feel and atmosphere of the show is very nostalgic. Many similarities from the X-files, E.T, and the Goonies can be found in Stranger Things which makes this series all the more magnificent. I came across Stranger Things and decided to give it a watch due to the mysterious synopsis. Since Netflix released all 8 episode at once, I was able to binge-watch the entire first season. I am sure this dark and mysterious story will give most people massive excitement in all 8 episodes. I hope the second season is just as good, if not better, because the season ends with an unexpected cliffhanger. As this is my first review, I cannot be certain what qualities a television show must exhibit in order to receive a high rating but personally, I think Stranger Things definitely deserves a 9/10.

author: iNickR
title: TV's Golden Age: Still Going
content:
I'll admit it took me until episode three of the first season to get into this show, 
but after that I gorged on it whenever I had the time. There's not much that I can say about Stranger Things that hasn't already been said. I watch a lot of TV and a lot of movies; and being a crew member in the industry for more than a quarter century I've seen both sides have good and bad years. The accolades and awards are well deserved for Netflix and the performers and artists of Stranger Things. This is TV's "Golden Age" and I'm glad to be a part of it - even if only as a loyal viewer. Stranger Things is one of the better shows on TV today...and that list is getting bigger (I encourage readers to check out some "Nordic Noir" for more exceptional TV).I will echo the words of those who spoke about the 80's nostalgia. Coming of age during the 1980's, I could relate to a lot of the more personal situations our protagonists were dealing with; relationships, school, bullies...I think most of us geeks out there had some flashbacks while watching....both good and bad.There are so many references and little inside jokes and homages throughout the first two seasons it's worth re-watching the entire series just to look for things in the background; or to listen really close to some of the dialogue. You may be pleasantly surprised at what you missed.Brilliant writing, well researched and thought-out production design, and acting worthy of an encore of one, perhaps two more seasons.

And this is just so good. The innocent, yet hard-reality, dark fringe of a story with beautifully done dichotomy of a warm familiar setting segueing into bizarre no-man's-land.Season 2
Is like Matrix 4, if the now-sisters continued that downward slope into cashing out on their franchise. The whole season 2 could have been done in the first 15 minutes of one episode of a spin-off. And even that shouldn't have been. If you are a tasteful fan of classic sci-fi's, and haven't seen the second season, you may want to skip this season all together. I cannot not see this failure now.

title: An amazing homage to '80s Steven Spielberg movies
content: I'm sure by now everyone knows about this show, so instead of writing the same stuff you've probably read already, I just want to focus on three things: 1. Yes, they did manage to give it an awesome '80s vibe, from the opening sequence to the end credits. Having grown up with these movies myself, I can attest to that. However, I think it will appeal to younger audiences as well. After all, there must be reasons that movies such as "The Goonies" and "E.T." remain memorable even now, other than the "'80s vibe". 2. The creators of the show (the Duffer brothers) have somewhat regretted having Winona Ryder's character acting so hysterically from the start. I disagree with that. That's EXACTLY how a real person would act if *spoiler* happened to her. I hate it when in most movies e.g. the hero loses someone very close to them, then they cry for a brief moment and then it's back to the action. That's ridiculous. 3. I liked how they gradually revealed pieces of the puzzle in every episode. No matter how clever your plot twist/secret is, if the building up period exceeds a certain point, then you'll have created too high expectations and it will be impossible to impress your viewers after that. I'm afraid that this will be a one off deal. I'm sure that the incredible success of the first season will lead to a second one, but given the plot and the ending, I doubt they'll be able to keep it to as high a level. In my honest opinion, the best case scenario would be if they wrote a similar story with a similar setting and maybe even have the same actors play different roles. I really, really wish they'll prove me wrong, but I'm afraid that a direct sequel is doomed to fail. Especially since this was supposed to be a one season show and they only discuss about making a second one because of all its unexpected success.

author: ellinaumburg
title: Wow..
content: Let me just start off by saying Stranger Things is such an amazing series. I love the story, and I love the characters. The storytelling in this show is phenomenal. That being said I believe this show is for a more mature audience. As a Christian, I think this show is a bit controversial because of its themes, sometimes death is inevitable in a show or a movie, it's life after all. However, there is a lot of gore in Season 4, more than I would like there to be. This is really the only turn off I can see for not watching it. The other seasons are amazing and showcase a little bit of gore compared to what we have here in Season four. There is a lot of swearing so just watch out for that. Many people believe that this show is Demonic, but if you look at it closely you'll understand it really isn't. There are a few scenes in season 4 with them being lifted up into the sky and their bones breaking and bending in unnatural ways. Stranger things has never had any spiritistic stuff in it (no demons, ghosts, evil spirits, etc.). All of it is based off of mystery, that is true. However it has a sci-fi rating for a reason, if it wanted to convey a more spiritistic, or demonic presence it would've landed the "fantasy" genre instead of Sci-fi. I feel like the mysterious vibe from it may bring off "unsettling vibes" but that is just, well the mystery aspect of it. Many people are scared of the unknown, so they tend to jump to conclusions about something before getting to fully understand it better. Similarly with Stranger Things, I believe it is a great show, but I believe children need to have a glimpse of maturity before even thinking about watching this show. It has suggestive themes in it and it may not be everyone's cup of tea. As for sex, there are only two scenes that have implied the characters having sex in Season1 and in Season 2, so there really is not a lot of Immorality (For those Christian parents out there wondering). As for drugs or smoking, season 1 Joyce buys a lot of cigarettes, but we only have a handful of scenes of her actually using them (not justifying it but she is a mother under a lot of stress). In season 4 there are brief mentions (Like 2 or 3) of either drug users or the drug itself. When it comes to drinking, there is only one scene in Season 1 where the teenager characters pop open a few beers, other than that there really is no drinking. In conclusion, I believe this show has it's issues (not one single show in this world is perfect), However It has beautiful story telling and an awesome plot that keeps you guessing, and makes your heart pounding, wondering for more answers about the never ending questions given. The characters are unique and amazing, and I believe it conveys a really good message about family and friendship, as well as "turning a new leaf" for a few characters. As a Christian, I believe this show can be viewed in moderation with maybe a few additives to make it more "friendly" to people. You can skip some of the scarier scenes (most of them don't reveal a lot about the plot). Try skipping some of the more gorier or suggestive scenes (again most don't reveal a lot about what is happening) to avoid feeling that "evil vibe". Lastly, just understand that just because a show may convey something, try not to jump to conclusions; If you're really bothered by it I would say wait a bit and ask friends/family members who have seen it to give you a better understanding, and Always look at the genre of a series before getting into it, otherwise you may be disappointed by the outcome of it. Stranger things is marked as a Sci-fi; Horror show. So it will have those elements in it. Something can be "horror" and scary but not be demonic. And Vice Versa. Last extra thing I kind of wanted to say is that there is something cool about this show. Not just talking about the 80's aesthetic, I mean how it brings people together, I've watched these kids (not-so-kids anymore) grow up on the screen. And It's amazing to feel somewhat apart of that. And the characters in this show are probably the biggest role models ever. I've really gotten to know myself in this show. Mostly because of Robin and Nancy, Robin showed me that it's okay to be myself. No matter my sexuality. And Nancy taught me to never give up. I'm forever grateful for this show.

author: Strombolii
title: Phenomenal in almost every aspect
content: This shows is one of those must-watch series that doesnt outstay its welcome. Although some of the seasons might seem linked together loosely/connected on the fly, it absolutely works.The sound design, the visual aesthetic, and the level of care given to fleshing out nearly every single character while driving an interesting and packed out story is all top level. Some characters suffer in later seasons as the ensemble grows, and there are one too many love sub plots with the Power of Friendship being extremely front and centre, but they do it well.Rewatchabaility is high, and the number of times you cry wont be low. Its gripping, its intense, it represents alternative kids, geeky kids, metal kids. It has organic representation, unlikely friendships, and great touches of fan service. The actors and cast are all phenomenal, and the sound design, again, is just so strong and original.It perhaps could take a few more risks, and it really suffered when that one filler episode came, but those are blips in the overall very strong storytelling. For other pop cultural comparisons, it is certainly blowing modern era Star Wars out of the water, and is certainly hitting consistently higher highs than Marvel. Many more emotionally driven moments, much more solid and labour-of-love writing, and although the budget is evidently lower, the visual effects rival those of any show you could name.A must watch, a true homage to horror and the 80s. Dont be fooled into thinking this is a kids show, this is the biggest, most well rounded and culturally impactful show since Breaking Bad and Game of Thrones (before it went downhill). I would expect to see this shoe honoured and homages for decades to come.

author: view_and_review
title: Needs Less Drama
content: There were some very nice aspects of Stranger Things. Personally, I was watching it for the sci-fi angle. It was more of an X-Files/Goonies/Beverly Hills 90210. The X-Files/Firestarter likeness was cool. Even the Goonies/E.T. type style was OK. The Beverly Hills 90210 teenage drama was sickening. I don't care who likes who, who's sleeping with who or who a sweet young girl is going to lose her virginity to. That very unnecessary aspect of the show very nearly ruined it.Well, that and Winona Ryder--she was awful. I couldn't take the show seriously whenever they put her exaggerated mug on the screen. Goodness, she was such a caricature. I didn't know if she was going for comedy, crazy or an Oscar. She greatly overplayed the distressed-I'm-not-crazy mother role. She was terrible.Strip away the teen love component and Winona Ryder then this was a solid sci-fi series. It's 1983 and a young kid named Will Byers (Noah Schnapp) goes missing. The mom, Joyce Byers (Winona Ryder) is convinced that he's alive and nearby. Coupled with that strange disappearance a young girl named Eleven (Millie Bobby Brown) shows up and is able to do some real Professor X-type stuff.The show centers around four distinct characters: Mike Wheeler (Finn Wolfhard), young nerd and leader of his pack. Joyce Byers, distressed mother. Jim Hopper (David Harbour), town sheriff and relentless searcher. Nancy Wheeler (Natalia Dyer), confused teenager in love looking for her friend. As I stated before; two of the characters' stories I couldn't care less about and the other two were the meat and potatoes for me. More bizarre happenings and less soap opera drama and it is a lot better show.

author: blackknight-51234
title: Things of diminishing returns
content: The early seasons are good. Different, innovative and genuinely entertaining. Good characters, good story, lots to like.Sadly, the further it ran, the more the quality declined.Firstly, there are far too many characters. The writers appear to have lost the courage or ability to kill characters off, meaning there are far too many of them with nothing to do.The gaps between seasons are far too long. Not only does this mean that you start seasons struggling to remember where you left off, but because of the sheer size of the cast, who everyone is. For final season, they add even more.Furthermore, everyone has aged out. None of the original cast resemble anything approaching school age. Most look like the full blown adults they are.The bad guy feels like he's been shoe horned in as an afterthought and really isn't that interesting.The physics make no sense. The monsters are impervious to bullets but get stopped in their tracks by a mother with a wine bottle.In the final season, everyone outside the main characters seems oblivious to what is going on. The town is closed off by the military under martial law, yet everyone carries on as if everything is fine.Lastly, I'm not sure why we need drawn out scenes regarding characters sexuality. They're exploring a parallel universe, I have zero interest in the sexual preferences of any of the characters. It's not "stunning" or "brave", it's predictable, dull and frankly ruins the suspension of disbelief. It's on a par with when a King Edward potato proclaimed that she was "going to be a Dad" in the Last of Us.It's a shame, this could have been a classic for the ages, instead, it went the same way as Game of Thrones.

author: Its-Arzan
title: A Goodbye That Feels Like Growing Up
content: Watching the end of Stranger Things felt less like completing a TV series and more like bidding farewell to a chapter of my own life.I began this journey years ago, during a time when life was simpler - when friendships were effortless, summers seemed endless, and the future didn't feel so burdensome. As the story progressed, the kids on screen matured... and so did I. That's the enchantment that Stranger Things achieved better than nearly any other show I've encountered.Season 1 was ICONIC, a burst of pure magic - mysterious, personal, and unforgettable. I will start crying in memories if I start a rewatch.Season 3 was pure NOSTLAGIC, captured nostalgia so exquisitely that it's painful to revisit now.Season 4 was PERFECT, demonstrated that the show could still aspire to greatness and actually achieve it.While the final season may not be flawless, it grasps something far more significant than mere shock value: it honors the memories. It doesn't attempt to dismantle everything. Instead, it allows you to linger with the characters, the moments, the music, and the realization that an era is coming to a close.This series wasn't solely about monsters or the Upside Down. It revolved around friendship, fear, love, and the journey of growing up - about cherishing childhood while recognizing that you can't remain there forever.As the credits rolled, I didn't feel anger or disappointment.I felt a sense of calm. Thankful. A bit hollow.And to be honest? That's precisely how goodbyes should feel.Thank you, Stranger Things.

author: TxMike
title: Netflix 8-episodes totaling roughly 6 hours, townsfolk dealing with the "upside down" world.
content: My wife and I watched this on Netflix streaming over 4 different viewing sessions, one or two episodes each time. Overall it is very entertaining although I don't share the lofty (9.2) IMDb rating.Set in the 1980s it appears to be inspired by "The Montauk Project: Experiments in Time" by Preston B. Nichols and Peter Moon, regarding supposed time travel experiments at the Montauk Air Force Base at the eastern tip of Long Island as part of the Montauk Project. A "time tunnel" was created and alien monsters traveled through it to menace the locals.Here Winona Ryder is Joyce Byers, single mother of two sons, one about 17 and the other about 11. A strange girl (Millie Bobby Brown as Eleven) shows up and the 4 young boys who are close friends take her in and hide her. It is clear that she is different and we find she has escaped from the top-secret experimental lab. She also has extra-normal powers.David Harbour is good as the local police chief Jim Hopper. He is instrumental in helping uncover all the secret activity and find Joyce's missing son.The movie contains lots of paranormal activity. When her son goes missing, we find into what they referred to as the "upside down world", Joyce is able to communicate with him through light flickers, even though she doesn't know where he is. He is actually very close to her but they can't see or hear each other directly.The ending sets it up for a continuation.Update September 2019: We dropped our Netflix subscription, I object to the heavy emphasis they put on what I consider "trashy" programming. So I was able to get season #2 on BluRay from my local library. My wife and I watched the first 3 episode and just weren't motivated to keep watching more. Not that it isn't good, for the right audience, we just no longer felt it was worth our attention and time, compared to all the other things we might want to watch. To us there was neither an interesting storyline or interesting characters to draw us in.Update DEC 2025: Billed now as the final season, and back with a NFLX subscription, I began to watch the first episode but didn't finish it. The characters and stories have changed so much over the years that I was not able to get invested in it.

author: JayWolfgramm
title: The Last of a Kind
content: "Stranger Things" was an event. Back when it premiered on Netflix 10 years ago, it dominated all the water cooler conversations. At Comic Con, everyone had a box of Eggo Waffles, a hospital gown and a bloody nose. The series then took over 10 years to release all its episodes. The series had gone through writers' strikes, actor strikes and a global pandemic.With all of those delays, there are some natural consequences that follow. The child actors age out of their roles, and a lot of the story feels disjointed.Season 1 feels like a Stephen King meets E. T. style horror.Season 2 takes the "Aliens" style sequel, focusing more on action instead of horror.Season 3... is its weakest season.Season 4 brings things back, creating a central focus and a big bad main villain to defeat.And Season 5 follows up on Season 4 and ties things up as if they had the whole thing planned out.It goes from a simple missing child story to a world ending threat story. author: SquigglyCrunch
title: Good Enough to Keep Me Interested, but Still Massively Flawed
content: Stranger Things follows a group of people within a small town who go looking for a young boy who has gone missing and ultimately realize that there's more to the mystery then they initially thought.Some of the mystery elements were pretty good, and I watched the first season because I was curious and mostly interested. It had it's moments of cool stuff, but that was maybe once every second episode.The show advertises itself as a horror, yet it fails to be scary. There was not a single moment at any point during season one did I feel even slightly unsettled or scared. It's more of a sci-mystery, but even then it's not that good. It lacks a substantial amount of originality, from the design of the monster to the presentation of the plot. Nothing about this show is special.Another thing is just the amount of flaws in the show. There were multiple points where I had several questions about how certain things happened. For example, at one point two characters are in the forest together. Let's call them 1 and 2 to avoid confusion. 1 finds something almost as soon as they get into the forest and calls out to 2, but he's nowhere in sight. So what, did 2 just sprint off in one direction? Did he put in earbuds and start listening to some heavy metal or something? Did he leave the forest? Then, 1 goes off somewhere on her own, 2 magically returns, not out of breath or anything (so he clearly didn't sprint off somewhere) and not wearing earbuds either, and he can suddenly hear 1 from a place totally opposite the forest. Again, no spoilers, but somehow 2 hears 1 from that place. And even if you try to argue that 2 has bad hearing, in an earlier episode he hears a scream loud and clear from the other side of that very same forest. It just doesn't make sense. Some of you will call this a nitpick, but it stood out so blatantly to me that I couldn't help but address it. And besides, I can only ignore so many nitpicks before it becomes a problem and I have to start docking points.The acting, please kill me, is awful. The children are horrendous. They're expressionless, character-less actors who have no talent. At one point two characters are arguing and one kid looks like he's about to fall asleep as he yells at the other character. That, or he's stoned out of his mind. Sure, he's underage, but that doesn't seem to stop kids. On top of that, Winona Ryder attempts to pull off the insane mother role, and it's clear that she's trying to be great, but she's not. I don't think Winona Ryder isn't talented, but she didn't pull off the performance she seemed to be trying to. Everyone else was pretty flat too, at least if they were important they were.The characters these actors portray are even worse. They're unbelievably flat and boring. Each one can easily be described in a single sentence.The show tries to make it look like it came out in the 80s, but its gets to be annoying with how hard it tries. It shoves all this 80s crap into every scene, and it feels like the Duffer Brothers are ramming all their 80s computers down our throats and movie posters up our butts. I think the conversation the Duffers had before the show was in their attic, surrounded by the stuff of their youth, and started like this: "Hey bro, what should we do with all this stuff from the 80s?" "Let's make a TV show" "Oh yeah, that's a great idea. But how will we get someone to produce it?" "Oh, we can just get Netflix to do it. They'll eat up anything, so long as they can make a couple bucks. Quantity over quality, like they always say" Furthermore, the 80s thing sacrifices a level of quality even. The first thing was a personal issue, not an actual flaw really. This is though. The CGI is awful. Painful even. Now I know, "It's trying to look like it was made in the 80s" but I don't care. The show proves that it knows what practical effects are, and whenever it decides to use those it looks great. But I can think of only a handful of times where it actually did that. So why didn't it use practical effects all the time? I don't know. It's stupid, though, that's for sure.And the writing, oh boy. It ranged from okay to awful to flat out not making sense. And what's funny is that I think some of the actors knew that, specifically the main child actor. His delivery was so bad sometimes I wondered if it was on purpose. Like he knew that the writing was awful and was pushing the limits as much as he could to see how poorly he could act without the director noticing. Just for fun, I guess.One more big flaw: the soundtrack. It switches between this repetitive, boring, and frankly annoying sound/noise and ill-suited songs. Seriously, none of the songs have any place in the show. At least not at the points they were used.Overall Stranger Things sucks. Yet like I said, it was, for the most part, good enough to keep me watching it until the end. Will I watch the other seasons if there are more? Not a chance. At gun point, maybe. But not of my own free will. I don't get why people love this show so much, but if you do then go right ahead. Obviously I'm either missing something or I'm just not as easily impressed as most people or something. I don't know, but I don't really care. In the end I would not recommend this show.

author: alekspredator87
title: The Frightening World of the Duffer Brothers
content: "Stranger Things" created by the Duffer brothers, has become a real phenomenon in the world of television. This series, which combines elements of science fiction, horror and nostalgia for the 1980s, has captured the hearts of millions of viewers around the world. Since its release, it has consistently pleased not only with exciting plots and atmosphere, but also with excellent acting.One of the key reasons for the success of the series is the play of young talented actors. Finn Wolfhard (Mike), Millie Bobby Brown (Eleven), Gaiten Matarazzo (Dustin), Caleb McLaughlin (Lucas), Sadie Sink (Max) and Noah Schnapp (Will) and many others demonstrate impressive depth and naturalness in their roles. Their characters are full of life and energy, and the chemistry between the actors makes each scene authentic and emotional. Watching the intertwining destinies of teenagers and their ability to be real friends, you remember how important all this is for children of transitional age. After all, it is then that they find real friends, support in life, those with whom people carry friendship through their whole lives. And looking back, as adults, people smile, remembering what a bright friendship there was in their childhood.It is worth noting Millie Bobby Brown, whose game conveys all the difficulties and vulnerability of the character Eleven, a girl with incredible abilities. The actress does an excellent job of showing the inner struggle and the gradual maturation of her character."Stranger Things" is often compared to the works of Stephen King, and for good reason. The series skillfully conveys the atmosphere of mystical events and explores the themes of friendship, fear and growing up, similar to such classic works by King as, for example, "It". The young heroes, faced with incomprehensible and frightening phenomena, resemble the heroes of King's stories about teenagers who, despite their young age, are forced to fight evil and protect their loved ones. This comparison highlights the skill of the creators of the series in creating fascinating and emotional stories.One of the strong aspects of the series is how the stakes and the intensity of events grow from season to season. The first season introduces viewers to the mysterious disappearance of Will and the appearance of strange phenomena in the small town of Hawkins. As the series progresses, viewers immerse themselves in the history of the Upside-Down World, learn more about the origin of Eleven's abilities and about the mysterious Hawkins laboratory. Each season introduces new characters and expands the mythology of the series, making the narrative even more exciting and layered. The creators successfully develop their characters and are not afraid to take risky plot moves, which makes watching even more exciting.An integral part of the success of the series is its soundtrack. The musical accompaniment of "Stranger Things" is a real tribute to the era of the 80s. The soundtrack includes both original compositions created by Michael Stein and Kyle Dixon from the band "Survive", as well as popular hits of the time. These melodies not only create an atmosphere and enhance emotions, but also become an important part of the narrative, immersing viewers in nostalgia and enhancing the authenticity of events on the screen. What a scene for the legendary song "Running up that hill", which was not particularly popular in the past, is worth now, after the release of the series. Now, this composition is well-known to many. It is because of her successful interweaving in one of the most important moments of the show.The visual part of the series also deserves praise. The visual effects, scenery and costumes are carefully crafted and create an atmosphere of mysticism and tension. The Duffer brothers and their team successfully demonstrate a world that seems both real and fantastic, where the supernatural and science fiction merge together."Stranger Things" is a series that combines a fascinating plot, deep characters and a nostalgic atmosphere of the 1980s. Young actors demonstrating incredible acting, an impressive soundtrack and increasing stakes from season to season make this project a must-see for all fans of mysticism. This is a real work of art that evokes both a sense of nostalgia and a desire to find out what happens next. "Stranger Things" is a show that not only entertains, but also makes you think about the importance of friendship, loyalty and bravery.8 out of 10.

author: trulstei
title: My god I wanted this to be a 10
content: What an amazing new series! I was getting tired of hearing about all these supposedly amazing TV shows, such as Game of Thrones, The Walking Dead and Breaking Bad that people always talk about, so when I heard there was a new entry to that list I said screw it, and jumped in, and boy was it great.At the beginning the show follows 5 different perspectives of the story, Mike and the gang, Joyce, Hopper, Nancy, and Jonathan. Even though there were a lot of characters I didn't struggle to remember any names, as I usually do. This isn't because they said their names a lot, but more because all of the characters felt like real people, they were believable.Later on the 5 perspectives change into 3, Mike and the gang, Nancy and Jonathan, and Hopper and Joyce. Each team are uncovering one piece of the puzzle, making it extremely satisfying when everyone teams up in the end, so that every character knows everything.Every writer nailed it, and every actor/actress did an extremely good job, so it is difficult to find flaws here, and I tried to ignore them, but the same one kept showing up.The biggest "problem" is that the CGI (special effects) -team was either too small for the job or didn't have a big enough budget to keep the quality consistent. I'll try keeping this spoiler free, but there is one scene with a knife and a big jump, where the special effects are just not believable and it really pulls you out of the experience. Hopefully you know what scene I'm talking about if you've seen the show.Now that I come to think of it this next part reminds me a lot of the situation the director of Jaws had when they were filming, which was that the shark didn't look very good, so they had to keep it off- screen for most of the film to not ruin it. It is very much the same with Stranger Things, because in fight scenes with the monster in the last episode the lights keep blinking a lot, not only did this save the CGI team a lot of work, but it also saved the viewers the feeling of this not being real. But there is nothing wrong with that, because they solved the problem, well the thing is that they sort of took it back, since in one of the last scenes with Eleven the monster simply doesn't look realistic enough.I would still be willing to give it a 10/10 if that was it, because everything else is just so well done, but the final small detail that made me go to a 9 was that the last episode had me thinking the episode was ending like 5 times. The final 4-6 scenes were directed in such a way that it always looked like the credits were about to come up, making me actually want the episode to end instead of the opposite.All in all, watch this show. I can actually guarantee you that you'll like it, if it was possible to give a 9.7 I would do that.Watch it.

author: ryan-bfd
title: Stranger Things just released a bolt of energy straight into the eighties sci-fi genre.
content: The story takes place in 1983 Hawkins, Indiana. When a middle school boy named Will mysteriously vanishes his three best friends, mother, brother and a local police chief become engrossed in supernatural events in an attempt to find him. The plot for this movie feels like something out of a Stephen King novel. It seems like the show is self-aware its own influences too. There are references made to eighties sci-fi horror films all throughout the series (Evil Dead, The Thing). So this isn't the most original show ever made, and I admit if I was just going off of the plot description, I probably wouldn't have invested my time in it. But this series offers something pretty interesting. It isn't something completely new, but it takes previous works and blends them together to create a story and style of its own. Imagine the Goonies and Twin Peaks colliding with a John Hughes film and a Stephen King novel and getting dropped in the middle of The Twilight Zone's universe. That best describes Stranger Things. Its creativity comes from its ability to mix influences and that's why it clings on to you with in the first episode. It provides something that is familiar but ultimately gives us something new.Eighties nostalgia is alive and well and you can clearly see its influences in the today's art-work, whether it be music, film or fashion. The only problem I've ever had with eighties-influenced art is when the artist makes something that is outdated and clearly would only work if been made in the eighties. However, Stranger Things is different. It wouldn't work as well if it was made in the eighties. The modern visual effects, directing, and cinematography compliment the series beautifully and make it easier to immerse yourself in this type of art. The modernization of this story gives it a component of clarity. While if this was made in the eighties, it would have gotten buried because it would just be stamped as another clichéd sci-fi thriller. But today, it stands out as a uniquely stylized and beautifully composed masterpiece. But it isn't just the style and visuals that keep you engaged. The story line twists enough to always keeps you guessing, but never enough to alienate or confuse you (like an M. Night Shyamalan film). The acting is phenomenal. Wynona Rider showcases her incredible acting chops to their full extent. She gives an absolutely heartbreaking performance. While the young actors in this film show us that their inexperience never gets the better of them. They never get overshadowed by their seasoned co-stars.One of the most admirable things about this series is that is stays well-grounded even with all the ridiculously abnormal activity. The charters never seem over-the-top or clichéd. Everyone in the series stays relatable. The story never gets confusing or incoherent. The blend of CGI with the natural backgrounds never gets sloppy or excessive. The score compliments the style beautifully. It never exaggerates a scene but keeps us submerged in the story by providing a signature eeriness to each scene.Stranger Things is truly another one of Netflix's crowning achievements. I look forward to the seasons to come.

The new story which is really a rehash of the previous one became too convoluted and felt like a reheated lasagna past its expiration date.If they had started with a totally fresh story it might have worked but it felt too similar as if starting over with a slightly different approach could make things seem all new again.I found season 3 to be quite painful to sit through because not only the delicious mystery present in 1 and 2 has vanished replaced by a sort of "dramedy" with the cast of characters seeming to struggle in their new quest to stay relevant.If season 3 had been the first, it might not have suffered as much in comparison with the 2 great seasons that preceded it but coming after such amazing and groundbreaking work, 3 has an indisputable feeling of been there done that.For this reason, even though I would rate season 1 a perfect 10 and season 2 a very strong 9, season 3 brings down my final rating to 6 stars. author: worshipevil
title: A good start... for an ending!
content: The first four episodes are absolutely crazy, and honestly, I still can't get over how intense everything becomes by the time you reach episode 4. It's wild how they managed to build up the atmosphere step by step, only to drop such a massive mid-final moment that feels almost like a season finale in itself. Episode 4 really hits differently - the pacing, the character moments, the way the scenes are put together - it all feels so sharp and deliberate. You can tell the creators knew exactly what they were doing, leaving you half satisfied and half desperate to see what comes next.What makes it even more fascinating is how much more you get out of it if you've actually seen the show on Broadway. If you've experienced the theatre version, suddenly so many small details, references, and stylistic choices in these episodes make much more sense. It's as if the series is constantly winking at the stage production, expanding certain elements while paying tribute to others. The way certain scenes are staged, the emotional beats, even some of the transitions - all of it feels like a love letter to the original performance. People who only know the screen adaptation will enjoy it, but those who saw it live get an entire extra layer of meaning.And the production quality is just stunning overall. You can really see how much care went into every frame, from the costumes to the lighting to the soundtrack. There's a kind of theatrical flair blended with a cinematic polish that gives the whole thing a unique vibe. It doesn't just feel like an adaptation - it feels like its own artistic event.All of this makes it almost unbearable to wait for what's coming next. Knowing that more is arriving around Christmas just adds to the excitement. The anticipation is real, and if the first four episodes are anything to go by, the rest is going to be unforgettable. I seriously can't wait for Christmas!

content: (I didn't include a synopsis because they're everywhere)When I first saw the trailer for this show a few weeks back, I immediately thought of R.L Stine and Stephen King. title: One of the best shows of our generation
content: Stranger Things is one of those rare shows that manages to feel both deeply nostalgic and completely fresh at the same time. The show takes time to make you care about everyone, whether it's a group of awkward, lovable kids on bikes, teenagers navigating love and loss, or flawed adults trying their best in impossible situations. The friendships feel genuine, the relationships evolve naturally, and the emotional beats hit hard without feeling forced. You don't just watch these characters like me, you grow up with them. The atmosphere is another major strength. The retro aesthetic, synth-heavy score, and careful production design create a mood that feels immersive and intentional. It's not just nostalgia for nostalgia's sake, it enhances the storytelling and raises the tension, especially when the horror elements come into play. The Upside Down is unsettling, creative, and memorable, making the supernatural threat feel truly dangerous.
