author: xx-99705
title: A Nostalgic Thriller with a Sprinkle of Silly
content: "Stranger Things" has quickly become a beloved TV series, capturing the hearts of viewers with its nostalgic '80s vibes, engaging storyline, and a mix of supernatural elements and government conspiracies. The show follows a group of kids in the fictional town of Hawkins, Indiana, as they uncover and battle otherworldly threats. It's a perfect blend of sci-fi, horror, and coming-of-age drama, making it a unique addition to the modern TV landscape.While the series excels in creating an intense atmosphere and building suspense, there's one aspect that can be a bit hard to overlook: the fact that a bunch of kids are seemingly responsible for saving the world. Don't get me wrong, the kids-Mike, Eleven, Dustin, Lucas, and the rest of the gang-are endearing, brave, and resourceful. But one can't help but wonder, where are the armies, police, FBI, and other authorities? Surely, a supernatural threat of this magnitude would warrant more than just a few kids and a handful of adults.The show does include some adult characters, like Chief Hopper and Joyce Byers, who play crucial roles in the fight against the Upside Down. However, the absence of a more substantial response from government agencies and military forces feels a bit unrealistic. It's almost as if Hawkins exists in a bubble where the fate of the world rests solely on the shoulders of these young heroes.Despite this slightly silly notion, "Stranger Things" remains an entertaining and captivating series. The chemistry between the cast, the nostalgic references, and the thrilling plot twists keep viewers hooked. It's a show that embraces its quirks and, in doing so, creates a world where the impossible becomes possible-even if it means a bunch of kids saving the planet.

I only made it through by frequently turning my head away from the absolute bloodbath on screen. The fun was gone, the series far from entertaining. There was so much less story so much more gorey. I'll miss the characters, but it's simply not worth sitting through another Season of all that yuck. I'm not a horror fan, obviously, and that is all that Stranger Things is now, just another horror story. I'd not be so frustrated if it didn't feel like such a bait and switch. All the initial charm is completely gone, what drew me to the series has so thoroughly vanished it doesn't even seem like the the same show. If you're going to watch, stop with Season Two. title: Tasteless Bubblegum

The car seem to wash themselves while being used.ST reproduces some kind of Meta-80ties, focusing only on Mainstream Mass Culture and ignoring the fact, that there has been many highly diverse subcultures.And why doesn't any kid have a computer? I grew up in Germany, I got my first in 79 and during the 80ties nearly all the boys in my area owned a Commodore, Atari or Sinclair.If you want a more realistic show about the 80tie, go and watch "Halt and Catch Fire".Edit: After watching Season 4 I have to add, that I misjudged the whole show. author: lilmsoblivious
title: Season 4 = Too Much Gore
content: I cannot adequately express how deeply disappointed and upset I am by the horrible turn the Duffer Brothers and Netflix have taken Stranger Things. The approval ratings only continue to soar because of a) the vast population of horror-lovers who hopped on the Stranger Things bandwagon and b) because people are just excited that Season 4 is FINALLY out; but I know MANY other fans who don't like thrillers but gave Stranger Things a chance and loved it, at least at first. Seasons 1 and 2 are more so thrillers than 'horror'-we love the creative storyline, the mystery-solving, the cinematography, the character development, all the iconic aspects of Stranger Things. Season 3 pushed the envelope with more gore and horror than the preceding seasons, and Season 4 is tenfold worse, AND has way more drug use. The images, sounds, demolition of the human body, satanic-like voices and hallucinations; it's strikingly dark, gory, demented, pure evil, and utterly disgusting... It's WAY different and these choices don't even make sense. Those of us who despise gore and horror are very angry and upset with the Duffer Brothers and Netflix for leading us on with a very intriguing story with mild, tolerable horror-thrill, really-in the initial seasons to now a full-blown gory horror show that leaves me feeling sick to my stomach and absolutely repulsed that so many people can watch such gruesome images and enjoy it. To love such, I think a person must be out-of-touch with their soul to a degree.Indeed, it seems the makers are catering to an entirely different crowd, in an effort to increase popularity and bring home more cash (like they need it); meanwhile, the rest of us feel betrayed and confused. Season 4 is a total botch in my opinion. There are more and more holes in the plot, and it's all related with the elements of horror that seem very forced. Many of their choices are uncalled for, don't make sense, and are totally uncharacteristic of the show. Rather than introducing a new monster villain, there are countless many other ways that the writers, directors, and producers could have and should have taken this season-don't throw in some OP villain who comes out of the blue (though he is tied into the storyline, but it seems that he wasn't a part of the plan back in Season 1, but I could be wrong) when y'all haven't even hashed out everything from the preceding seasons! For instance, they could have geared it toward better explaining how the supposed experimenting with psychedelic drugs mentioned in Season 2 produced telepathic babies and provide some more of the backstory there with El/Jane's mom, how the Russians still somehow have access to the upside down and have a demogorgon, etc. There is some explanation in the 7th episode, but all the others in season 4 are not very important to the overall plot. More over, it's inappropriate to target "Mormons" by misrepresenting a large religion. It's never cool to pick on people for their religious beliefs, but the media regularly pokes fun at LDS members and always get away with it. Just another way that season 4 stoops to a lower level.If the Duffer Brothers and Netflix wanted to make a super gory, nasty horror show that's totally trying to be trendy and appeal to the worldly members of society, then MAKE A NEW SHOW. Don't ruin our beloved Stranger Things! I wish that Season 4 would be redacted and altered so as to not include the entirely unnecessary disturbing content. I know this isn't gonna happen, so at the very least, I hope some similar viewers will save themselves the heartache and spare their minds from having those horrible scenes forever etched in their memories by just not watching Season 4. Unequivocally, it should be rated TV-MA for how repulsive and gory it is. Maybe some YouTuber or VidAngel will make an edited version so we don't have to wade through the muck to get the good scraps of the story. One can hope.Smh @ the Duffer Brothers, Netflix, & all who influenced the disgusting turn of Season 4 for the worse. You have damaged my already injured view of the goodness of humanity. Please don't let us down with Season 5!

author: jalib-66193
title: Decent but glaringly flawed
content:
I am late to this party and to me the biggest surprise is how obvious the flaws are and how they have never been addressed, they are all painfully obvious to see and ridiculously simple to fix1: Mike
Mike is by a very wide margin the worst element of the show, not only is he the least interesting character but also in a show of corrupt "scientists" and immoral human experimentation one of the most unlikeable. He doesn't care about being a good friend, ignoring friends who have been through hell and back despite pretending to care desperately about getting them home. He is so obnoxiously self centered he twists every single conversation to be about him. From the very start of the show his one personality trait, despite being a literal child in season 1, is believing he is in love with eleven, which is already ridiculous because they are both literal children and eleven doesn't know basic English and has never spent time around people her age so the story arc of them having "feelings" for each other after knowing each other for 3 days and saying maybe 8 words to each other is objectively bad, but it is another flaw in Mike's character because while he is a complete tool to his friends, family and people in the town, he acts as if eleven is the one person he truly cares about, but guess what? He's a manipulative, self centered, arrogant prick to her too, he has no personality, no character arc, no character development, after the point of being the plot device to introduce eleven to the environment he serves literally zero purpose, he is insufferable to characters in the show and insufferable for us to watch, he is a truly awful character.2: Nancy
Nancy has the potential to be a great character, without spoiling anything, she is both brave and smart, she takes more proactive steps than any other character in the show except Hopper. However, she is deeply flawed because her character is reduced to being arm candy. She is smart, resourceful with a strong moral compass and more stones than any male her age, but her entire screen time she apparently needs to be accompanied by one of 2 male characters, she does badass stuff, but she is never allowed to do it herself and she is never allowed to be a leader, she is painted as a character whose life and personality revolves entirely around who she is dating at the time, she is never allowed to stand on her own 2 feet, despite objectively being more willing and capable than the male characters the writers force her to be attached at the hip to. She is a good character, with all the potential to be a great one, if the writers would just let her be.3: Hopper
Hopper is the saving grace of the show, his flaw is a different angle to the above 2, mike is outright awful, Nancy could shine but the writers wont let her, Hoppers flaw is that he is too good, by which I mean he is overpowered. He is my favourite character and he carries the show on his back, I am not caught up with the show yet, but if he dies as far as i'm concerned the show dies with him, which may sound like an odd critique, but the show is supposed to be a drama with horror themes, having a character like Hopper who can single handedly infilitrate government labs, single handedly survive hostile environments that teams of trained and armed soldiers didn't last 2 minutes in, single handedly deal with every problem in the show from small town crimes, to corrupt government officials, to off the books experiments to other worldly threats and breeze through all of it, it takes away a lot of the tension and atmosphere. Again i will reiterate, he carries the show, watching him do a combination of detective work and action scenes are by far the best scenes in the show, but I can't help wishing that it had been handled better, make it more interesting than a character who effectively has god mode turned on and can single handedly fix every problem in the show takes away from the drama and tension that the rest of the screen time is spent hyping up.Those are my reasons for giving the show the rating i have, I am mid way through season 3 and so far am enjoying it, but at the same time every episode has the same issues I have listed, I keep hoping that the writers would have addressed the obvious weaknesses but so far they double down on them, the longer the show goes on, the less relevant and more annoying mike gets, the more Nancy is reduced to helpless female/damsel in distress who can't possibly navigate the world without one of her incompetent male peers "protecting" her and Hopper remains a superman tirelessly solving any and all problems that arise with no support and no struggle. The complacency with the writing gets more and more obvious and they sabotage their own creation by refusing to address it.

author: tomerb-10768
title: Stranger Things: A Nostalgic Trip Best Left Untaken
content: The Duffer Brothers' "Stranger Things" has undeniably captured the cultural zeitgeist, fueled by a potent cocktail of 80s nostalgia, Spielbergian homages, and a dash of Stephen King-esque horror. Yet, beneath the veneer of retro charm lies a glaring flaw that, for me, undermines the entire experience: the insufferable behavior of its core characters, the children.From the outset, the young protagonists of "Stranger Things" come across as less endearing and more exasperating. Their dialogue, often peppered with forced pop culture references and juvenile insults, feels contrived and grating. The constant bickering and petty squabbles, intended to portray a realistic camaraderie, instead come across as whiny and immature.This bratty behavior extends beyond mere verbal sparring. The characters' actions are frequently driven by impulsive decisions, a lack of respect for authority, and a general disregard for consequences. They consistently put themselves and others in danger, often exacerbating already perilous situations with their reckless antics.While some may argue that this portrayal of youthful rebellion is essential to the show's narrative, it ultimately detracts from the overall viewing experience. It becomes difficult to root for characters who are so consistently unlikeable, their flaws overshadowing any redeeming qualities they may possess.Furthermore, the show's reliance on these juvenile characters as the primary drivers of the plot stretches the bounds of believability. These children, with their limited understanding of the supernatural forces at play, are consistently the ones who unravel the mysteries, confront the monsters, and save the day. This narrative contrivance undermines the tension and suspense, as it becomes clear that no matter how dire the situation, these plucky youngsters will inevitably prevail.Of course, "Stranger Things" offers other redeeming qualities. The visual effects are impressive, the creature design is suitably terrifying, and the adult actors deliver compelling performances. However, these elements are not enough to compensate for the show's central flaw: its insufferable child characters.In conclusion, "Stranger Things" is a show that is ultimately undone by its own protagonists. Their bratty behavior, reckless actions, and constant reliance on plot contrivances make them difficult to root for and detract from the overall viewing experience. While the show may appeal to those seeking a nostalgic trip back to the 80s, for me, it's a journey best left untaken.

content: The opening of season 4 sees the Duffer brothers go out of their way to establish a hetero max landscape where any form of hetero-normative courtship is the rule but suggestion of other representation is aggressively banished. There's being faithful to the 80s but then there's just being outright prejudice. This tragic turned evil negative (implied sissy) gay sterotype is well documented and it's troubling to see the Duffers resurrecting it without any sense of self awareness or historical sensitivity.Over-all Stranger Things is plagued by the adult Duffer's perpetual adolecence. This is made stark in the fantastical visual choices which are in fact typical of male pubecsent fantasy centred as they are around an anxiety, fear and fasination with bodily function, most notably here, the rear-end, faeces and any 'whiff' of the banished yet associated homosexuality. Tubes of brown colon filled creepers emerge as multiple penis substitute phallus, spreading across a convincing Dali / Elm Street franchise inspired alt world, while flower headed carniverous pansies feed like wild animals. The symbolism is really quite stark.The Duffers have used the homophobia of the 80s as an excuse to exercise their own latent fears unchecked and once again prove that if you put cart blanche film making power in the hands of hetero males they just take it as a right to unleash their prejudices. The gay movement has spent 40 years critiquing and attempting to lay to rest LGBTQ cinematic prejudice, a task initiated by emerging queer theorists of the 1980s. In this light, Stranger Things is a shocking mark of cinemtaic immaturity for which the Duffers should be held to account.In the immortal words of the hit gay 80s band 'Frankie Goes to Hollywood' , "Relax, don't do it, when you want to go to it, relax don't do it when you want to cum..." and we hope series 5 will address and put right much this review raises. title: Nostalgia on Life Support
content: Stranger Things Season 5 is what happens when a show survives entirely on vibes long after it's run out of ideas.The writing is a mess of retcons that treat continuity like a suggestion. The Upside Down, once mysterious and unsettling, is now overexplained, contradicted, and conveniently rewritten whenever the plot gets stuck. Stakes don't matter because the rules never stop changing.Every other line is a sarcastic quip. No emotion is allowed to land without being undercut by a joke, as if the show is embarrassed by sincerity. Grief, fear, and danger are all flattened into the same smug tone, draining scenes of any real weight.The acting feels tired, hollow, and just downright bad. Characters have become caricatures of themselves, delivering algorithm-approved monologues followed by Marvel-style banter that kills whatever impact they might've had.Worst of all, Season 5 feels afraid. Afraid to be quiet, afraid to be weird, afraid to actually end. It doesn't trust its audience or its story. Instead of a finale, it's nostalgia on life support. Loud, overstuffed, and strangely empty.The early seasons worked because they trusted mystery, restraint, and emotional sincerity. Season 5 feels like a show that knows it's iconic and is desperately trying not to mess that up. Ironically ensuring that it does.

author: Sheenq
title: Mid
content: I really wanted to love the final episode of Stranger Things Season 5, but honestly, it just didn't land for me. For a show that defined itself with strong character moments, real tension, and unforgettable finales in earlier seasons, this ending felt strangely underwhelming and way too safe. It's not terrible, but for a series finale, "not terrible" just isn't good enough.The biggest issue is the payoff-or lack of it. After so much buildup across the season, the final confrontation feels rushed and oddly low-impact. Big moments are introduced and resolved too quickly, which kills the emotional weight they're supposed to carry. Things that should feel devastating or triumphant barely have time to sink in before the episode moves on. It's like the show is checking boxes instead of letting moments breathe.Character endings are another letdown. Some arcs feel wrapped up purely out of obligation, not because they naturally reached a satisfying conclusion. A few characters get emotional send-offs that feel earned, but others are sidelined or resolved with vague, almost lazy closure. For a show that made us care so deeply about its cast, the imbalance is frustrating.The tone is also all over the place. One minute it's trying to be dark and emotional, the next it's throwing in humor or nostalgia that undercuts the stakes. Instead of enhancing the ending, those callbacks feel distracting, like the episode is more concerned with reminding you of past greatness than delivering something new and powerful.Visually, it's solid. The effects, music, and production are all fine-but that's expected at this point. None of that can make up for an ending that feels emotionally muted and narratively rushed.In the end, the finale isn't a complete disaster, which is why it gets a 3/10 instead of lower. But for a show as iconic as Stranger Things, the final episode should have felt bold, heartbreaking, and unforgettable. Instead, it feels cautious, uneven, and forgettable-and that's the biggest disappointment of all.

It felt nostalgic-I really connected with the RPGs we used to play, loved the soundtrack, and enjoyed all the references to the movies we grew up watching. None of my favorite characters died, which made me genuinely happy!I think the Duffer brothers enjoy mystery and ambiguity, keeping everything playful while staying coherent within the universe of fiction and the RPG elements so heavily referenced throughout the series. They like to leave space for the audience's own interpretations, so imagination isn't constrained. Showing everything in detail would break the pacing and make the story feel exhausting.Leaving some questions unanswered encourages the audience to think more, discuss, and become emotionally involved. That's part of building a universe and a fanbase-one that can expand through spin-off series, games, comics, and books that may eventually offer more answers.

author: cozaiz
title: Stranger Things - Overall Series Review (6/10)
content: Stranger Things started off very strong, and season 1 is easily the best season of the whole show. It nailed the 80s vibe, introduced the characters really well, and had a darker, creepier atmosphere compared to what came later. Watching the kids grow up over the series is one of the show's biggest strengths, and their personalities were genuinely well written early on.After season 1, the show slowly began to decline. Season 2 wasn't bad, but it didn't feel as tight or as mysterious as the first season. Some story choices didn't land very well, and while certain episodes had meaning, they weren't executed in the most engaging way. The introduction of bigger threats also took away some of the mystery that made season 1 so effective.Season 3 became extremely popular and brought in new characters and a new setting, which was refreshing at first. However, this is where the show started leaning more into corny jokes and lighter tone instead of strong storytelling. It felt less serious and more childish than the earlier seasons, and some plotlines felt random rather than natural.Season 4 improved things again in terms of scale and emotion. The new villain and darker themes helped bring back some intensity, and there were some genuinely great scenes. It had stronger moments than seasons 2 and 3, but it still didn't reach the level of season 1.Season 5 was easily the weakest season for me. It felt padded with filler, had a lot of repetitive planning scenes, and the dialogue was noticeably worse than previous seasons. Instead of feeling like a proper conclusion, it came across as underwhelming and poorly structured compared to what the show used to be.Overall, Stranger Things has great characters and a strong start, but it loses focus as it goes on. Season 1 remains the highlight, while later seasons rely more on action and fan service than solid writing.Final rating: 6/10.

author: sadman_sakibayon3
title: Goodbye, Stranger Things
content: There are goodbyes that happen loudly, with words, with explanations, with closure. And then there are goodbyes like this one. Quiet. Almost accidental. You close a screen, the room returns to its ordinary shape, and yet something inside you knows that a door has just closed for good. Goodbye, Stranger Things is not just about the end of a television series. It is about the moment we realize that a certain version of ourselves will never return.When Stranger Things first entered our lives, it did not arrive as a spectacle. It arrived like a memory we did not know we were missing. A small town. Empty roads. Children on bicycles pedaling through silence. A sky that felt wider than the world we lived in. It reminded us of a time when fear was still something we faced together, not alone behind screens. Watching it felt less like consuming entertainment and more like stepping into a shared emotional shelter.Over the years, Stranger Things became a ritual. Not just something we watched, but something we returned to. After long days, after disappointments, after news that made the world feel heavier than it should, Hawkins waited for us. The show did not promise happiness. It promised connection. And that promise mattered more.At its heart, Stranger Things was never about monsters or alternate dimensions. It was about children learning that the world is darker than they imagined, and choosing to love anyway. It was about friendship that survives fear, loyalty that refuses to bend, and innocence that cracks but does not completely disappear. That is why its ending hurts. Because what ends is not a plot, but a feeling.At its heart, Stranger Things was never about monsters or alternate dimensions. It was about children learning that the world is darker than they imagined, and choosing to love anyway. It was about friendship that survives fear, loyalty that refuses to bend, and innocence that cracks but does not completely disappear. That is why its ending hurts. Because what ends is not a plot, but a feeling.Eleven was never just a character with supernatural abilities. She was a wounded soul learning the language of care. Her power came from pain, but her strength came from tenderness. Watching her grow felt like watching someone reclaim their right to exist gently in a world that had used them harshly. When her story settles into silence, it feels like losing someone who taught us that survival does not have to make us cruel.Mike, Dustin, Lucas, and Will were not heroic in the traditional sense. They were afraid. They made mistakes. They doubted themselves. And that was precisely why they mattered. Will, especially, carried a quiet grief that many recognized but few spoke about. His silences said more than his words ever could. In him lived the truth that some battles leave marks that friendship alone cannot erase. Seeing him on screen felt like seeing the unspoken parts of ourselves reflected without judgment.Stranger Things understood something rare. That growing up is not a clean transition. It is messy, uneven, and filled with losses we do not know how to name. As seasons passed, the characters aged. And so did we. The jokes changed. The tone darkened. The simplicity faded. Somewhere between the first episode and the last, childhood slipped away, both for them and for us.This is where the grief truly lives. Not in the ending, but in the realization that we can never go back to how it felt the first time. The first time we watched kids ride bicycles into danger without knowing what was waiting. The first time the world felt mysterious instead of exhausting. Stranger Things became a marker of time. Before it, and after it.There is a spiritual lesson hidden inside this goodbye, though it is never spoken aloud. Everything that arrives must also leave. Clinging turns memory into pain. Letting go turns it into meaning. Stranger Things did not owe us permanence. It gave us presence. And that is enough.As viewers, we often believe stories exist to distract us from reality. Stranger Things did something else. It helped us face it. It reminded us that fear does not disappear, but it becomes bearable when shared. That darkness exists, but so does loyalty. That loss is inevitable, but love leaves traces.Now that it is over, something strange happens. We feel empty, yet full. Sad, yet grateful. The show ends, but what it awakened remains. The desire to protect what is fragile. The courage to stand beside others when things feel impossible. The memory of a time when stories felt like safe houses.The screen goes black. The music fades. There is no dramatic farewell. Just a quiet understanding. Some stories do not ask to be remembered loudly. They ask to be carried softly.Goodbye, Stranger Things. You were never just a show. You were a place we lived in for a while. And places like that never truly disappear.They wait, patiently, inside us.

author: BradenTheRater
title: Hellfire Lives!
content: "Stranger Things" is a wonderful, binge-able, and mysterious series that is untouchable and undefeated. I'm going to go season by season and rate each individual season.Season 1. The first season was undoubtedly amazing and was a great start to the mysteries starting to unravel. The pacing in the first few episodes were pretty slow, so it was a bit hard to get into the series. But after that I warmed up to it and ended up loving it. A great start to the iconic ensemble of "Stranger Things" Season 1 gets a 9/10.Season 2: The second season started out slow, but it did introduce a crucial character into the show, and delved into more of Will's problems when he went missing. This season also contained my third and tied for second favorite episode, "The Mind Flayer" and "The Gate" I love "The Gate" so much because of the last school dance scene. In what world does your girlfriend walk in as soon as "Every Breath You Take" plays? The perfect situation for Mike and Lucas! And I can't say why I loved "The Mind Flayer" without spoiling anything. Overall, Season 2 was a great season to continue the series. Season 2 gets a 9.3/10Season 3. This was probably my least favorite season due to the predictability and how many cliches there were. If you don't know what that is, it's basically an unoriginal idea used in many science fiction stories. And there were a lot of those in Season 3, but it was still good nonetheless. The season went into more detail on the kids lives and the story, and it had its ups and downs. Season 3 gets a 8.5/10.Season 4. This was definitely my favorite season and included some of the best episodes including my personal favorite, "Dear Billy". Such an iconic and perfect episode, nothing is left out, and nothing takes away from the glory of this episode. Emotionally powerful, and it shows us how great this TV show is. It also basically solidifies the anthem for "Stranger Things" which is "Running Up That Hill", by Kate Bush. We also have the other tied-for-second favorite episode, "The Massacre at Hawkins Lab". It ties together so many holes in the plot and reveals a major plot twist and character development. In conclusion, Season 4 was the best and greatest season in "Stranger Things" Season 4 gets a 9.9/10.Season 5. This season tied together and concluded the show, but it also left open big plot holes. And I can't really give examples without spoiling anything, so I'm not gonna. Season 5's episode "Sorcerer" was very good, and it delved into more of Will's background and history, as the rest of the season does later on. (The Bridge ahem.) All jokes aside, the season finale is way better the ratings say, and it provides a satisfying ending to this legendary show. Season 5 gets a 9.5/10So, we've gone through all the seasons. We can safely say "Stranger Things" is an iconic series with some of the best soundtracks, ensembles, and acting in TV show history."I've loved you every day since. I love you on your good days. I love you on your bad days. I love you with your powers, I love you without your powers. I love you for exactly who you are. You're my superhero."

author: TyronianCritic
title: GOT ENDING
content:
Season 1:7,8/10The performances are incredible - the kids and adults alike bring energy, emotion, and charisma that drive the story. Visuals and production design fully capture the 80s mood, while suspense and horror moments are tight and well-executed. Dialogue is punchy, but certain character arcs and subplots could use more depth. Still, it's an entertaining ride with tension, heart, and moments of brilliance. Tyronian Critic: 7,8/10Season 2:7,5/10The season builds tension and delivers strong visuals and atmosphere, yet Eleven's role doesn't carry the narrative until the very end, reducing her presence in key moments. Some character arcs also feel rushed, making the episode slightly less compelling than earlier peaks. Dialogue is solid, but pacing issues prevent full immersion. Tyronian Critic: 7.5/10.Season 3:8,2/10Season 3 delivers a thrilling visual spectacle and the cast keeps its charm alive, with the characters fully engaging and entertaining. However, pacing is often unclear, and the tension only truly peaks in the final two episodes. Teen drama doesn't fully resonate, and the adults have shifted from dramatic anchors to comic relief, changing the tone in ways that don't always land. The ending offers a never-ending spectacle that's visually impressive but feels a bit out of place. Tyronian Critic: 8.2/10 - an emotional rollercoaster with strong characters, charm intact, but storytelling uneven, in addition, the plot is unclear due to the lack of motivationsSeason 4:8,5/10This season is a visual feast - striking cinematography, intense gore, and masterful character development make it the most immersive entry yet. The Upside Down is portrayed with jaw-dropping beauty, and the cultural impact of the show has never felt stronger. Volume 1 delivers tension-packed episodes filled with twists, suspense, and engagement that keep viewers on edge.However, some side characters are underdeveloped and occupy screen time that could have been better spent on the main arcs. Certain storylines drag unnecessarily, and the final two episodes feel rushed compared to the meticulous pacing of the first seven. Despite these flaws, the main characters shine, the suspense is high, and the season delivers memorable cinematic moments. Tyronian Critic: 8.5/10 - an impressive, high-stakes season with minor pacing issues and uneven character focus.Season 5: 5.5/10
The performances largely decline, with only a few actors still delivering moments of brilliance. Many characters feel unnecessary, and the villain's buildup is weak and fails to deliver tension or stakes. Dialogue is clunky and uninspired, with the writing often feeling directionless, relying on spectacle rather than substance. Plot twists appear without explanation or proper setup, making the season a chain of disappointment rather than a cohesive story. Tyronian Critic: 5.5/10 - ambitious in vision, but ultimately underwhelming and chaotic.

author: Faraz-241
title: A masterpiece but not without flaws
content: My Review of Stranger ThingsIf I want to talk about Stranger Things, I have to say it's the show that changed my life. It all started when a friend told me, "You should watch this amazing series called Stranger Things." I replied, "No, I don't like shows that seem like childish dramas." And he said, "Just watch one episode."Later that day, I went home, and weirdly enough, The Tonight Show with Jimmy Fallon was interviewing one of the actors from the series. That moment made me think, Alright, I'll give it a try - just one episode. But one episode turned into two... two into three... and after the third, I was completely hooked.That first night, I ended up watching five episodes straight. People who know me and follow my reviews probably remember my review of The Last of Us season two and Five Nights at Freddy's 2. Honestly, I'd say I know the FNAF franchise better than almost anyone right now.That's why Stranger Things felt so special to me - it beautifully, and somehow authentically, recreated the soul of the 1980s era. The mix of retro '80s vibes with the Upside Down and the lost kids created a world so unique that no other series has a universe quite like it.Each character is written so well that you can truly understand and feel them. Of course, like every masterpiece, it has its flaws. For me, season three wrapped up the story perfectly, while seasons four and five felt a bit unnecessary. Even though I still hope Netflix makes a sixth season someday, the truth is that seasons four and five just weren't as strong as the earlier ones.Still, Stranger Things is absolutely the best series I've ever watched. It's the kind of show that stays in your mind even after it's over - you just can't stop thinking about it. Saying goodbye to the Upside Down and Hawkins was honestly harder for me than saying goodbye to any other fictional world.

author: timdasilva
title: Dr. Holmes, Smell Ya Later
content: 9.5 years. 5 seasons. 42 episodes... each building something extraordinary. An epic story of friendship and inter-dimensional demons, with supernatural surprises, titillating twists & turns, and magnificent mystery from beginning to end.Stranger Things isn't just a television series, it's an adventure. author: Maverick_41
title: A Confident Genre Blend with Memorable High Points
content: Stranger Things is an excellent genre mix of science fiction, horror, mystery, and drama. Set in the small town of Hawkins, Indiana, what begins as a seemingly simple story about missing children quickly unfolds into a much larger mystery involving an unknown and dangerous world.The series excels at weaving together multiple storylines of varying importance into one compelling overall narrative. At times it is light-hearted and does not take itself too seriously, while at other moments it becomes highly dramatic and emotionally heavy, with a sense of tragedy the viewer can truly feel. The large cast of characters works well both together and individually, each contributing to the variety and entertainment value of the series. In an era where special effects are getting worse, Stranger Things stands out as a strong counterexample. The 1980s setting is recreated brilliantly, sometimes deliberately over the top, but always with a striking and effective visual style.The few weaknesses of the series lie mainly in its tendency to overexplain parts of the story. The audience could be trusted more to draw its own conclusions about the plot. Additionally, the final season features extremely long episodes of up to two hours, and a tighter edit could have improved the pacing.The series reaches its peak in season four, with episodes seven and my personal favorite, episode four, standing out as absolute masterpieces.Overall Stranger Things stands out as an atmospheric series that successfully combines genres.

author: 1RandomFan
title: A Phenomenon That Mostly Delivers
content: Going into Stranger Things, I wasn't sure if it would live up to the hype. But season after season, it proved why it became such a cultural phenomenon. It's a great show. Not perfect-but undeniably great.What makes it work so well is the heart. At its core, it's about friendship. The bond between Mike, Dustin, Lucas, Max, and Eleven is what carries the show through all the Demogorgons, Mind Flayers, and trips to the Upside Down. The mix of '80s nostalgia, horror, sci-fi, and coming-of-age drama feels natural rather than forced. It knows how to balance humor, emotion, and suspense in a way that keeps you invested.Season 1 is still the magic formula. It's tight, mysterious, and emotionally grounded. Season 2 expands the world nicely, even if it has a few pacing hiccups. Season 4 swings big and mostly pulls it off with some of the show's most intense and cinematic moments.Season 3, though, is probably the weakest in my opinion. It leans heavier into the bright summer aesthetic and comedy, which isn't bad-but it feels slightly less focused and more over-the-top compared to the grounded tension of earlier seasons. It's still fun and entertaining, but it doesn't hit with the same emotional weight.The performances are another huge strength. Watching the younger cast grow into their roles has been one of the most satisfying parts of the series. The show also isn't afraid to take risks, and when it hits, it really hits.Stranger Things may not be flawless, but it earns its place as one of Netflix's flagship series. It blends nostalgia with genuine heart and suspense in a way few shows manage. Great characters, strong atmosphere, and memorable moments make it an easy 8 out of 10 for me.

author: Hyushi
title: Stranger Things
content: Watching Stranger Things feels like discovering a quiet town running normally on the surface while something beneath it is interfering with the signal.What makes the show so effective is how clearly it establishes its baseline before introducing disruption. The friendships feel genuine. The routines feel stable. So when anomalies start appearing, you sense the disturbance immediately. It's not random chaos - it's interference.The series balances character and spectacle with impressive control. Emotional bonds are the infrastructure. The larger threats amplify tension, but the core strength comes from loyalty, curiosity, and collaboration. When pressure increases, the group adapts rather than fragments.Tonally, it manages nostalgia without becoming dependent on it. The atmosphere is deliberate - synthesised tension, dim lighting, and that constant feeling that something just outside perception is watching. It understands pacing: escalate, breathe, escalate again.As seasons progress, the scope expands, but the heart remains intact. Even when the scale increases, the show keeps its focus on connection and resilience. That consistency is what prevents it from feeling bloated.Verdict: Immersive, emotionally grounded, and expertly calibrated - Stranger Things proves that even when the world glitches, strong foundations hold.

title: Things happend strangerly !!!!

title: Stranger Things is the most popular series Netflix has ever made and the most relevant in the world of streaming.

The plot is quite simple and generic, but it works so well because of its simplicity and the charisma of its characters. Everything was going well until the third season.At first, the series stood out for its nostalgic aesthetic and references to classic films, and I honestly thought the series finale would be the same as the second season's, because it provides a truly satisfying ending and leaves almost no room for a continuation. And here comes the real problem, the long wait between seasons; the third season premiered in 2019, the fourth season in 2022, and the final season in 2025. What I mean is that with so much waiting, the general interest in the series is fading, Or at least that's what happened to me; when the final season premiered, I practically had no desire to watch it, and another problem is the length of the episodes-most of them are an hour long, and the last one 2 hours.In the almost 10 years that this series lasted, it made 5 seasons, while other series such as Supernatural, for example, made 9 seasons of 20 episodes and still had time left over for more. Perhaps using Supernatural as an example isn't the right thing to do, but it's my point of view. Why, despite the bad things, are there also good things, such as the main villain Vecna, who, despite being generic, carries a large part of the series from his first appearance.Overall, Stranger Things is a good show, which was a total revolution when it premiered. title: Stranger Things: A Gripping Sci-Fi Thriller Review
content: Stranger Things is a science-fiction horror series set in the 1980s in the small town of Hawkins. author: Anisha-467
title: "Stranger Things: A Perfect Blend of Mystery, Friendship, and 80s Nostalgia"
content: Stranger Things is one of the most engaging and nostalgic science fiction series of the modern era. Created by Matt Duffer and Ross Duffer, the show beautifully combines supernatural horror, emotional storytelling, and 1980s nostalgia. Set in the small fictional town of Hawkins, Indiana, the series begins with the mysterious disappearance of a young boy, Will Byers. As his friends search for him, they encounter a strange girl with telekinetic powers named Eleven, who escaped from a secret government laboratory.One of the strongest aspects of Stranger Things is its compelling characters and their relationships. The friendship between Mike, Dustin, Lucas, and Will feels genuine and heartwarming, capturing the innocence and loyalty of childhood friendships. Eleven's character arc is especially powerful, as viewers watch her slowly discover her identity, emotions, and sense of belonging. Characters like Jim Hopper and Joyce Byers add emotional depth to the story, portraying determination and parental love in the face of terrifying circumstances.The series also stands out because of its thrilling storyline involving a parallel dimension called the Upside Down. The presence of terrifying creatures such as the Demogorgon creates suspense and keeps viewers constantly on edge. Each season expands the mystery, blending horror, adventure, and emotional drama in a way that keeps audiences invested.Another remarkable feature of the show is its nostalgic tribute to 1980s pop culture. From the music and fashion to references to classic films and games like Dungeons & Dragons, the series perfectly recreates the atmosphere of the era. The synth-heavy soundtrack and retro cinematography further enhance this nostalgic experience.Overall, Stranger Things successfully balances suspense, emotional storytelling, and nostalgic charm. Its strong characters, intriguing plot, and unique supernatural elements make it a memorable and highly addictive series. The show has captivated audiences worldwide and continues to be one of the most popular productions on Netflix.

author: Yusuf015
title: Saying Goodbye After All These Years
content: Following this story for nearly a decade, this finale felt respectful and emotionally earned.Stranger Things was never just a show for me - it was a period of life. While the Hawkins storyline is clearly closed, some character arcs (especially Mike's) are left intentionally open-ended, which feels more realistic than disappointing.The final season doesn't rush to wrap everything up. Instead, it focuses on emotion, atmosphere, and paying tribute to what made the earlier seasons special. Not every question gets an answer - and that's okay. This was always a coming-of-age story, and growing up rarely comes with perfect closure.Does it have flaws? Yes.But the feeling it leaves behind is strong, sincere, and lasting.For me, Stranger Things delivered a finale worthy of the journey.

author: cherold
title: Captures that '80s magic
content: There is no reason, in terms of story, for Stranger Things to take place in the '80s. But the '80s atmosphere - the dial phones, the chain smoking, Winona Ryder - are there to clue you in on the inspiration for this movie, which is pretty much every supernatural movie from the 80s with a focus on kids. E.T., Poltergeist, that sort of thing.The wondrous thing is how dead-on this tribute. It's not just the clothes and hair, but the style of acting, the scripting approach, the structure, all hold true to their inspiration. You've got the young nerdy kids, the horny, unsure teenagers, the monster, the mysterious one with the power, the bad science/government people, the conflicted investigator, the tearful mom.You could argue that this entire season is simply a pastiche made up of recycled elements, and I wouldn't disagree, but it really feels less like a copy and more like something of that era, as though the writers had fallen into a coma in 1985, woke up and got to working.While it doesn't have the high style of the Spielberg films that are a primary influence, it does have the likability. The story is consistently engaging and fun, the acting is excellent, and the movie has sufficient laughs and tears to satisfy.

author: Lovegood13
title: A great series undone by bad unimaginative writing.
content: When I first watched Stranger Things Season 1 years ago, I genuinely thought it was one of the greatest shows of the decade. I loved how it reminded me of Freaks and Geeks. It was a perfect blend of quirky humour, eerie otherworldly mystery, childhood nostalgia, and gripping suspense centred on the search for Will. I remember feeling deeply sorry for Eleven, wanting to adopt her and protect her at all costs. Seeing what the writers ultimately did with her character is honestly heartbreaking and incredibly disappointing.It's clear that much of the story was made up as it went along after Season 1, but Season 2 still managed to work. After that, the show seemed to lose its original mood and identity. Season 3, while flawed, was still enjoyable and passable. Season 4 was a mess structurally, yet it was somewhat saved by the incredible performances of Jamie Campbell Bower and Sadie Sink.Season 5, however, is where everything completely fell apart for me and the reason I'm giving the show such a low rating. The story abandoned what once made Stranger Things special and instead leaned into a Marvel-style formula full of quick action scenes and shallow, meaningless storytelling. There's no real overarching message left. If anything, it feels like the message is that abused children never get a happy ending. So many characters forgotten, character development stunted, countless plot points left unexplained, and the finale felt unimaginative, sloppy, and rushed.I'm honestly upset with the Duffer Brothers for creating something so wonderful, only to ruin it in the end.

author: gogoschka-1
title: A nostalgic callback to the stories from my youth - but also a beautifully shot supernatural tale with charming performances and great production values
content: There were two dominating forces in the eighties that had a lasting effect on my cinematic taste for ever after and also resulted in my undying love for fantasy, sci-fi and horror stories: Steven Spielberg and Stephen King. I guess it isn't an overstatement to say "The Two Steves" probably influenced and shaped the imagination - the dreams AND the nightmares - of an entire generation.The main factor why I loved their movies and books was that kids roughly my own age figured so prominently in many of them. King wrote 'Firestarter', 'It' and 'Stand By Me', and Spielberg either directed or produced (via his company Amblin) 'E.T.', 'The Goonies' and 'Gremlins'. Those were stories where the young protagonists encountered aliens and monsters or where they themselves had supernatural powers - or where they just went on an adventure (to find a body or a long lost treasure) with grown-ups largely out of the picture. Now if you've seen 'Stranger Things', that should sound pretty familiar, right?Of course it does: because 'Stranger Things' deliberately pays homage to all those stories - and it does it very, very well. And it's not a rip-off, it's a love letter. The show emulates the themes and a certain style from those eighties treasures, and while it is a (for me) very welcome callback to some of the favorite stories from my youth, it's also very much its own thing. I won't give away the plot here (I guess you get a pretty good picture what it's about from what I wrote above), but I would like to mention that it's beautifully shot, the effects and generally the production values are top-notch, and the period-inspired music is fantastic. The biggest shout-out, however, has to go to the ensemble of actors, especially the kids who play the protagonists: their charming performances are the key to why the show works as well as it does.To sum it all up: If you're an eighties kid like me, this show is a must. For everyone else, it might depend a bit more on whether you're a genre fan or not, but if you do like supernatural stories, 'Stranger Things' is a treat. author: Eneshrn
title: Nine Years of Build-Up, One Rushed Goodbye
content: Despite all the fuss on the internet, I tried to watch ST Season 5 impartially and finished it today, so my impressions are still fresh. After watching the finale, the only thing I can say is this: I'm disappointed.I first watched this series when I was 13, just after Season 3 had been released. It had a huge impact on me right away, and from that point on, I waited for each new season with the same excitement. Six years have passed, and now the series I loved so much-one I grew up with-has finally ended. Instead of feeling fulfilled, I feel betrayed.Over the first four seasons, the series genuinely expanded its own universe. Whether through its enemies, its characters, or the events it depicted, it kept developing while, most importantly, staying consistent with the rules it had established. Season 5, however, threw everything that had been built over those four seasons and many years straight into the trash-and that is why I'm so angry.In the earlier seasons, entering the Upside Down was a major event. In Season 5, that weight is completely discarded, even though the air there is supposed to be poisonous. Suddenly, we're told that Hopper has been there dozens of times, which is absurd. That was the first piece of nonsense introduced in Season 5. The air was toxic. In Season 4, there were bats-there should have been Demogorgons. Being able to come and go so easily destroyed all the tension the series had carefully built. If Hopper really went in and out that often, how did he fail to notice that massive wall? If the goal was to expand the universe, why wasn't this hinted at as early as Season 1, the way the Vecna storyline was gradually seeded? Especially when the creators kept emphasizing that this was leading to a finale, the wall feels completely inconsistent.Let's talk about the Abyss. I'll call it that because I didn't even bother to learn its official name. Yes, it was an interesting idea, but it needed to be hinted at long before it appeared. Instead, it felt forced and rushed. This is an entirely different dimension, after all. Yet the moment our characters step into it, they adapt instantly and start chatting about trivial things as if nothing is wrong. Is that supposed to feel normal? You've entered a completely unknown place. There could be countless creatures you've never seen before. I don't want to listen to Steve and Jonathan talk about meaningless nonsense in a setting like that. And if I have to listen, then at least give me dialogue worth hearing. Instead, the writing leans heavily on clichés.Vecna and the Mind Flayer were both overused-especially the Mind Flayer, which had been built up as a slowly growing threat since Season 1. You showed it every season. Even before Season 5 aired, the marketing kept insisting that Vecna wasn't the true enemy. I've followed this series for six years, but you've been investing in the Mind Flayer for nine. So what's the payoff? Bullets that can't even hurt Demogorgons somehow damage what's supposed to be a godlike force in the universe. That's absurd. A creature that has received this much buildup should never be discarded so easily. The same goes for Vecna. You attempted to explore his past, but you failed to make it work. The most promising character in the series was wasted. You could have done so much more with him. The actor playing Henry was particularly strong and well-suited for this role-but in the end, none of it came together.While we're on the subject of the actor who played Henry, let's talk about the acting overall. I think this problem actually started in Season 4. There wasn't a particularly strong performance among the main cast, at least in terms of acting, but it didn't bother me back then because the atmosphere carried everything. The mood, the tension, the direction-they did the heavy lifting. But this season... this season is a complete disaster. None of the performances managed to convey genuine emotion. What I watched felt entirely lifeless, almost mechanical. I felt nothing. There is a significant decline in the performances of all the main characters except Dustin. The character Derek evoked more emotion than most of the main cast, and that is a terrible sign. When a minor character leaves a stronger emotional impact than characters we've followed for years, something has gone seriously wrong.And then there's the fan service scattered throughout this season. The entire spirit of the show feels dead. There were countless action scenes, yet not a single one managed to excite me-because I already knew you wouldn't kill off any of the main characters. Even the scene where Steve falls reeks of fan service. So much tension was drained from the story that I could barely sit through the action scenes in the final episode. Tension was always the lifeblood of this series, and you sacrificed it just to please a small, vocal portion of the audience. You shouldn't have destroyed that tension for people like me-viewers who genuinely loved this show and followed it for years.Then comes Will's conversation, encouraged by Robin, about his sexual identity. Let me explain why this scene felt so absurd. This is the 1980s, in the United States. LGBT people were not accepted the way they are today; society was deeply hostile and divided. On top of that, the world was literally facing extinction. And in the middle of all this, Will delivers a ten-minute speech about not liking girls. In that context, this scene feels completely disconnected from reality. A character like Hopper-written as a hardened, emotionally closed-off man shaped by that era-would not have responded calmly or supportively. The show ignores its own historical setting and character logic to force a modern conversation into a moment where it simply doesn't belong.I wanted to see Will's confession. It deserved to happen. But not in front of everyone, and not with the world on the brink of collapse. If you want an example of how this could have been handled properly, look at Robin's confession to Steve in Season 3. It was natural, spontaneous, and emotionally grounded. That is how such a moment could have existed in an '80s setting. This conversation should have been between Will and Mike. It should have been intimate, quiet, and earned-not forced into the story at the worst possible moment. Instead, it ended up damaging an already unstable season even further.I have to conclude my review here, or no one will read this. I have much more to say, but this is where I'll stop. The series has finally ended. Even though it ended badly, it has, at least, come to a close. If this season hadn't been weighed down by inconsistencies, excessive fan service, weak performances, and the decision to keep every character alive purely to pave the way for future spin-offs, we might have ended up with something at least acceptable. There was endless hype about this being the best season yet. Expectations were pushed sky-high, and still, it failed to deliver. In the end, the creators will probably be satisfied. The franchise will be milked further through new spin-offs, slowly draining whatever remains of its soul. And yet, despite everything, I'm still glad this series was part of my life for so many years. I'm glad I watched it. Out of respect for the earlier seasons and what this show once meant to me, I won't lower my overall rating any further.Thank you for reading.Overall Rating: 7/10.

author: 2Yung4This
title: Could've been one of the goods
content: Stranger Things started off in a solid place. I really loved the first two seasons, it felt fresh at the time-simple, focused, and driven by mystery rather than spectacle. Seasons 1 and 2 are easily the strongest because the story was contained, the cast was small, and the tone felt natural. The kids felt like actual kids, the danger felt real, and the show knew when to hold back instead of constantly trying to escalate.After that, the series clearly overstays its welcome. The concept gets stretched thinner with every season, yet Netflix takes years between releases for seasons that are only 8-9 episodes long. The wait is never justified by what we actually get. Over time, the show became one of the most overhyped pieces of media in recent years while mostly hovering around average in terms of writing and structure.The biggest issue is the complete lack of stakes. The writers are visibly afraid to kill off any main characters, which removes all tension. The core cast survives absurd, impossible situations again and again, so there is never a real sense of danger. Instead, the show relies on killing disposable new characters or faceless soldiers to fake consequences. When viewers know the main characters are untouchable, nothing feels earned.This problem is perfectly summed up by Max's storyline. Her arc was emotionally complete and thematically appropriate for a tragic ending, yet the show refuses to commit. Keeping her alive adds no meaningful narrative value and only reinforces the feeling that the writers will not follow through on consequences. It feels less like a creative decision and more like a refusal to let go of popular characters. As a result, the story loses weight, and emotional moments feel hollow.The growing cast also works against the show. There are now too many characters, many of whom have very little to do but are kept around anyway. Instead of tightening the story, the show keeps expanding sideways. Characters who once felt essential now feel like background filler, hanging around because the show does not know how to move on from them.The adults are another weak point. Their behavior makes little sense as the series progresses. Allowing children to repeatedly handle world-ending threats is already hard to believe, but the decision for families to continue living in Hawkins-after it becomes an obvious supernatural disaster zone-is absurd. The idea that the government or military would allow people to remain there completely breaks immersion. These choices make the plot feel sloppy and convenient rather than thought-out.The characters themselves also lose their charm over time. They worked in the first two seasons because they were kids dealing with something far bigger than themselves. As they grow older, the writing does not evolve with them. Many of them feel out of place, underwritten, or stuck repeating the same beats, relying more on nostalgia than strong character development.Zooming out, this fits a larger Netflix pattern. The platform frequently cancels creative or well-written shows while continuing to push popular but mediocre ones. The focus seems to be on engagement numbers and brand recognition rather than long-term quality. With Netflix expanding further into major studio properties, the trend does not inspire confidence for the future of mainstream entertainment.Overall, Stranger Things is not a terrible show, but it is far from the masterpiece it is often presented as. It peaked early, dragged on far too long, and lost its sense of danger along the way. What started as a tight, mysterious story became bloated, safe, and predictable-and that is ultimately its biggest failure.

title: Amazing
content: I found this programme not long before series 5 premiered. Yes, I know, where had I been hiding right? However, this late discovery put me in a very unique position, I got to binge watch right the way through to the end. This meant I was immune to the hype, unfrustrated by the long late between each series and free from seeing or hearing any fan opinion, spoilers or critic ripping. Turns out I completely love Stranger Things! I love the plot, the twists and turns and all the characters, even the annoying ones were essential. I love the Stephen King salutes and, unless I am very mistaken, the doff of the caps to Game of Thrones and even the Alien franchise. There is only one reason why I didn't score this show a ten (deep breath) the long-winded, overly sentimental buddy I love you speeches between the main characters during the penultimate and the last episodes. When the pace is quick and my heart's going at ten to the dozen, when I'm on the edge of my seat, I don't want to hear these long drawn out bits of mush. I have no problem with sentimentality, but please don't make them so frequent and so long! Rather than make me cry they made me feel like just turning the telly off an hour from the end.However, I'm so glad I didn't. Mush was put aside and the brilliant ending shone through. It ended how it started and how it ran through its middle: fantastic fantasy. I've given nothing away, no spoilers, no real critique, just my own humble opinion. Do with it what thy will.
